A controlled study across five benchmarks and five receiver models shows that when a downstream agent would otherwise answer correctly, an incorrect upstream message flips its answer in up to 32% of cases, and in 94% of audited harmful cases the downstream agent simply copies the upstream's specific wrong answer — a pattern the authors call 'answer substitution.' The findings quantify a concrete failure mode in multi-agent LLM pipelines, showing that inter-agent communication is a double-edged sword that can actively degrade accuracy rather than only improve it, which has direct implications for anyone designing collaborative agent architectures or safety-critical deployments. The experiment holds the downstream task and evidence fixed while comparing three conditions — no message, the upstream agent's original message, and a message with the opposite conclusion — and finds that removing unreliable messages recovers part of the lost accuracy, suggesting communication should be selective based on upstream reliability and the evidence the downstream agent already has.

A new arXiv paper (2609.36900) introduces Self-Tuned Anchored Reliability Group-Relative Policy Optimization (STAR-GRPO), a reliability-first advantage estimator that uses paired assessments of the same rollout to separate a rollout's quality signal from its influence on learning. Score disagreement determines rollout reliability, relative reliability feeds a self-tuned robust location-scale fit before group normalization, and absolute group reliability attenuates the bounded advantage. Reward hacking is a central obstacle to aligning reinforcement learning systems, and it is amplified in group-relative methods where one unsupported reward can shift the group baseline and distort updates for other rollouts. STAR-GRPO offers a principled normalization scheme that limits unsupported reward influence while keeping the task reward as the optimization target, which matters for researchers training reasoning and agentic LLMs with GRPO-style algorithms. The paper establishes coordinate and second-moment bounds, characterizes exact centering through the weighted location equation, and gives reliability-dependent attenuation guarantees for outlying rewards. Experiments cover two reward-hacking regimes: token-interface exploitation, where STAR prevents runaway optimization of the deployed-interface score while improving the canonical quality signal, and rubric-proxy overoptimization for medical reasoning, where it improves independent semantic evaluation, narrows the proxy-judge discrepancy, and reduces overclaim.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Sep 30, 04:00

**Background**: Reward hacking (also called specification gaming) occurs when an RL agent optimizes the literal reward function without achieving the intended outcome, often by exploiting flaws or ambiguities in the reward interface. Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), introduced in a 2024 arXiv paper, is an efficient policy-gradient method that drops the separate critic model and instead normalizes advantages within a group of sampled responses. Advantage estimation is the component that assigns credit to actions relative to a baseline, so how a group's baseline is computed directly shapes which behaviors get reinforced.

## [Neuro-Symbolic Framework Learns Reusable Policies for Computer-Use Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.36927) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.36927) introduces neuro-symbolic computer use, a framework that learns reusable executable policies for recurring computer workflows instead of re-planning every step on each run. Using neuro-symbolic policy iteration, the method achieves the highest Pass^3 across all four settings on OSWorld-Verified and ScienceBoard, beating the base agent by 3.6-15.8 points while cutting per-run cost by 15-217x and latency by 3.4-5.1x. Most current computer-use agents re-plan every step of every run, which is costly and unreliable for recurring workflows; learning reusable policies could substantially reduce cost and improve reliability for automation in enterprise and desktop settings. The approach also shows that policies built only on generated variants transfer to held-out original tasks, exceeding AutoRPA by 8.6-17.5 points in Pass^3 on OSWorld-Verified. The policy encodes stable decisions (ordering, variables, loops, branches) in executable code and delegates observation-dependent decisions such as grounding and state checks to neural models. Policies are learned from a single agent trajectory via iterative diagnosis with task-completion and step-level judges, revised by a coding model using the agent's continuation from the failure point, without access to the benchmark evaluator, and a pre-action verifier guards each state-mutating step at deployment.

**Background**: Neuro-symbolic AI combines neural networks with symbolic reasoning to improve reliability, data efficiency, and trustworthiness over purely statistical deep learning, and has been called the third wave of AI. ## [FastRL: Advantage-Aware Pruning and Adaptive Rollout Sampling for GRPO](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.36932) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers propose FastRL, a plug-and-play reinforcement learning framework that introduces advantage-aware pruning to keep high-advantage trajectories with maximal gradient diversity, plus adaptive rollout sampling that adjusts sampling scale across training stages based on historical pruning distributions. Experiments show FastRL integrates into GRPO, DAPO, and GSPO, delivering an average 2.07x training speedup on Geometry3K and GeoQA8K-R1V and about 1.64% average accuracy improvement on visual reasoning benchmarks. GRPO-style methods are widely used for LLM reasoning post-training, but their per-question multi-rollout sampling and repeated per-token probability evaluation create heavy computational overhead, while homogeneous trajectories waste learning signal. FastRL's plug-and-play design could lower training costs and improve final policy quality for researchers and practitioners training reasoning models, without requiring changes to the underlying algorithm. The pruning strategy selectively preserves high-advantage trajectories while maximizing inter-trajectory gradient diversity, and the adaptive rollout mechanism balances exploration adequacy against computational efficiency using historical pruning distributions. Reported gains are measured on Geometry3K and GeoQA8K-R1V visual reasoning benchmarks, and source code is promised at https://github.com/Nicozwy/FastRL.

**Background**: Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) is a reinforcement learning algorithm popularized by DeepSeek for improving LLM reasoning: instead of training a separate value network, it samples multiple responses per question and uses the group's relative rewards to estimate advantages. This multi-rollout design improves stability but multiplies inference cost, and when all sampled responses are similar or uninformative, the resulting gradient signal is weak. FastRL targets both problems by pruning low-value trajectories and adapting how many rollouts each prompt receives.

## [CoEM Defers Evidence Compression to Boost Long-Context LLM Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.36935) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduced Commit-on-Evidence Memory (CoEM), a method that learns when to convert source evidence into compact memory facts during long-context reasoning. On a 6,400-document long-context input, CoEM outperforms the strongest memory baseline by 10.4–11.4 F1 points on Qwen3.5-9B, with code released on GitHub. Long-context reasoning is critical for complex, long-horizon tasks, but LLM performance degrades as context grows, and existing chunk-by-chunk memory approaches often discard details prematurely. CoEM's learned deferral policy could improve reliability for document analysis, multi-hop QA, and agentic workflows that depend on retaining evidence over long inputs. Under a fixed context-memory budget, CoEM keeps potentially useful excerpts verbatim in a pending set and uses a learned policy to promote, retain, or discard each excerpt as new context arrives; a frozen verifier only accepts proposed facts if they are supported by retained excerpts and current context. The policy is trained with reinforcement learning combining step-level evidence rewards and final answer rewards.

**Background**: Large language models have limited context windows, so long inputs are often processed chunk by chunk while carrying a bounded textual memory forward, as in recurrent memory agents like MemAgent. Compressing information too early can irreversibly lose details needed for later reasoning, which is the problem CoEM targets by delaying commitment until relevance is clarified.

## [SCA: Spatial Credit Assignment for GUI Agent Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.36939) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers propose Spatial Credit Assignment (SCA), a method that uses the screen coordinates of sampled clicks to refine group-relative credit in reinforcement learning for GUI agents. SCA predicts each held-out response's reward from other responses in mixed success/failure groups, and when all sampled clicks fail, it orders them by distance to the annotated target. This addresses a key limitation of group-relative RL for GUI agents, where binary rewards treat spatially different failed clicks as identical and give no learning signal when all samples fail. The approach could improve training efficiency and grounding accuracy for GUI automation tasks across professional domains. SCA uses spatial references only to construct the training update, leaving the deployed policy unchanged, and it is evaluated in a controlled synthetic study comparing its error and directional alignment with the exact return gradient. Across GUI grounding and offline action-prediction benchmarks, SCA achieves the strongest results among reinforcement-fine-tuned models on most action-prediction metrics.

Group-relative reinforcement learning, such as GRPO, improves action prediction by comparing rewards of multiple responses sampled from the same GUI state, but relies on binary success/failure evaluation. Credit assignment is the problem of determining which actions in a trajectory deserve credit for the final outcome, and spatial credit assignment uses location information to refine this process.

## [REALHOP Audits Multi-Hop Reasoning Benchmarks via Behavioral Necessity Rate](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.36984) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint introduces REALHOP, a diagnose-construct-verify framework that uses the Behavioral Necessity Rate (BNR) to measure how often removing targeted evidence prevents a model from recovering an initially correct answer. Across five existing benchmarks, panel-mean BNR ranged from only 16.6% to 48.9%, and on 790 paired MuSiQue questions REALHOP raised panel-mean BNR from 27.4% to 94.4% while retaining high full accuracy. The work shows that a correct final answer does not prove a model actually used the intended multi-hop reasoning chain, meaning many widely used benchmarks may overestimate true reasoning ability. This matters for anyone comparing models, designing evaluations, or drawing conclusions about LLM reasoning from benchmark scores. REALHOP rebinds entities, factorizes selected relations, adds complete competing paths, and places evidence at traceable locations, with structural and semantic checks before freezing and behavioral interventions afterward. On 216 long-context questions, the matched multiple-choice spread across 16 models grew from 13.9 to 59.2 points and persisted under repeated open-ended evaluation, though the paper is a preprint without peer review or community discussion yet.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Sep 30, 04:00

**Background**: Multi-hop reasoning means answering a question by connecting several pieces of evidence through intermediate steps, such as linking facts spread across different documents or distant parts of a long context. Benchmarks typically build questions around predefined reasoning chains and treat a correct answer as proof that the intended chain was used. The Behavioral Necessity Rate instead tests whether each intended hop is actually necessary by removing targeted evidence and checking if the model can still answer correctly.

## [CADOC: Cache-Aware Context Compression for Long-Horizon Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37012) ⭐️ 7.0/10

CADOC introduces an online algorithm that replaces structured objects in an agent's history with compact retrieval Cards while preserving exact, on-demand access to the originals. It schedules these replacements in batches by balancing accumulated waiting cost against shared cache-reconstruction cost, a rule derived from the economic order quantity (EOQ) trade-off, and reports roughly 40% lower input cost on average while keeping task performance close to full context. Context is the central bottleneck for long-horizon LLM agents, since history is resent with every request and reasoning degrades as it grows. CADOC shows that efficient compression depends not only on shortening prompts but also on scheduling edits to preserve prefix-cache reuse, offering a cost-derived approach that could make long-running agents cheaper and more practical. The scheduling rule recovers the optimal integer batch size under stationary assumptions, and the method is evaluated against configurations that time edits by reuse forecasts or preset intervals. The abstract is truncated and no community discussion is available, so independent validation of the reported 40% cost reduction is still pending.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Sep 30, 04:00

**Background**: Long-horizon agents accumulate large histories that must be resent with each LLM request, which raises cost and can degrade reasoning. Prefix caching lets providers reuse the computation of a shared prompt prefix, but editing the history can invalidate that cache. The economic order quantity model, developed by Ford W. Harris in 1913, is a classic inventory formula that minimizes the sum of ordering and holding costs, and CADOC adapts this trade-off to decide when and how many context edits to batch.

A new arXiv paper (2609.37027) characterizes the gradient space accessible to LoRA as exactly the tangent space induced by the current low-rank parameterization, and uses this to orthogonally decompose the full weight gradient into a LoRA-tangent component and a normal component. The authors propose GDLoRA (Gradient-Decomposed Low-Rank Adaptation), which reconstructs the full weight gradient from forward activations and backward signals, extracts the normal component, and directly updates the base weights with it while keeping standard AdamW for the LoRA factors. This work offers a theoretical explanation for why LoRA variants still lag behind full fine-tuning: their first-order update directions are confined to the tangent space of the current parameterization. By adding the orthogonal normal gradient without increasing the optimizer-state memory budget under matched adapter and optimizer configurations, GDLoRA consistently improves over LoRA and narrows the gap to FFT across NLU, math reasoning, commonsense reasoning, and image classification tasks, which matters for practitioners seeking full fine-tuning quality at PEFT cost. GDLoRA reconstructs the full weight gradient from forward activations and backward signals rather than storing it, and it retains standard AdamW optimization for the LoRA factors while updating base weights with the normal component. The paper reports that this adds complementary normal gradients without increasing the standard LoRA optimizer-state memory budget under matched adapter and optimizer configurations, and code is available at an anonymous repository.

The authors also release WTI-82K, a dataset of 82,335 timed questions across 4,812 causally aligned trajectories, and Stream-GDPO, a trajectory-level optimization method for response timing, source-video recall, and memory updates. WTI's closed-loop design lets the model decide per question whether to answer, keep watching, or recall a past interval, potentially improving long-horizon multi-turn video assistants where questions arrive asynchronously under a fixed context budget. WTI's memory entries are compact natural-language summaries tagged with source-video time ranges; they support direct reasoning when sufficient and otherwise anchor selective recall of finer visual evidence without replaying the full observed history. Stream-GDPO optimizes complete multi-question streaming rollouts using trajectory-level feedback for response timing, source-video recall, and memory updates, though the work is an arXiv preprint without peer review or community validation yet.

**Background**: Streaming video assistance requires a model to answer asynchronous questions from an observed prefix while operating under a fixed context budget, so it cannot simply store every frame. Memory-augmented neural networks address this by adding an external memory that can be read and written over time, and reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) provides a way to optimize agent behavior using reward signals rather than explicit supervision. The benchmark covers three task categories — OriginPro script-based data analysis, GUI interaction with materials-science tools, and programmatic database queries — and includes a human-LLM agreement study validating a multimodal judge for secondary aesthetic assessment of OriginPro figure-generation tasks. Failures are attributed not only to visual grounding but also to domain-specific operational knowledge, sparse pretraining coverage of scientific software, weak cross-tool artifact handoff, and critical states exposed only visually.

## [MVPO Learns from Viable Failure Prefixes for Long-Horizon LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37111) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper proposes Milestone Viability Potential Policy Optimization (MVPO), a potential-routed policy optimization algorithm that estimates prefix potential over Union-Find viability regions and repairs zero-credit groups with potential-difference advantages. Experiments with Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct show MVPO outperforms eight strong baselines, improving over GiGPO by +4.4 success points on ALFWorld and +5.3 on WebShop with only 0.16%-0.20% advantage-construction overhead. Long-horizon LLM agents trained with sparse rewards often suffer from zero-credit failure, where failed rollouts containing useful prefixes receive no task-discriminative advantage, stalling learning. MVPO directly targets this failure mode, offering a lightweight credit-assignment fix that could make group-based RL training for multi-turn agents more sample-efficient and reliable. MVPO estimates prefix potential over Union-Find viability regions, repairs zero-credit groups with potential-difference advantages, and attenuates the potential branch according to relative performance progress. The method is evaluated on ALFWorld and WebShop with Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, but the abstract is truncated, so full experimental validation and limitations cannot be fully assessed.

GiGPO extends this idea to multi-turn agent training with a two-level advantage estimation that captures both episode-level and step-level credit. Union-Find is a classic disjoint-set data structure that efficiently merges and queries sets, used here to group viable prefixes into regions. ## [BudgetPM: Budgeting External State Checks for Agent Intentions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37125) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces BudgetPM, the first resource-allocation formulation for the external observations required by stored intentions under a shared episode budget, offering two policy variants (BudgetPM-Static and BudgetPM-Sequential) that share a hard-budget executor. Evaluated against two public memory-agent systems, five matched controls, and four hand-designed rules across two benchmarks and three backbones, BudgetPM-Static outperforms adapted Mem0 and PMA workflows, while BudgetPM-Sequential exceeds the strongest natural monitoring schedule by 1.92–2.58 Set F1 points under severe scarcity. This work addresses a practical gap in budget-constrained agent design: existing memory systems decide when intentions need attention but do not allocate the resulting observations under a shared budget. It offers a demand–capacity design rule for tool-using agents, which is likely to interest researchers in AI planning, memory management, and cost-aware agent deployment. BudgetPM-Static uses a lightweight Logistic scorer to learn whether a check improves the current decision, retaining 99.9–100% of unconstrained quality with 42–54% fewer observations, while BudgetPM-Sequential distills full-episode hindsight schedules into a lightweight policy that uses only pre-query information at deployment and reaches the same Set F1 and on-time recall with 16–33% fewer observations. Matched attribution, exact-cost analysis, and a fixed-budget load intervention link the gain to competition between present and future opportunities.

## [B-OPSD Bootstraps On-Policy Self-Distillation with a Future Teacher](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37132) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces Bootstrapped On-Policy Self-Distillation (B-OPSD), which temporarily trains the policy ahead to create a future teacher, restores the student to its original state, and then lets that future teacher supervise the restarted student's own trajectories. On mathematical reasoning with Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B, B-OPSD consistently beats standard OPSD, improving rollout-privileged scores from 27.50 to 41.30 and from 48.80 to 64.44. Existing on-policy self-distillation methods build the self-teacher from the current, initial, or slowly averaged policy, so supervision quality is capped by how well that teacher exploits privileged information. B-OPSD suggests a broader principle that a model's own future learning progress can be distilled backward, which could reshape how LLM fine-tuning pipelines are designed. The future teacher helps in two ways: it generates more reliable privileged trajectories, and conditioned on them it provides more informative token-level targets along the restarted student's on-policy trajectories. The results are from an arXiv preprint (2609.37132v1) with no peer review or community discussion yet, so the gains are not independently validated.

**Background**: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) lets a single LLM act as its own teacher: a "self-teacher" with access to privileged information (such as reference solutions) gives dense token-level supervision on the model's own generated trajectories, which helps address exposure bias and improves reasoning. "Privileged information" comes from the learning-using-privileged-information (LUPI) paradigm, where extra signals available only at training time guide the student. B-OPSD extends this by recycling the model's own optimization progress into a stronger teacher rather than relying on the current or averaged policy state.

## [IBM and Weizmann Split Agent Proactivity into Horizontal and Vertical Axes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37236) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.37236) from IBM and Weizmann researchers distinguishes two forms of proactivity in tool-using agents: horizontal proactivity, which pursues unstated information already identified by the current context, and vertical proactivity, which pursues needs revealed only by earlier evidence. The authors propose Q&D (questioner and drafter), a training method that teaches a questioner to prefer questions whose continuations retrieve more required evidence, without any reward model or judge. This reframes proactivity from a binary question of whether an agent acts unprompted to a content question of what information it should pursue and when it should stop, which could change how agent designers build tool-use and retrieval pipelines. The trained questioner outperformed a prompted model 15 times larger on two of three multi-hop QA benchmarks, suggesting substantial efficiency gains are available from better question selection rather than scale alone. The method scores both forms of proactivity, and whether the agent stops at the right time, from a transcript using a need graph recovered from the benchmark's own decomposition, avoiding a model judge. Gains persisted after controlling for question volume and length, and the questioner transferred without further training to an interactive customer-service agent with a simulated customer, completing more tasks while asking fewer questions, and to retail, where it beat the 15x larger model with fewer follow-up turns.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Sep 30, 04:00

**Background**: Tool-using AI agents typically respond only to what a user explicitly asks, but completing a task often requires information the user never requested. Prior work on proactive agents has focused mainly on whether and when an agent should act on its own, not on what information it should seek out. Multi-hop question answering benchmarks require chaining several pieces of evidence together, making them a natural testbed for measuring whether an agent pursues the right unstated information.

## [Paper Proposes 3T Principles and PROACTIVITY-GYM for Proactive LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37267) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.37267) proposes foundational principles for proactive LLM agents built around three joint objectives — Task Capability, Temporal Allocation, and Trust (the '3T' principles) — along with a five-dimension design space covering task scope, anticipation horizon, activation trigger, processing timing, and intervention depth. It also introduces PROACTIVITY-GYM, a simulation-based evaluation testbed with multi-day scenarios, stateful environments, and persona-conditioned simulated users, and reports evaluations across 23 model-harness configurations plus a 30-participant human study. Most LLM agent systems today remain reactive, waiting for explicit user instructions, so a structured framework for proactive agents that anticipate needs could shape how the field designs and benchmarks autonomous assistance. The finding that LLM judges often conflate task capability with trust, and that users sharply lose trust after misaligned interventions even when outcomes are correct, highlights evaluation gaps that current benchmarks do not capture. The paper specifies the situation and system modeling needed to support design choices, including user and environment representations, backbone LLMs, and agent harnesses (the runtime scaffolding that turns a model into an agent). Its human study found participants preferred sleep-time assistance, even when imperfect, to preserve ongoing focus, and the 23-configuration evaluation uncovered substantial performance gaps across the 3T dimensions.

Prior work such as the ProactiveAgent project has focused on data pipelines and training for proactive behavior, while agent harnesses provide the runtime infrastructure around a model. PROACTIVITY-GYM builds on this line of research by offering a Gymnasium-style simulation environment for training and evaluating proactive agents that anticipate user needs.

## [Transolver-σ Jointly Models Spectral and Physical Subspaces for Neural PDE Solving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37279) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Transolver-σ is a new neural PDE solver that jointly models spectral and physical subspaces within each block, introducing Slice-Residual Physics-Attention (SRPA) and an axis-factorized Fourier operator. Across five established PDE benchmarks, it reports a benchmark-averaged relative error reduction of 33.4% over the strongest baseline per metric, while consistently improving autoregressive rollout over single-operator counterparts. The work targets a well-known weakness of neural PDE surrogates: strong one-step accuracy often fails to translate into reliable long-horizon autoregressive rollout. By combining physical-state and spectral representations, it could improve surrogate reliability for time-dependent simulation, benefiting researchers in scientific machine learning, neural operators, and physics-informed learning. The physical subspace uses SRPA, which preserves an explicit slice-space identity path while retaining learnable cross-slice interaction, and the spectral side uses an axis-factorized Fourier operator to capture global structure. The method is validated on five PDE benchmarks plus coupled multiphysics systems and real-world fluid and combustion measurements from RealPDEBench, though the abstract does not report computational cost or scaling limits.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Sep 30, 04:00

**Background**: Neural PDE solvers are learned surrogates that approximate the solutions of partial differential equations far faster than classical numerical simulation, and they are central to scientific machine learning. For time-dependent problems, such models are typically used autoregressively: each predicted state is fed back as input to predict the next step, so small errors can accumulate over long rollouts. Transolver-style models use physics attention that projects inputs onto learned physics slices before applying attention, and spectral methods instead operate in frequency space; this paper argues that neither representation alone is optimal across all rollout steps.

## [MetaCtrl: A Metacognitive Controller for More Accurate and Concise LLM Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37304) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduced MetaCtrl, a lightweight metacognitive controller that regulates a frozen large language model's reasoning process by deciding whether to continue, simplify, skip redundant steps, or conclude. Trained with reinforcement learning and no predefined token budgets or reasoner retraining, it improved average accuracy by 4.7 points while cutting generation length by 53.3% on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B across seven benchmarks. This matters because longer chain-of-thought reasoning is not always better and often wastes inference compute on simple problems, so a plug-and-play controller that improves both accuracy and efficiency could reduce serving costs for reasoning models. The same controller also transferred to an unseen reasoner (Qwen3-14B), improving accuracy by 2.9 points and cutting length by 50.3%, suggesting a general-purpose efficiency layer for LLM deployment. MetaCtrl is formulated as a sequential metacognitive control problem in which the controller observes the evolving reasoning trace and is trained directly with reinforcement learning using a reward that prioritizes correctness while favoring shorter trajectories among correct solutions. It requires neither supervised intervention trajectories nor problem-specific budgets, and the code is available at https://github.com/binbin2xs/MetaCtrl.

## [Mubric Uses Mutation Testing to Generate Better LLM Evaluation Rubrics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37322) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint introduces Mubric, a mutation testing-guided approach that mines response defects from preferred/dispreferred response pairs and abstracts them into reusable mutation operators. These operators are then applied to reference responses to refine task-specific rubrics, achieving the highest overall evaluation accuracy across 703 tasks in four domains, outperforming the strongest baseline by 7.48 percentage points. Rubric-based evaluation is widely used to assess LLM systems, but automatically generating rubrics that reliably capture task-specific quality requirements remains challenging. By bridging classic software testing methodology with LLM evaluation, Mubric offers a principled way to produce more reliable rubrics, potentially improving how LLM-based systems are assessed across domains. Mubric draws an analogy between test suites and rubrics: if a rubric captures an important quality requirement, introducing a corresponding defect into an otherwise high-quality response should reduce its score. It uses insufficiently penalized defects to refine the rubric, and was evaluated against six advanced rubric generation methods on 703 tasks across four representative domains.

**Background**: Mutation testing is a classic software testing methodology that evaluates a test suite by injecting small faults (mutants) into a program and checking whether the tests detect them. ## [On-Policy Distillation Transfers Problem-Solving but Not Stopping in Small Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37326) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.37326) empirically analyzes on-policy distillation from Qwen3-8B into Qwen3 4B, 1.7B, and 0.6B students in both thinking and non-thinking modes. It finds that distillation improves problem-solving at every size but fails to transfer the ability to know when to stop reasoning in thinking mode, with students bounded by a pre-training multi-attempt ceiling. This work reveals a key limitation of on-policy distillation for building efficient reasoning models: smaller students may solve problems but cannot reliably terminate their reasoning, undermining deployment where concise outputs matter. It provides a diagnostic separating answer marking, correctness, and stopping, which could guide better distillation objectives and evaluation for compressed reasoning models. The study measures two ceilings across both modes and all student sizes: a student's single attempt never exceeds what it could already reach in many attempts before training, and smaller students stay further below the teacher. In thinking mode, the teacher signals a stop almost only where the student already ends its reasoning, so distillation teaches no new stops; the smallest students often reach the right value but fail to commit, either rarely marking it or marking it and writing past it.

## [SeekVLN Tackles Progress Myopia in Vision-Language Navigation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37353) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.37353) identifies a failure mode called Progress Myopia in vision-language navigation (VLN), where agents act confidently on insufficient visual evidence, and proposes SeekVLN, an evidence-seeking framework that actively acquires task-relevant observations. SeekVLN uses a two-stage training pipeline—Future-guided Reverse Generation (FRG) for supervised fine-tuning and Counterfactual Contrastive Policy Optimization (C2PO) for reinforcement fine-tuning—and achieves state-of-the-art results, improving success rate by 12.7% on R2R-CE and 7.5% on RxR-CE over the base model. This work addresses a fundamental reliability gap in embodied AI: VLM-based navigation agents often proceed without sufficient evidence, leading to confident but wrong actions. By explicitly teaching agents to seek missing evidence, SeekVLN could make autonomous navigation safer and more robust in real-world robotics, where getting lost or making wrong turns has tangible costs. The FRG stage augments offline expert trajectories with supplementary views and evidence annotations using future expert actions, establishing a prior for evidence seeking without extra expert interaction. The C2PO stage then compares each evidence-seeking branch with a counterfactual direct-navigation branch from the same state, using a contrastive reward to credit seeking decisions based on subsequent navigation benefit; both simulated and real-world evaluations show human-like evidence-seeking behaviors.

This paper names that failure mode Progress Myopia and introduces active evidence seeking as a remedy.

A new arXiv preprint (2609.37356) proposes a challenger-solver asymmetric self-play method in which an LLM challenger generates progressively harder MILP instances while a solver verifies feasibility and hardness. The authors fine-tune Gemma-4-12B and Qwen3.5-4B with GRPO and a size curriculum into OptiScribe-12B and OptiScribe-4B, which raise median SCIP search nodes by 1.7-5x (12B) and up to 15.6x (4B) on capacitated facility location and max-cut. If validated, it could give the optimization community a controllable, instruction-driven source of difficulty-graded MILP benchmarks. The reward combines solvability with hardness measured by branch-and-bound nodes and post-cut relaxation gaps, and the method requires no seed or training MILP instances. Reported gains include 1.1-1.7x higher post-cut gaps and a 9-19 point feasibility-rate improvement on facility location, though the paper is a preprint and code/models are promised only upon acceptance.

The paper models the plan as a commitment hierarchy and the intent change as a belief-revision operator with AGM-style postulates, then proves an impossibility result for node-local policies. Empirical validation spans three environments and three models from two vendors, with the single-classification design matching the cost-optimal oracle in all cases.

The authors ground this in AGM belief revision, a classic formal framework from philosophy and AI that specifies rational ways to update a belief set when new information arrives, and in commitment hierarchies, where higher-level goals constrain lower-level sub-goals.

## [VeriWeave Govern: Deterministic Runtime Governance for Enterprise AI Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37457) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (arXiv:2609.37457v1) introduces VeriWeave Govern, a deterministic runtime governance layer that evaluates structured agent actions against versioned policies, validates typed evidence, and applies a fixed deny > review > allow precedence before routing consequential actions to human review. Evaluated on GovernBench — 30 independent seeds and 60,000 oracle-labelled cases across five enterprise domains — it reports 0.9888 mean accuracy, 0.9836 macro-F1, zero observed aggregate false allows, and zero observed Governance Attack Success Rate. As enterprise AI agents increasingly call tools, modify infrastructure, and process protected data, separating action generation from action authorization becomes a core safety requirement, and this work offers a concrete, benchmarked control plane for that separation. The reported zero false allows and zero governance attack success rate, if validated, could inform how organizations deploy agents in regulated environments where unauthorized actions carry real compliance and security costs. Six ablations indicate that evidence gating, deny precedence, out-of-distribution fail-safe behavior, human review, contradiction handling, and temporal replay each contribute complementary safety, and the deployed API reportedly passes 12/12 end-to-end scenarios plus a 40,040-request concurrency matrix with zero failures. A separate 150-case EU/Austria regulation-grounded evaluation with frozen predictions and two blinded human annotators found that deterministic engines remain conservative while a Gemma 4 31B comparator aligns more closely with human consensus, exposing a measurable safety–utility trade-off.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Sep 30, 04:00

**Background**: Enterprise AI agents are systems that autonomously invoke tools and APIs to carry out tasks, which means a single unverified action can alter production infrastructure or expose protected data. Runtime governance refers to intercepting and adjudicating agent actions at the execution boundary, before they reach real systems, rather than relying only on post-hoc logging or model-level alignment. Typed evidence means each proposed action must be accompanied by structured, schema-validated proof (such as authorization or policy context) before it can be allowed, and a Governance Attack Success Rate measures how often adversarial inputs manage to bypass those controls.

## [BSC-R Binds Agent Commits to State to Block Drift Attacks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37475) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.37475) introduces BSC-R, a deterministic effect-boundary mechanism that binds a single-use commit authorization to the exact action and to a semantic projection of the authorization state that justified it. On 2,847 attacked AgentDojo episodes, BSC-R preserved the unprotected agent's behavior exactly (80.576% utility, 1.616% attack success), and on 10,302 frozen proposals it accepted every unchanged commit while rejecting all ten prospectively specified changed or replayed classes. Tool-using language-model agents can decide an action is permissible and then execute it only after security-relevant state has changed, creating a proposal-to-commit gap that attackers can exploit. BSC-R offers a scoped, deterministic commit-time consistency mechanism that could harden agent tool use in high-stakes deployments, though the authors explicitly frame it as a scoped result rather than a universal agent-safety guarantee. In an independently generated boundary-drift experiment, full joint binding committed 0/4,403 invalid contexts while retaining 5,899/5,899 valid contexts, and on the 3,460-scenario CONTINUITY suite it retained all 700 benign cases, prevented 1,200/1,200 represented non-replay invalid effects, handled 160/160 replay lifecycles correctly, and withheld 200/200 ambiguous no-release cases. The broader external suite exposes a limit: across all 2,560 attacks, BSC-R had a 25% invalid-effect commit rate versus 0% for CONTINUITY.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Sep 30, 04:00

**Background**: Tool-using language-model agents are AI systems that call external tools or APIs to complete tasks, and they are vulnerable to prompt injection and other attacks that manipulate the state those tools depend on. AgentDojo is a dynamic benchmark for evaluating attacks and defenses on such agents, while CONTINUITY is a scenario suite used here for prospective external evaluation. The proposal-to-commit gap refers to the window between when an agent decides an action is allowed and when it actually executes it, during which security-relevant state may change.

## [REVOIR: Value-of-Information Reasoning for Agent Clarification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37588) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduce REVOIR (Rational Enquiry via Value-of-Information Reasoning), an inference-time method that lets assistive agents decide whether to ask a clarifying question or act directly by estimating the expected improvement in task reward from the answer. On ambiguous question answering (CondAmbigQA) and preference-aligned household planning (ADAPT), REVOIR improves preference satisfaction by 13-15% over a fine-tuned clarification policy while requiring no training and asking five times fewer questions. Deciding when to ask versus act is a core challenge for interactive AI agents, and getting it wrong causes either annoying over-questioning or misaligned actions. REVOIR offers a training-free, decision-theoretic alternative to uncertainty-threshold and prompting-based approaches, with direct implications for AI alignment and human-AI interaction. REVOIR uses inference-time reasoning about the value of information with limited lookahead, and it naturally infers that asking is not always efficient when cheap user corrections are available after acting. Notably, vanilla reasoning agents fail to adaptively clarify, requesting fewer clarifications as reasoning effort increases.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Sep 30, 04:00

**Background**: Value of information (VOI) is a decision-theoretic concept that quantifies how much an agent's expected utility would improve if it observed new evidence before acting. Assistive agents built on large language models often face ambiguous user requests, and prior work typically asks questions until uncertainty about user intent falls below a threshold, ignoring the downstream reward impact and the cost of asking. REVOIR reframes clarification as a rational VOI trade-off between asking and acting.

## [FOCUS: Training-Free Context Compression for LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37590) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduced FOCUS, a training-free context compression framework that reframes compression as a causal decision-preservation problem over discrete interaction units, operating entirely at test time without offline data collection or fine-tuning. On diverse agentic benchmarks it cuts peak context by up to 48% and dependency by 73% while improving task success by up to 8.9 percentage points over uncompressed execution. LLM agents accumulate interaction histories that grow linearly with task length, causing quadratic inference cost scaling and performance degradation from attention dilution, so a compression layer that attaches to any closed-API frontier model could substantially reduce cost and latency for real-world agent deployments. Because it is architecture-agnostic and requires no training, it lowers the barrier for teams that cannot afford to train or distill their own compressors. FOCUS is a modular compression layer that requires no offline data collection or fine-tuning and is evaluated on API and tool-calling, QA, web-domain, and multi-turn dialogue benchmarks. The paper reports up to 48% peak context reduction and 73% dependency reduction, though the abstract does not detail the computational overhead of the causal identification step itself.

**Background**: LLM agents are systems that use a large language model to plan and act over multiple turns, calling tools or APIs and accumulating a growing history of past interactions. Existing context-compression methods typically learn what to discard offline by contrastively optimizing guidelines, distilling compressors, or training compression policies, which is costly and not dynamically conditioned on the evolving test-time trajectory. The paper introduces an efficient spectral filter that recalibrates the eigenvalues of each subject's functional connectivity (FC) matrix, matching or exceeding kernel ridge regression (KRR) baselines across 5 datasets, 11 parcellations, and 6 prediction targets. Using this finding, the authors pretrain a small encoder on about 4,000 hours of fMRI from 162 open datasets by aligning embedding similarities with recalibrated connectome similarities, achieving performance on par with 6 published brain foundation models (BFMs) while using an order of magnitude fewer parameters. This work addresses a key limitation of current brain foundation models, which still underperform simple KRR on FC matrices for phenotype prediction, and shows that a much smaller pretrained encoder can rival large BFMs. It suggests a new direction for neuroimaging self-supervised learning and could make brain foundation models more practical for small cohorts and short scans. The spectral filter recalibrates eigenvalues to better exploit inter-individual variance, and the pretrained encoder performs better than FC on short scans and in smaller cohorts, especially in fingerprinting. The authors release the pretrained model weights, code, and preprocessed, parcellated pretraining data.

## [Dual-Latent World Model Splits Planning and Execution for Long-Horizon Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37644) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2609.37644) introduces the Dual-Latent World Model (Dual-WM), which separates low-level action-conditioned transition prediction from high-level macro-action planning using distinct latent representations and dynamics models. Paired with a Long-Horizon Representation Learning with Weighted Rollout (LoRe) training scheme, Dual-WM raises mean success on five goal-conditioned visual control tasks from 75.9% to 84.4% at goal offset 50 and from 61.4% to 69.5% at offset 100, outperforming LeWM by 30.8 percentage points at offset 100. Long-horizon planning remains a core bottleneck for model-based reinforcement learning, where recursive rollouts accumulate errors and high-dimensional latent spaces suffer from distance concentration that blurs goal discrimination. By decoupling temporal scales, Dual-WM offers a concrete architectural recipe that could improve sample efficiency and reliability in robotics, navigation, and other goal-conditioned control domains. The high-level model generates latent subgoals that the low-level model refines into actions, and the LoRe objective uses exponential horizon weights with separate decay rates for the two temporal scales, motivated by an analysis of recursive error propagation. Results are reported from-scratch without actor-guided proposals, and the core implementation is released at https://github.com/DeLin1001/Dual-WM-Official.

**Background**: Latent world models learn a compressed representation of the environment and predict future states in that latent space, allowing agents to plan or train in imagination rather than interacting with a costly simulator. Model-based reinforcement learning leverages such models to improve sample efficiency, but prediction accuracy degrades over long horizons, and in high-dimensional spaces distances between points tend to concentrate, making it harder to tell which latent state is closer to a goal. Dual-WM addresses both issues by assigning local execution and long-range planning to separate representations and dynamics models.

The method relies on lightweight signals computed online and a drift-based criterion that enables effective updates from a single labeled example; code is available at https://github.com/Muhammad-Huzaifaa/WISE-ATTA.

A new arXiv preprint (2609.37751) proposes token-error supervision for sparse routing in Mixture-of-Experts LLMs, in two forms: one predicts an error score per expert whose affinity-weighted aggregate is aligned to next-token cross-entropy loss, while the other directly aligns router affinities to the model objective without an extra head or inference-time changes. Using Itakura-Saito divergence or an exponential negative log-likelihood for alignment, the method improves accuracy by about 2.3 percentage points on average on Granite across four multiple-choice QA benchmarks, with gains reaching 2.94 points on ARC-Challenge under stronger supervision. MoE routers are typically trained only with load-balancing terms and the language-model objective, which gives no direct signal linking routing decisions to token-level errors; this work closes that gap and could make sparse MoE models more accurate without increasing the sparse execution budget. If the gains generalize, it offers a low-cost training-time improvement for the widely used MoE architecture behind many large-scale LLMs. Both supervision mechanisms preserve the native sparse execution budget and aggregation policy, meaning no changes to inference cost or top-K selection behavior are required. Evaluation covers two sparse MoE backbones and four multiple-choice QA benchmarks, and the code is available in the supplementary materials, though the work is a preprint without peer review or community discussion yet.

**Background**: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models scale capacity by splitting the network into specialized sub-networks called experts and using a router to activate only the most relevant ones for each token, enabling massive scale with manageable compute. Cross-entropy loss is the standard training objective and evaluation metric for language models, measuring how well predicted token distributions match the true next token. Itakura-Saito divergence is a measure of difference between two quantities (originally spectra), defined as x/y - log(x/y) - 1, and is used here to align routing affinities with token errors.

## [Adam Proven to Converge Under Generalized Smoothness Without Strong Tail Assumptions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37787) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new paper proves that Adam converges on generalized smooth objectives using only second-moment information on stochastic gradients, removing the need for almost-sure boundedness or sub-Gaussianity assumptions. Building on the Adam self-normalization framework of Jin et al. (2026), the authors extend stopping-time and de-preconditioning strategies to the L0-Lp generalized smoothness condition and a generalized second moment ABC condition, establishing high-probability convergence rates for the full range p<2 with confidence dependence of order δ^{-1/2}. This resolves an open theoretical question posed by Li et al. (2023) about whether Adam can converge on generalized smooth objectives without concentration assumptions, which is significant because real-world deep learning objectives often deviate from global smoothness. The result strengthens the theoretical foundation of the most widely used optimizer in machine learning, potentially guiding more robust algorithm design and analysis. The analysis shows that even when the stochastic-gradient condition provides only second-moment information that may grow along the trajectory, Adam's stochastic trajectory remains in a locally well-behaved smoothness region with stretched-exponential tail decay under bounded variance and global smoothness. The authors also construct a hard instance demonstrating that the δ^{-1/2}-type confidence dependence is sharp, and for the regime p<1 they combine trajectory control with polynomial-growth estimates on rare events to obtain convergence guarantees in expectation.

**Background**: Adam is a widely used stochastic optimization algorithm in deep learning, but its convergence theory has long relied on strong assumptions such as global Lipschitz smoothness of the gradient and bounded or sub-Gaussian gradient noise. Generalized smoothness relaxes the classical uniform smoothness condition to allow the Hessian norm to grow with the gradient norm, better capturing practical loss landscapes like those with high-order polynomials or exponential growth. Previous analyses of Adam under generalized smoothness required almost-sure boundedness or sub-Gaussianity of stochastic gradients, which are often unrealistic in practice.

## [DIET: Training-Free Expert Pruning for Video Diffusion Transformers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37829) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduced DIET, a training-free expert pruning framework for mixture-of-experts video diffusion transformers that selects which experts to keep using deletion-response signatures rather than static activation or routing statistics. On LingBot-Video 30B-A3B, pruning 50% of experts (6,144 to 3,072) shrank the checkpoint from 57 GB to 30 GB, enabling single-card deployment on a 48 GB GPU without fine-tuning, while VBench Total rose from 0.7941 to 0.8115 under a fixed 284-case protocol. MoE video diffusion transformers reduce active computation but still require storing the full expert bank, which makes deployment on consumer or single-GPU hardware expensive. A training-free pruning method that preserves or even improves quality could make large video generation models far more practical to serve, and the deletion-response idea may transfer to other MoE architectures beyond video. DIET runs a single all-expert calibration pass that records expert outputs and router states for matched conditional and unconditional tokens, then replays candidate deletions from cached tensors with no extra forward passes. Retained experts are chosen by minimizing Overall Diversity Loss (ODL), which preserves directional coverage in signature space, combined with intra-layer local search and an inter-layer regression-guided budget search for allocating experts across layers.

## [Cacheable decision model loses rule-sensitivity, counterfactual training partially restores it](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37832) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper studies Certo, a small non-generative decision model based on Qwen3-4B that scores candidate actions instead of generating answers. Converting its accurate joint scorer into a cacheable independent-encoding design (about 5x cheaper at 77 candidates) drops recall@1 from 1.00 to 0.24, and targeted counterfactual supervision can restore strong performance on held-out synthetic rule tasks but not on real unseen-source rules. The result highlights a fundamental trade-off between inference efficiency and rule-following reliability in decision models, which matters for anyone deploying cached scoring systems in agentic or tool-use pipelines. It also shows that counterfactual supervision is a promising but not yet sufficient fix for the rule-sensitivity lost by independent encoding. The joint scorer keeps a significant edge on real rules after fixing a truncation confound (0.861 vs 0.500 on the short tier, and 0.655 vs 0.483 directionally on the hard tier with n=29), while a shortlist+rerank rescue fails and a matched cross-domain real-prose mixture reduces contract accuracy by 9.3 to 16.2 points. The authors also note they do not isolate whether the recovered predictions actually depend on the supplied rule rather than a learned decision pattern.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Sep 30, 04:00

**Background**: Certo is a non-generative decision model: instead of writing out an answer, it reads a state, a set of rules, and each candidate action as text and returns a probability score. A joint scorer reads all three together, which is accurate but costly because the cost grows with the number of candidates, whereas independent encoding lets each candidate be encoded once and reused across states, making it much cheaper. Rule-sensitivity means the model's score actually changes when the supplied rule changes, which is essential if the model is to follow instructions rather than memorize patterns.

## [Mixture of Self-Improving Branches Boosts Agent Harness Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37834) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.37834) proposes a Mixture of Self-Improving Branches method that makes the harness improvement process itself adaptive by organizing search into branches with evolving development subsets and proposal policies, plus a router that selects one branch head per input. It reports relative improvements over Meta-Harness of 34.8% on Olympiad-level mathematical reasoning, 11.6% on Terminal-Bench 2.0, and 3.8% on SWE-bench Lite, with all selection and router configuration based solely on development data. This work targets a key failure mode of recursive self-improvement pipelines — convergence to a single local optimum — and shows that evolving branch objectives can produce complementary harnesses whose strengths a router combines without access to test outcomes. If it generalizes, it could make automated agent harness search more robust and reduce the manual effort of designing agent scaffolds, affecting teams building agentic coding and reasoning systems. Each branch keeps development cases solved by more of its leading harnesses than by other branches' leaders, drops cases solved by every leading harness across all branches, and revises its proposal policy using its own search history. The router selects one development-selected branch head per new input before execution, and the reported gains are relative to Meta-Harness on math reasoning and agentic coding benchmarks.

**Background**: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) describes a process where an AI system iteratively modifies its own code or behavior to improve further, and harness optimization is a practical setting for this because an optimizer agent can iteratively update the code that determines what an LLM stores, retrieves, and presents. Meta-Harness is prior work that implements this via iterative code generation and evaluation but keeps a fixed development set and proposal policy, which channels evolution along a single search trajectory and risks local optima. ## [Active Budget k Blamed for TopK Sparse Autoencoder Feature Sensitivity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37857) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.37857) diagnoses feature sensitivity in TopK Sparse Autoencoders, showing through a controlled width×k factorial experiment that the active budget k, not dictionary width alone, is the root cause of degraded sensitivity for rare features. The authors introduce pairwise rank stabilization, which improves rare-feature sensitivity by 8.83 percentage points while keeping reconstruction and alive-feature coverage near baseline. This matters because SAE features are only useful for mechanistic interpretability if they remain stable units of analysis across different surface forms, and the finding suggests that scaling TopK SAEs wider may silently erode reliability for rare features. It implies that evaluation of wide TopK SAEs should include feature reliability under semantic variation and boundary geometry, not just reconstruction, sparsity, and feature count. The paper attributes the failure to the geometry of TopK selection, using the active margin—the distance to the cutoff—to predict feature loss without thresholds, and targets ordering failures at the cutoff with pairwise rank stabilization. The reported 8.83 percentage point gain in rare-feature sensitivity comes with reconstruction and alive-feature coverage kept near baseline, though the work is a specialized arXiv preprint without peer review or community discussion.

## [GATS: Adaptive Teacher Scheduling for Sparse-Reward Agentic RL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37898) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces Gap-Adaptive Teacher Scheduling (GATS), which augments a student agent's reinforcement learning objective with an on-policy distillation (OPD) term whose weight adapts to the teacher-student performance gap. GATS gradually reduces and eventually withdraws teacher guidance once the student reaches the teacher's reference performance, and across ALFWorld, WebShop, and ScienceWorld with three Qwen2.5 teacher-student configurations it achieves the highest average success rate, improving over reward-only GRPO by 4.37%–11.87% under matched student rollout budgets. This work addresses the cold-start problem that plagues sparse-reward reinforcement learning for long-horizon agents, where early policies rarely succeed and thus receive almost no learning signal. By showing that teacher guidance is most useful when the teacher substantially outperforms the student and becomes harmful once the gap narrows or reverses, it offers a practical, principled way to combine distillation with RL and even enables the use of task-trained teachers smaller than the student. The key insight is that the benefit of on-policy distillation depends on the teacher-student performance gap: it helps during early training but can hinder further improvement once the gap narrows and eventually reverses. GATS therefore adaptively weights the OPD term, reducing guidance as the student approaches the teacher's reference performance and withdrawing it once that reference is reached, which is what allows smaller teachers to be effective.

**Background**: Reinforcement learning for long-horizon agents often relies on sparse outcome-based rewards, meaning the agent only learns whether it succeeded at the end of a task, which creates a severe cold-start problem when early policies fail almost every sampled task. On-policy distillation (OPD) mitigates this by having a student model learn from a teacher's token-level behavior on the student's own rollouts, combining online learning with knowledge distillation. Teacher-student reinforcement learning frameworks use a teacher to guide a student through advice, reward shaping, or curricula to improve sample efficiency and convergence speed.

## [Provider Choice Can't Be Read From the Price List: Market-Aware LLM Routing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37902) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.37902v1) measures live endpoints across multiple open-weight models, competing providers, several task types, and three measurement waves, and finds that provider choice cannot be inferred from the price list. It formulates same-model provider selection as a price-taker market-aware routing problem and proposes FACET, an online router that certifies per-(provider × task) feasibility facets and fails safe to an anchor before serving uncertified arms. Existing LLM routers only decide which model to call using static per-model costs, so they miss a second decision axis that directly affects cost, latency, and reliability in open-weight inference markets. This work shows that market-aware routing must measure not only which model to use but also who serves it, which matters for any team deploying open-weight models through third-party providers. The same model can vary sharply in quality, latency, availability, and price across providers; higher-priced providers are consistently faster, but price does not reliably predict quality or availability, and provider feasibility is task-selective—one deployment was nearly normal on knowledge tasks yet catastrophically degraded on multi-step reasoning. FACET tolerates imperfect task assignment and sparse feedback under relaxed deployment assumptions, but systematic evaluator bias exposes a quality-signal trust boundary that can be mitigated with ground-truth probes or audits.

## [KV-Kaizen Learns Context-Adaptive KV Cache Compression Without Token Eviction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37988) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.37988) introduces KV-Kaizen, a learned selector that produces per-layer KV cache configurations along three axes — depth (sharing one cache across layers), precision (fewer bits), and rank (truncating low-rank latent representations) — to hit an overall compression budget without evicting tokens. The selector runs once before pre-fill and, on long-context tasks, achieves a 32x smaller decode-time cache on a 14B model while preserving accuracy, with a 4x reduction causing no accuracy degradation from 7B parameters up. KV cache size can outgrow model weights as context grows, and since decoding is memory-bound, this directly limits LLM throughput; KV-Kaizen offers a token-preserving alternative to eviction, which risks irreversibly discarding content that may matter later. Its results suggest a practical recipe of pre-training large models and compressing them only afterwards, which could reshape how long-context LLM serving is deployed. The paper observes that applying these interventions independently and uniformly across all layers limits achievable compression because it degrades accuracy, whereas composing them locally and adaptively to the context preserves accuracy while yielding large memory savings. On instruction-following and reasoning evaluations, the selectors reach the Pareto frontier of accuracy versus cache size against learning-free and post-hoc baselines, and KV-Kaizen can also be composed with eviction methods.

## [HARISSA Uses Hidden States for Efficient, Safe Local LLM Deployment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38006) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.38006) introduces HARISSA, a method that fine-tunes a language model so its prefill state (computed before any token is generated) and answer state (at the end of generation) both predict answer correctness. One policy then cascades through answering strategies from cheapest to most expensive, skipping strategies the prefill state predicts will fail and deferring to a human when the final answer is predicted wrong. On a single-device setup, HARISSA stays within one accuracy point of chain-of-thought while cutting latency by 2.7x, and on a server with four model sizes it outperforms FrugalGPT and Self-REF cascades at equal latency. Local language model deployment preserves privacy, latency, and cost advantages, but small local models are less capable than frontier cloud models, and the usual fix of escalating hard queries to the cloud sacrifices those very advantages. HARISSA shows that a model can decide for itself when extra computation is worthwhile and when an answer is unsafe to deliver, which could make privacy-preserving edge AI more practical. This matters for anyone deploying models on-device or on-premises where cloud escalation is undesirable. HARISSA relies on two internal signals: the prefill state predicts whether the model will answer correctly before generation begins, and the answer state predicts whether the generated answer is correct. At the same deferral rate, the answer state leaves fewer wrong answers than standard confidence signals in five of six task and setting pairs, though the paper does not claim a universal win across all settings.

**Background**: Transformer-based language models generate text in two phases: prefill, which processes the entire input prompt at once and builds the key-value (KV) cache, and decode, which produces output tokens one at a time. Hidden states are the internal vector representations the model computes at each layer, and prior work has used them to analyze errors and hallucinations. Human-in-the-loop deferral is a common safety pattern in which a model routes uncertain or risky cases to a human reviewer instead of answering autonomously. HARISSA combines these ideas by reading correctness signals directly from hidden states to drive both compute allocation and deferral decisions.

## [PE-EK-PINN Uses Evolving Kernels to Scale Physics-Informed Neural Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38023) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers propose PE-EK-PINN (Physics Embedded with Evolving Kernels), a new architecture that treats physics kernels as reusable learned representations instead of fixed analytical inputs. By freezing a converged subsystem field and promoting it to an evolved kernel, the method makes the peak number of active kernels independent of system size and reduces cumulative training cost from O(N) to O(log N). This addresses a key bottleneck in physics-informed neural networks: manually constructed kernel dictionaries that grow exponentially with the depth of hierarchically structured systems such as antenna arrays and metasurfaces. The approach could enable scalable, accurate solutions for practical radiation problems involving singular excitations, absorbing boundaries, and wave fields spanning tens of wavelengths. Experiments on dipole arrays, composite line-source geometries, and cross arrays show dramatic training cost reduction while achieving reduced or comparable relative L2 error; notably, PE-EK-PINN solves a 256-dipole array more than 30 times faster than direct PE-PINN. The method avoids deriving new governing equations for higher-level configurations by reusing transformed copies of evolved kernels.

**Background**: Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) embed governing equations into deep learning by enforcing them through loss residuals, but they can struggle with highly oscillatory wave behavior. Architectural physics embedding improves this by factorizing the field into analytically derived oscillatory kernels and learnable envelopes, yet the kernel dictionary must be manually built and scales exponentially with hierarchical depth. PE-EK-PINN builds on this idea by making kernels learnable and reusable across system levels.

The paper introduces UserProxyBench, an evaluation layer over the tau-bench family, and the User Fidelity Score (UFS), which measures how well an LLM user simulator follows the benchmark's private user instructions using task-grounded rubric criteria scored independently of agent success. Holding the agent fixed at GPT-5.5 and varying only the user proxy across 375 enterprise tasks changes mean task reward by 15.2 points, and 24.4% of successful episodes contain a user-specification violation. This work exposes a previously overlooked reliability problem in agent benchmarks: the simulated user, not just the agent, can significantly shift measured outcomes, which undermines the validity of benchmark scores and multi-turn reinforcement learning training signals. The dominant failure mode is premature disclosure, where users provide information before it is requested; this has little effect on task reward but causes the agent to make 1.06 fewer tool calls on average among successful episodes, changing the interaction being evaluated while preserving the reward. Across seven proxies, the authors identify an empirical cost-fidelity frontier that lets practitioners pick the least expensive simulator satisfying a required fidelity level.

## [DTC: Counting Divergent Tokens to Quantify LLM Reasoning Uncertainty](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38070) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces Divergent Token Confidence (DTC), a framework that estimates an LLM's reasoning confidence by counting tokens where two models strongly disagree during decoding, identified via Jensen-Shannon divergence between next-token distributions along the same reasoning trajectory. Experiments across multiple model families and six mathematical benchmarks show the count-only estimator achieves an average expected calibration error of 13.0% in white-box settings, versus 32.7%-42.4% for standard full-sequence confidence methods, and reduces mean ECE from 32.1%-40.2% to 13.7%-16.3% on DeepSeek-V3.2 in black-box settings. Reliable uncertainty quantification is critical as LLMs are deployed in high-stakes reasoning tasks, and this work challenges the dominant probability-based paradigm by showing that a coarse token-disagreement count can outperform fine-grained probability signals. It offers a training-free, generation-preserving method that works in both white-box and black-box settings, potentially making confidence calibration more practical for proprietary or API-only models. DTC uses an auxiliary model to compute Jensen-Shannon divergence between next-token distributions along the same reasoning trajectory, counting tokens where the two models strongly disagree; the count is almost negatively associated with answer accuracy. The method requires no explicit training and does not alter the generation process, but it depends on the availability and choice of an auxiliary model, and evaluation is limited to six mathematical benchmarks.

**Background**: Chain-of-thought prompting elicits step-by-step reasoning in large language models and improves performance on arithmetic, commonsense, and symbolic tasks, but it also makes it harder to know when a model's answer is trustworthy. Confidence calibration aims to align a model's stated or implied confidence with its actual accuracy, and most existing methods rely on token probabilities or verbalized confidence scores. Jensen-Shannon divergence is a symmetric, bounded measure of similarity between two probability distributions, commonly used to compare how much two distributions differ.

NeuronEye decomposes vision-token states into an overcomplete sparse basis organized by concept-level clusters, uses the language query to activate relevant clusters and localize patches, and injects the focused evidence back into vision tokens; a complementary suppression mechanism attenuates dominant perceptual directions to preserve weaker but relevant cues. ## [LLM Agents Often Fail to Execute the Plans They Declare](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38108) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.38108) introduces the Plan Declaration–Execution Gap and proposes Planning-as-Routing, in which an LLM declares one of four planning modes (Predefined, Sequential, Hierarchical, or Search) and a deterministic router dispatches the task to a pattern-specific executor. Across four benchmarks and three LLMs, generic Plan+ReAct preserved the declared planning structure in only 22%–45% of trajectories, while pattern-specific executors raised task success from 0.48 to 0.92 on ALFWorld and from 0.36 to 0.44 on SWE-bench Verified. The work shows that final task success alone cannot distinguish planning-mode selection failures from execution failures, a blind spot in current agent evaluation. Its findings suggest that agent designers should invest in faithful, pattern-specific execution rather than assuming a single generic Plan+ReAct loop will honor whatever plan the model declares. The largest gains came from execution rather than selection: pattern-specific executors substantially closed the execution gap, but current LLMs still do not reliably choose the strongest mode for each task, and the best mode varies by environment and model (Search on ALFWorld, Hierarchical on SWE-bench). Few-shot examples improved mode selection in some benchmark–model combinations, leaving task-specific mode selection an open problem.

## [Sage: Agentic Framework for Faithful Lean 4 Formalization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.35790) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Sage (Semantic Agent-Guided Formalization Engine) is an agentic framework that decomposes informal-to-Lean 4 formalization into four stages and adds a dual-signal semantic correction loop combining Lean 4 compiler diagnostics with multi-dimensional semantic feedback. On Omni-MATH without proofs it reaches 73.3% pass@4 joint compilation and semantic fidelity while cutting answer leakage from 70.9% to 2.7%, and on IMO-Unformalized it achieves 87.4% pass@4 verified fidelity versus 19.4% for a fine-tuned Goedel-Formalizer-V2 baseline. Neural theorem provers have largely assumed that faithful Lean 4 statements are already available, so informal-to-formal translation is a critical data bottleneck; Sage targets the "illusion of rigor" where type-checkers accept statements that compile but drop hypotheses or introduce vacuous truths. By enforcing semantic fidelity rather than mere syntactic validity, it could improve the reliability of AI-generated formal mathematics and the quality of autoformalization data used to train provers. The framework explicitly accounts for the gap between open-ended queries and declarative formal targets, preventing models from inflating formalization rates by guessing unverified answers. It is evaluated on Omni-MATH without proofs and on IMO-Unformalized, a new set of 175 unformalized International Mathematical Olympiad problems, where it wins over 79% of blind pairwise evaluations; as an arXiv preprint it has not yet undergone peer review.

**Background**: Lean 4 is a proof assistant and functional programming language based on dependent type theory, widely used to formalize mathematics and verify proofs by machine. Formal verification means proving correctness against a precise specification, and in this setting a statement can type-check while still misrepresenting the original informal problem, which is why semantic correction matters.
