## [Binarization Flattens the Score Space: Why LLM Judges Need Three Grades](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.35797) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.35797) shows that collapsing LLM judge verdicts into pass/fail ({0,1}) hides proportional changes in an unreported score scale, because a policy can stretch that scale toward or away from the single cutoff without ever crossing it. The authors prove under a joint-Gaussian model that adding a third grade introduces a second threshold and removes this affine stretch ambiguity, and they validate this on MATH and SciBench outputs from one seven-criterion judge, where all 14 constructed criterionwise stretches were invisible after binarization but visible with three grades. This matters for anyone using LLM judges as reward signals in reinforcement learning or evaluation pipelines, because a policy can exploit the binarization blind spot to inflate its reward without changing any reported verdict. The proposed fix—keeping at least three grades—is a cheap, practical change that closes one concrete loophole in reward modeling and LLM-as-a-judge evaluation. At n=1,024, a test given both population laws had at least 96.5% power at a 1.5× stress, and the shared-factor reference approximation fit MATH and SciBench but not HealthBench, delineating its empirical scope. The authors caution that three grades do not eliminate all blind spots: arbitrary within-grade changes and fixed-covariance, loading-aligned mean shifts—the signature of a sycophancy-shaped lift the panel reads as competence—remain indistinguishable from genuine improvement, so gains along that remaining direction still need external validation.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Sep 30, 04:00

**Background**: LLM judges are increasingly used as automated reward models to train policies on objectives that deterministic verifiers cannot easily check, such as helpfulness or reasoning quality. In practice, these judges often output a binary pass/fail verdict per criterion, which is simple to aggregate but discards information about how well a response met each criterion. This paper formalizes that loss of information as an affine ambiguity in an unobserved score space and proposes a three-grade scale (fully, partially, or not met, rewarded as {0, 0.5, 1}) as a minimal remedy.

## [Environment Steering Enforces Runtime Safety for LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.35807) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2609.35807) proposes Environment Steering, a runtime data-flow-control mechanism that models the agent and harness execution state as database tables, tracks record-level data flows, and checks them against declarative policies during execution. On the AgentDyn benchmark, it achieves a 0% attack success rate while improving task success rate over a no-defense baseline. Existing defenses either constrain agents before execution, modify tool inputs/outputs, or rely on LLM judges, which can depend on model behavior or block unsafe actions without helping the agent recover. Environment Steering shifts enforcement into the execution environment itself, potentially offering a more robust and model-agnostic safety layer for tool-using LLM agents. The approach tracks record-level data flows against declarative policies and, when violations are detected, provides policy- and context-specific feedback that steers the agent toward safe trajectories rather than simply halting it. Results are reported on AgentDyn, a dynamic open-ended benchmark with 60 tasks and 560 injection test cases, but the work is a preprint without peer review.

**Background**: LLM agents can make unsafe tool calls even when instructed to behave safely, and indirect prompt injection is a common attack vector in which malicious instructions hidden in tool outputs or retrieved content hijack the agent. AgentDyn is a dynamic, open-ended security benchmark covering Shopping, GitHub, and Daily Life scenarios, designed to test whether agent defenses remain deployable in realistic environments. Data-flow control, inspired by database-style taint tracking, labels data and tracks its propagation across tool calls so that multi-hop exfiltration can be caught even when each individual step looks legitimate.

A new arXiv paper introduces Memory Adaptation for Task-Conditioned Execution (MATE), a deterministic post-retrieval procedure that converts previously successful trajectories into execution-oriented memory for embodied agents. MATE removes obsolete control context, extracts condition-action-effect transitions, applies verified action normalization, selects a task-dependent representation, and serializes the result under a fixed budget without additional LLM inference. Controlled comparisons show that verified action normalization is the principal mechanism restoring the utility of retrieved experience.

## [Lookahead-R: Budget-Aware Tool Retrieval via Execution-Centric Planning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.35811) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Lookahead-R reformulates tool retrieval for LLM agents as a resource-constrained sequential decision-making problem, introducing a lightweight execution-aware surrogate world model that jointly predicts tool execution success, latency cost, and semantic utility without invoking real APIs. This world model drives a cost-sensitive, uncertainty-guided Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) that navigates the tool space under strict budget constraints, achieving an NDCG@5 of 91.40% on the challenging ToolBench I3 split, outperforming the state-of-the-art ToolGen (90.16%) by 1.24%. Tool retrieval is a critical bottleneck for LLM-based agents operating over large, heterogeneous API ecosystems, and existing approaches face an inherent trade-off between fast but semantically imprecise retrieval and accurate but prohibitively slow execution-based validation. Lookahead-R's planning-based framework offers a superior accuracy-efficiency trade-off, potentially enabling more practical and scalable agent systems that can select tools effectively under real-world latency and cost constraints. The surrogate world model predicts execution success, latency cost, and semantic utility jointly, and ablation studies confirm that explicit latency modeling is the key discriminative signal for identifying high-quality tools under resource constraints. The approach is evaluated on the large-scale ToolBench benchmark across all test scenarios, with the most challenging I3 split showing the reported NDCG@5 improvement.

**Background**: Tool retrieval for LLM agents involves selecting the most appropriate tools from a large, heterogeneous API ecosystem to accomplish a given task. Semantic retrievers match queries to tool descriptions based on text similarity but often fail to capture functional compatibility, a problem known as the semantic-functional gap. Execution-based validation improves precision by actually running candidate tools but incurs prohibitive latency, creating a trade-off. Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) is a heuristic search algorithm that balances exploration and exploitation in decision processes, and surrogate world models are lightweight predictors used to estimate outcomes without costly real-world evaluations.

## [BreakingWeb Turns Task Difficulty Into a Programmable Property](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.35814) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper introduces BreakingWeb, a benchmark that constructs challenging browser-use tasks by applying deterministic, detectable, and recoverable interventions to tasks that agents already solve. It contains 519 clean/intervention task pairs across seven self-hosted websites and 29 intervention families, and evaluation of six strong browser-use agents shows interventions cut pass rates by 22.9% on average and overturn nearly half of cleanly solved tasks. This approach makes difficulty a controllable, diagnosable property of the environment rather than an expensive side effect of collecting ever-newer tasks, which could substantially improve how browser-use agents and other web agents are evaluated. It also reveals that most agent failures are belief failures, where agents declare success even though the required change never happened, pointing to a concrete reliability gap for real-world deployment. Each intervention preserves the user instruction, latent target, and backend success criterion while changing the environment at different web stack layers, and is annotated with the cognitive primitive it primarily loads. Humans lose only 10.0% on a first attempt and 5.7% after one familiarisation attempt, whereas 75% of the six agents' failures end with a declared success despite the required change never happening.

Researchers propose Less Uniform Diffusion (LUDI), a new uniform diffusion language model (UDLM) framework that replaces the over-uniform training objective with a less uniform loss directing each reverse transition toward the clean token, and adds per-token time embeddings for confidence-based few-step sampling. They continue-train a 7B autoregressive model into LUDI-7B, which achieves a 3-token-per-step speedup over autoregressive decoding and competitive performance against masked diffusion baselines. The core technical contributions are a less uniform loss that directs each reverse transition toward the clean token, and per-token time embeddings that provide token-level corruption hints for confidence-based few-step sampling. LUDI-7B is obtained by continue-training an existing 7B autoregressive model rather than pretraining from scratch, and it achieves a 3-token-per-step speedup while remaining competitive with masked diffusion baselines.

## [Test-Aware LLM Mutant Generation Boosts Mutation Testing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.35841) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper proposes test-aware mutant generation, in which an LLM receives the problem statement, canonical solution, and base unit tests in a single prompt and must produce a nontrivial mutant that passes those base tests. Evaluated across five LLMs (Gemini 3.1 Pro, Gemini 3 Flash, GPT 5.1 Codex Mini, GPT 4.1 Mini, Qwen3-32B) on HumanEval and MBPP, the method achieves verified fault rates of 87.7% and 79.1%, far exceeding test-blind prompting (12.2% and 23.0%) and the rule-based tool mutmut (4.4% and 5.7%). Mutation testing is a powerful way to measure test-suite quality, but traditional rule-based tools flood developers with trivial or equivalent mutants, making the technique costly in practice. By making LLM-generated mutants test-aware, this work shifts mutation testing from untargeted bug injection toward targeted discovery of real gaps in existing test suites, potentially making the technique more practical for real-world software projects. The extended EvalPlus test suites serve as an automated oracle to verify whether surviving mutants represent genuine bugs, and while fault subtlety (the fraction of extended tests a mutant fails) is comparable across all three methods, test-aware prompting minimizes the computational cost per verified fault compared to test-blind prompting. The work is an arXiv preprint without peer review, so its impact is not yet validated by the community.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Sep 30, 04:00

**Background**: Mutation testing evaluates test-suite adequacy by injecting small synthetic faults (mutants) into program code and checking whether existing tests catch them; a mutant that survives indicates a gap in the test suite. Traditional rule-based tools often generate many trivial, redundant, or equivalent mutants — mutants that are semantically identical to the original program — which limits practical adoption. Recent LLM-based approaches generate more realistic faults but are mostly test-blind, seeing only the source code and unable to reason about what existing tests already cover. HumanEval and MBPP are standard Python code-generation benchmarks, and EvalPlus extends them with more rigorous test suites.

## [Mara Chain Turns Rejected AI Configurations into Refinement Stepping Stones](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.35855) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.35855) introduces Mara Chain, a refinement procedure that retains rejected candidate configurations and iteratively refines them using evidence accumulated across prior attempts, rather than discarding them as in standard propose-evaluate-select pipelines. Evaluated on AppWorld skill optimization, TerminalBench 2.1 harness optimization, and MuSiQue retrieval-pipeline optimization, Mara Chain outperforms GEPA, ACE, and SkillOpt-Lite by up to 20.5% relative performance on AppWorld while reaching the target score with 65.5% fewer rollouts than GEPA. Most deployed AI system optimization today focuses on editing prompts, skills, harnesses, and code rather than model weights, and standard selection procedures throw away failed candidates that often contain critical information. By reusing failures, Mara Chain reduces the number of expensive rollouts needed and could make auto-evolution of AI systems more sample-efficient and less prone to revisiting the same failure modes. Mara Chain limits each refinement chain to a fixed depth and applies Pareto-filtered Top-N selection to bound the candidate pool, which keeps the search tractable. On TerminalBench 2.1 it improves pass rate by 20.2 and 22.5 percentage points over AHE and Meta-Harness respectively, and on MuSiQue it improves test nDCG@10 and Recall@10 by 0.104 and 0.131 over a hand-written retrieval pipeline.

## [Detectability Gap Reveals Hidden Heterogeneity in Hallucination Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.35860) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.35860) analyzes hallucination detection across four language models and three factual QA datasets, partitioning hallucinations into high-agreement (Ghost) and low-agreement (Flickering) regimes and finding an apparent detectability gap of 0.35 to 0.46 AUC. Because the statistics defining the regimes and measuring the gap are strongly coupled (|ρ| ≈ 0.94 to 1.00), the authors treat the raw result as a property of agreement-based detection, then freeze regime assignments and show the asymmetry persists in all 12 model-dataset settings with bootstrap 95% intervals excluding zero. This work shows that aggregate detection metrics conceal persistent, model-dependent heterogeneity in language model failures, meaning a single AUC number can mask which errors are actually detectable. It motivates regime-conditioned evaluation and has implications for AI safety and reliability, since systems relying on sampling-based consistency may systematically miss certain hallucination types. A stricter test using individual diffusion trajectories with no cross-seed information preserves the asymmetry across all three LLaDA datasets (p < 0.005) and directionally across all three Dream datasets, with one reaching significance. The hard regime's prevalence varies substantially across models (16% to 77%), and matched prompts frequently change regimes between models.

**Background**: Sampling-based consistency is a widely used hallucination detection approach: a model is prompted multiple times, and if its answers disagree across samples, the response is flagged as likely hallucinated. Hallucinations are factually incorrect or fabricated outputs from language models, and detection performance is typically measured with AUC (Area Under the ROC Curve), which captures how well a classifier separates hallucinated from correct answers. This paper asks not just how well such detectors work overall, but which specific errors they systematically fail to catch.

## [CruxBench: Benchmarking LLMs' Ability to Discover Valuable Subquestions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.35879) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduced CruxBench, a benchmark that grades LLM-generated subquestions (cruxes) by their Value of Information — how much a proposed question shifts beliefs about a target forecasting question. It was evaluated across eight models on 293 target forecasting questions, and while VOI correlated strongly with independent capability measures (r=0.90), even frontier LLMs only narrowly beat a random-timing baseline. Most LLM benchmarks only check answer accuracy against fixed labels, but many real-world tasks hinge on knowing which questions are worth asking in the first place. CruxBench targets this under-evaluated capability of information discovery, and its design could shape future research on LLM forecasting and problem decomposition. CruxBench combines three properties: it is contamination-resistant by construction because ground truth comes from future world events, it is open-ended since submissions are free-form text rather than a single numeric answer, and it is grounded because informativeness is measured against quantified changes in real-world beliefs. The finding that frontier models barely exceed a random-timing baseline suggests information discovery remains a hard, largely unsolved problem.

**Background**: Value of Information (VOI) is a decision-theoretic concept describing the maximum benefit that additional information can provide in reducing uncertainty or cost. In forecasting, a crux is an intermediate subquestion whose answer meaningfully updates one's belief about the ultimate target question. Benchmarks like ForecastBench have already used future events to create contamination-free tests of LLM forecasting, and CruxBench extends this idea from predicting outcomes to identifying which questions to ask.

A new arXiv paper (2609.35886) introduces three artifacts for measuring and mitigating fraud in agentic commerce: a taxonomy of agentic commerce fraud separating five observation levels, the Agentic Commerce Bench (ACB) covering twenty fraud classes derived from production aggregates (1,647 catalogued service operations and 1,068 settlements), and gordonguard, an open-source detector stack and offline harness. Calibrating to a stated false-positive budget yields a 6.5% clean flag rate replicated across three independent generations, but leaves eight of twenty classes no better than chance, and a widely used agent security scanner scores zero on all four reasoning-observable classes. As AI agents gain spend authority and settle payments without per-action human confirmation, traditional identity-based fraud checks fail because a counterparty can be exactly who it claims to be yet still overcharge. The taxonomy separates five observation levels (agent reasoning, wire, settlement rail, counterparty, principal) from request-level and history-level evidence, recording which levels can observe which attacks; six of the twenty fraud classes involve a counterparty that is exactly who it claims to be. A measured median payment of $0.007 means one human review costs 143 times the value of the payment it examines, placing a hard constraint on deployment.

## [New Defense Blocks LLM Semantic Cache Poisoning Attacks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.35908) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2609.35908) exposes a cache poisoning vulnerability in LLM semantic caches, where attackers cache malicious answers under queries that are highly similar to benign ones. The authors propose a defense that exploits a rewrite-residual structure in adversarial queries, using Deletion Gain and an Answer Check to block 82.0% to 98.2% of poisoned entries at a 5% false-positive rate with negligible serving overhead. Semantic caching is widely deployed to cut LLM serving costs and latency, so a poisoning flaw means attackers can bypass the model, its system prompt, and safety checks to replay malicious answers to innocent users. This work provides a practical, low-overhead defense for a critical layer of production LLM infrastructure. The vulnerability stems from an information-bottleneck gap: query embeddings lose information needed to distinguish valid from invalid cache hits, limiting any matching algorithm that uses only embeddings. The defense recovers this information from the raw cache key text by searching shortened variants for similarity gains (Deletion Gain) and testing whether removed text contributes to the stored answer (Answer Check), with a proof that Deletion Gain stays positive under certain conditions.

**Background**: Semantic caches speed up LLM serving by reusing previously generated answers for queries that are semantically similar, rather than calling the model again. Retrieval is typically based on embedding similarity, such as cosine similarity between query vectors. The information bottleneck method is an information-theoretic framework for finding the best tradeoff between compression and preserving relevant information, and it is used here to explain why embeddings alone cannot guarantee answer validity.

## [UNBIND: Inference-Time Steering to Unlearn Code from LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.35913) ⭐️ 7.0/10

UNBIND introduces an inference-time directional steering framework that selectively unlearns specific code implementations from code LLMs while keeping model weights frozen. Evaluated against fourteen baselines across two code models and two corpora, it reduces target code reproduction by 97.3% to 99.1% (F-BLEU) while solving at most two fewer HumanEval+ and six fewer MBPP+ problems than the original models. Code LLMs are trained on massive code corpora and can memorize implementations that later raise copyright or security concerns, so selective unlearning is becoming a practical requirement. UNBIND shows that forgetting can be achieved at inference time without retraining or weight modification, which could make compliance with takedown and licensing requests far cheaper for model providers. The method separates which hidden states correspond to the target code from how to suppress its reproduction, constructing distinct directions for each objective. In repeated extraction tests under a fixed budget, the number of targets yielding exact spans of at least 50 tokens drops from 188–262 to 0–2 out of 300 per setting, no extracted span reaches 100 tokens, and the mean best recovery ratio ranges from 0.43% to 6.45%.

Exploratory analyses show that most leading systems' misses occur on cues they heard, that systems beat the null almost entirely on items that state the rule, and that describing the voice or stating the rule each recovers part of the shortfall, leaving a gap on emotion.

A new arXiv preprint (2609.35948) develops intrinsic dense associative memories on Riemannian manifolds by casting memory storage as Epanechnikov kernel-density mode seeking. It proves that geodesic memory always retains isolated patterns, while volume-corrected memory obeys a sharp Ricci-curvature threshold where positive curvature can erase memories in high dimensions and negative curvature reinforces them. This reframes curvature from a passive property of data into an active design variable for associative memory, with potential implications for machine learning architectures, geometric deep learning, and neuroscience models of memory. It also provides rigorous capacity scaling laws that could guide the construction of more reliable memory systems on non-Euclidean data such as hierarchies and graphs. The paper derives geodesic capacity scalings of q_beta^{-1/2} for retaining every pattern and q_beta^{-1} for a typical one, where q_beta is the pairwise kernel-overlap probability. It shows that designed N-pattern configurations can realize all 2^N-1 subset modes, whereas random data at the storage threshold yield only a Poisson number of modes, and it establishes exact one-step recall via Riemannian mean shift.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Sep 30, 04:00

**Background**: Dense associative memories, also known as modern Hopfield networks, generalize classical Hopfield networks by using sharply peaked energy functions to achieve super-linear or even exponential storage capacity relative to the number of feature neurons. Kernel density estimation is a statistical method that smooths data into a continuous density curve, and the Epanechnikov kernel is a common choice for this. Riemannian manifolds are curved spaces where distance and volume behave differently from flat Euclidean space, and Ricci curvature characterizes how volumes distort under parallel transport, making it central to the threshold results in this paper.

## [ROSS selectively supervises historical self-generated rollouts for LLM post-training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.35954) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper introduces ROSS (Relearning from Self-Generated Rollouts through Selective Supervision), a method that preserves the full historical trajectory as context while applying loss only to selected model-generated continuations. On Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, ROSS improves the six-benchmark multi-teacher on-policy distillation average from 58.40% to 62.20% and SWE-bench Verified from 64.20% to 68.40%. The work shows that historical self-generated rollouts, typically discarded as stale after the policy updates, contain reusable behavioral experience that can yield further gains through offline supervised fine-tuning without additional policy rollouts. This could reduce the compute cost of post-training and benefit researchers working on reinforcement learning, on-policy distillation, and agentic LLM training. ROSS applies loss only to selected model-generated continuations while keeping the full historical trajectory as context, filtering out mistakes, abandoned attempts, and redundant actions that should not be imitated. It was evaluated across domain-specific reinforcement learning, multi-teacher on-policy distillation, and agentic reinforcement learning, consistently improving upstream checkpoints on mathematics, code generation, instruction following, and software engineering benchmarks.

**Background**: Large language model post-training commonly uses reinforcement learning and on-policy distillation, in which the model generates its own rollouts (trajectories of tokens or actions) that are then used as training material. On-policy distillation trains a student model on samples from its own evolving policy while a teacher provides dense token-level supervision, addressing the distribution mismatch of static imitation. Once the policy advances, however, earlier rollouts are usually treated as stale and discarded, even though they may still be compatible with the later policy and preserve useful behaviors.

## [First Systematic Multi-Agent Vision-and-Language Navigation Benchmark and Method](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.35965) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper presents the first systematic formalization of multi-agent Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) as a constrained coordination problem, where missions consist of subtasks with dependency and resource constraints such as presence locks and holding chains. It introduces MAVLN, a benchmark with 11,724 episodes across 145 scenes and teams of up to four agents under three instruction regimes, along with TRISS, a coordination-ready system combining an LLM-based subtask scheduler, shared topological memory, and conflict-aware execution. This work extends VLN from single-agent instruction following to multi-robot team coordination, a critical step toward real-world applications where tasks exceed any individual robot's capabilities. The benchmark and baseline provide a foundation for evaluating and advancing multi-agent embodied AI, potentially impacting robotics, logistics, and search-and-rescue. MAVLN includes 11,724 episodes across 145 scenes with teams of up to four agents under three instruction regimes, and comes with tailored constraint-aware metrics. TRISS couples an LLM-based subtask scheduler, a shared topological memory that turns each agent's exploration into team knowledge, and a conflict-aware execution mechanism that realizes simultaneous intentions as collision-free routes; experiments show substantial room for improvement across scheduling, planning, and execution.

## [LLMs Show Layerwise Causal Structure in Cyclic Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.35970) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2609.35970) reports that across Llama, Qwen, Gemma, and Mistral model families, transformer layers show a consistent progression when solving cyclic relational reasoning tasks: intermediate layers encode the inferred relationship between two tokens, while later layers build a joint representation of all three tokens to predict the next token. The authors also identify geometrically structured but causally inert token relationships, and find that restricting models to causally relevant joint representations actually improves next-token prediction accuracy. This work advances mechanistic interpretability by linking the geometry of internal representations to their causal role in computation, offering a concrete mechanism for how transformers compose relational information. Such insights could inform model design, debugging, and targeted interventions that improve compositional reasoning reliability in LLMs. The study uses ensembles of prompts spanning cyclic concepts—months, hours, weekdays, and musical notes—and combines geometric and causal analyses across multiple model families. Notably, the finding that restricting models to causally relevant joint representations improves accuracy suggests that some internal computations may be redundant or even detrimental to next-token prediction.

**Background**: Mechanistic interpretability aims to reverse-engineer the internal computations of neural networks, especially transformer-based language models, by identifying interpretable features and circuits. Prior work has shown that transformer representations evolve across layers, with earlier layers capturing more local or contextualized features and later layers encoding more abstract information. Cyclic relational reasoning tasks, such as inferring the next element in a sequence of months or weekdays, require models to combine multiple token relationships, making them a useful testbed for studying compositional reasoning.

## [LLM-Guided AI Develops Local Infrared Subtraction for Particle Physics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.36007) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2609.36007) presents AI-developed local infrared subtraction methods that build on projection to Born and EFT matching, with an LLM producing two implementations under human physics guidance: a neural network that fits the Born contact by matching to EFT cumulants, and an analytic construction that keeps Born momenta fixed while integrating over radiation. The authors reconstruct full NLO corrections for massless 3- and 4-jet production in electron-positron annihilation and make an attempt at NNLO dijet production, with predictions agreeing well with EERAD3. Infrared subtraction is a central bottleneck for higher-order QCD calculations, and this work shows that AI can help construct subtraction terms and improve their numerical integration, potentially simplifying calculations that normally require slicing parameters. If validated, the approach could lower the computational barrier for precision collider predictions and broaden who can perform such calculations. The framework separates an integrable radiation term from a finite Born-kinematics contribution called the Born contact, determined using the EFT singular distribution in an N-jettiness resolution observable; the resulting local subtraction formula has no slicing parameter and reuses existing lower-order radiation calculations and EFT singular predictions. Notably, the numerical calculation and projection-network training were done on a 2020 Apple M1 MacBook without GPU acceleration, and appendices extend the local subtraction to 3-jet NNLO with explicit radiation maps and a proposed contact formula.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Sep 30, 04:00

**Background**: In perturbative QCD, fixed-order calculations of jet cross sections suffer from infrared divergences when emitted gluons become soft or collinear, and subtraction schemes cancel these divergences by adding and subtracting auxiliary terms. Traditional schemes often introduce a slicing parameter that must be taken very small, which can cause numerical instability, so local subtraction methods aim to remove that parameter entirely. N-jettiness is an event-shape observable that measures how N-jet-like an event is, and effective field theory (EFT) provides singular distributions in such observables that can be matched to fixed-order calculations. This paper applies large language models to help design such subtraction terms, an example of the growing 'AI for science' trend.

## [TORQUE Optimizes Which Coordinates to Preserve Before and After Random Rotation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.36032) ⭐️ 7.0/10

TORQUE introduces a framework that jointly optimizes how many and which coordinates to preserve at high precision both before and after random rotation, under a fixed overall expected bit budget. The authors derive a quantization error upper bound and prove that top-k pre-rotation retention minimizes it for each k, reducing the search over coordinate subsets to an optimization over k. This work could improve the tradeoff between reconstruction accuracy and storage cost in vector quantization, benefiting applications such as nearest-neighbor retrieval, KV-cache compression, and activation compression. It offers a practical, theoretically grounded refinement to the widely used random-rotation quantization pipeline. The method uses offline codebooks and parallel parameter selection for practical implementation, and the fast optimizer relies on the proven top-k retention property. Numerical evaluation under the Gaussian model and experiments on nearest-neighbor retrieval, KV-cache compression, and activation compression demonstrate an improved accuracy-storage tradeoff.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Sep 30, 04:00

**Background**: Random rotations are a common preprocessing step for quantization: they make normalized coordinate distributions approximately Gaussian, enabling the use of codebooks optimized offline. Vector quantization is a lossy compression technique that represents high-dimensional vectors using a finite set of prototype vectors, and it is widely used in data compression and large-scale nearest-neighbor search. TORQUE builds on this pipeline by deciding which coordinates to keep at high precision before and after the rotation.

## [Neural Networks Learn Spectra Directly from Domain Geometry](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.36047) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.36047) proposes two neural network surrogate models that learn the spectrum of differential operators directly from domain geometry, avoiding expensive PDE solves during optimization. The first model encodes star-shaped domains via Fourier coefficients with a light MLP and achieves 0.2% precision, while the second uses the landscape function, indicator function, and its gradient with a Gram-Schmidt process to output orthogonal eigenfunctions, reaching 1% mean relative error on the first ten eigenvalues versus 4% for an FNO baseline. This work could significantly accelerate shape optimization problems that depend on eigenvalues, such as designing photonic crystals, acoustic cavities, or quantum structures, by replacing costly repeated PDE solves with fast differentiable neural surrogates. It also demonstrates that neural networks can recover classical spectral optima like the disk for the first eigenvalue, bridging machine learning and spectral geometry. The Fourier-coefficient model satisfies the eigenvalue scaling law through coefficient rescaling and achieves rotation/reflection invariance by averaging outputs over transformed inputs. The landscape model generalizes from synthetic shapes to classical image datasets, but replacing the landscape function with a signed distance function (SDF) worsened both prediction and optimization errors.

**Background**: Spectral optimization seeks a domain shape that minimizes or maximizes a functional of the eigenvalues of a differential operator, such as the Laplace operator. Traditional approaches rely on numerical PDE solvers, which are computationally expensive when embedded in an optimization loop. Neural surrogates, including Fourier Neural Operators (FNOs), have emerged as fast differentiable alternatives, and the landscape function is a known tool in spectral geometry that captures eigenvalue information for Schrödinger-type operators.

## [Mnemon: Dual-System Memory Agent for LLM Long-Term Recall](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.36059) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Mnemon, a new arXiv paper, proposes a memory agent that keeps conversations as raw dated records and splits memory work into fast System 1 relevance judgments by a decision model called Jev and slow System 2 search planning by an LLM. With gpt-4.1-mini answering, it scores 91.7% on LoCoMo and 83.8% on LongMemEval-S using under 4k tokens of context per question, and with a reasoning model it reaches 92.2% and 94.4% respectively. Most long-term memory systems for LLM agents rewrite conversations into facts, graphs, or typed memories at write time, which locks in decisions before the query is known. Mnemon's write-nothing-decided approach lets the same agent read any store that returns dated records, and its cost per question grows only 1.11x from 100K to 10M tokens of history on BEAM, which matters for agents that must run cheaply over very long histories. Mnemon uses explicit budgets to turn Jev's many small yes/no judgments into a compact View for an unchanged answering model, and a background pass consolidates each record once into topic timelines, value histories, and standing instructions linked to the records. On the same records, Jev separates gold evidence better than two LLMs and is 3-11 times faster, though the paper reports results only on LoCoMo, LongMemEval-S, and BEAM.

**Background**: Dual-process theory, popularized by psychologist Daniel Kahneman, describes thinking as two modes: fast, automatic System 1 and slow, deliberate System 2. Long-term memory for LLM agents is the problem of letting an assistant use conversation history it can no longer fit in its context window, and existing systems typically compress or rewrite that history at write time. Mnemon applies the dual-process split to this problem, using a small decision model for many fast relevance and recency judgments and an LLM only for the slower planning and composition steps.

## [Probing How Neural Routing Solvers Make Decisions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.36063) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.36063) analyzes the internal decision-making mechanisms of three autoregressive neural combinatorial optimization models — AM and POMO (heavy-encoder, light-decoder) and LEHD (light-encoder, heavy-decoder) — using behavioral analyses, representation probing, and causal interventions. It finds that AM and POMO follow a persistent geometric pattern during solution construction, while LEHD encodes linearly accessible information about multiple future actions and relies on current-node representations for local decisions and start-node representations for broader route navigation. Neural combinatorial optimization models have achieved strong empirical results but remain largely black boxes, so this mechanistic interpretability study could inform more transparent and better-designed solvers. It also highlights how architectural choices (heavy encoder vs. heavy decoder) produce fundamentally different internal decision-making strategies, which matters for researchers designing generalizable routing solvers. The study spans the Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP) and the Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem (CVRP), and cross-instance alignment analyses show that LEHD maps current-node representations into a relatively shared latent region that may serve as a stable reference for evaluating subsequent decisions. Code and additional visualizations are available at the NCO-Interpretability GitHub repository.

## [PHASE: A Physiology-Guided Hierarchical Foundation Model for Intracranial EEG](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.36087) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduced PHASE, a physiology-guided foundation model for intracranial EEG (iEEG) that makes directly measurable physiological characteristics explicit learning targets, combining them with masked latent prediction in a temporal stage (PHASE-T) and a spatiotemporal stage (PHASE-ST). Pretrained on heterogeneous recordings from 222 participants across nine clinical sites, frozen PHASE-T outperforms every evaluated foundation model by up to 31% on all five Omni-iEEG clinical tasks, while fine-tuned PHASE-T surpasses task-specific models to set a new state of the art. Existing iEEG foundation models learn by reconstructing or predicting inputs, leaving the retention of clinically meaningful physiological characteristics implicit, and they remain below task-specific models on broad clinical benchmarks when used frozen. By making these characteristics explicit learning targets, PHASE could improve clinical applications such as seizure-onset-zone identification and generalize better to unseen institutions with few or no local labels, benefiting both the neurotech and clinical AI communities. PHASE-T benefits from physiological supervision, outperforming matched ablation variants trained with latent prediction alone or auxiliary waveform reconstruction on every task, and it generalizes to unseen institutions with few or no local labels. PHASE-ST further improves seizure-onset-zone identification over PHASE-T and, when frozen, decodes sound volume and pitch on BrainTreebank better than published models, even though pretraining contains no ictal recordings or anatomical labels.

## [Modality Gap in VLMs Is Approximately Rank-One, Study Finds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.36101) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.36101) shows that across CLIP and SigLIP encoders, a single dominant direction captures 94.4–99.9% of the squared norm of the image-text mean separation, meaning the modality gap is approximately rank-one. The authors decompose the similarity score to identify three task-specific roles for the gap direction, explaining why gap modification can improve, degrade, or restore performance in zero-shot classification, standard retrieval, and mixed-modal retrieval. This provides a unified geometric explanation for previously contradictory findings about the modality gap, giving researchers a principled basis for deciding when and how to intervene on the gap in similarity-based vision-language systems. It could influence future work on contrastive learning and cross-modal alignment, especially for practitioners tuning CLIP-style models for classification versus retrieval. In zero-shot classification, query-side fixed gap-offset subtraction is exactly equivalent to an additive class bias; in standard cross-modal retrieval, projecting out the gap direction and renormalising residuals discards candidate-specific norm information, causing a multiplicative ranking distortion. A geometry-derived exponent tracks the grid-search optimum with Spearman rho = 0.93 and restores performance in some settings, though gains transfer unevenly, and residual semantic structure after removal limits the rank-one account.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Sep 30, 04:00

**Background**: Contrastive vision-language models such as CLIP and SigLIP are trained to align matched image-text pairs in a shared embedding space, yet image and text representations still cluster separately — a phenomenon known as the modality gap. Prior work reported conflicting effects of modifying this gap: reducing it can help zero-shot classification and cross-modal alignment, while removing gap-related structure can hurt image-text retrieval. This paper uses geometric analysis, including rank-one matrix approximation ideas, to reconcile those divergent results.

## [ThinQuant Cuts LLM Rotation Calibration to Minutes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.36120) ⭐️ 7.0/10

ThinQuant introduces a scalable rotation learning method for weight and activation quantization of large language models, combining geometric data selection with an exact optimization reduction. For Llama-3-70B under W4A4KV4 quantization, it completes rotation calibration in under 12 minutes with a WikiText-2 perplexity of 5.63, versus 7.55 and 111 minutes for DartQuant, and it also scales to Llama-3.1-405B on a single H200 GPU in just over 2 hours. Rotation-based quantization is key to deploying large models at low bit-widths, but existing methods like SpinQuant and DartQuant struggle to scale to the largest architectures. ThinQuant's dramatic reduction in calibration data and compute could make 4-bit weight-and-activation quantization practical for frontier-scale models on modest hardware. The method selects calibration activations via the geometric structure of their convex hull, showing that a carefully chosen set orders of magnitude smaller can match state-of-the-art performance. Because the selected activations span an r-dimensional subspace with r<d, optimizing a d×d rotation reduces to a d×r matrix on the Stiefel manifold, solved with an ADMM algorithm using thin matrix updates.

## [DSpine injects causal conditioning across drafter depth for speculative decoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.36173) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper proposes DSpine, a speculative drafter that performs gated adjacent causal injection at every backbone layer, writing each predecessor's predicted feature into its successor so the causal chain unfolds over network depth while all positions update in parallel. On Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B across seven math, code, and chat benchmarks, DSpine achieves the longest acceptance length at both temperatures, raising the Qwen3-8B mean at temperature zero from DFlash's 3.77 to 4.82 (+27.8%) and delivering 23.3% higher serving throughput than DFlash in SGLang. Speculative decoding is a key inference-time optimization for large language models, and parallel drafting methods often suffer from inconsistent continuations that shorten the accepted prefix. DSpine's layer-wise causal conditioning addresses this limitation, potentially improving acceptance rates and throughput for real-world LLM serving systems, which matters to researchers and practitioners optimizing inference efficiency. The method uses a unified transfer space built from the target model's output embeddings to unify layer-wise injection with predecessor-conditioned decoding, and applies layer-wise output-embedding supervision to promote predicted features in shallow layers. Fused kernels and a transition cache enable efficient parallel execution within SGLang, though the evaluation is limited to Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B models.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Sep 30, 04:00

**Background**: Speculative decoding accelerates autoregressive LLM inference by having a smaller draft model propose multiple candidate tokens that a larger target model verifies in a single forward pass, preserving the target model's output distribution. Parallel speculative drafting generates multiple candidates in one backbone pass, but independent token selection can produce inconsistent continuations that reduce the accepted prefix length. Existing methods often leave conditional decoding to a lightweight module after the backbone, limiting how much predecessor information reaches successor positions.

## [ProVer Targets Pivotal Decisions to Improve Credit Assignment in Agentic RL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.36178) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduce ProVer, a framework that improves credit assignment in agentic reinforcement learning by having an agentic judge contrast successful and failed trajectories to propose a potentially pivotal segment, then verifying that segment by estimating its advantage from differences in terminal success rates of current-policy continuations sampled before and after it. Across ALFWorld, WebShop, and SearchQA, ProVer achieves the strongest average performance at both model scales, with relative improvements over GRPO of 9.91% and 7.12% for Qwen3.5-2B and Qwen3.5-4B, respectively. This work addresses a known limitation of GRPO, which uniformly assigns trajectory-level advantages to all policy tokens and thus fails to distinguish consequential decisions from less relevant ones. By grounding local credit in observed outcomes rather than trusting model judgment alone, ProVer could make agentic RL training more sample-efficient and interpretable, benefiting researchers and practitioners training LLM agents on long-horizon tasks. ProVer uses model judgment only to select where to verify, avoiding exhaustive evaluation of every intermediate state, and it achieves gains with modest additional generation overhead even without a frontier-scale judge model. The approach is evaluated on ALFWorld, WebShop, and SearchQA, and the paper is an arXiv preprint (arXiv:2609.36178v1) that has not yet undergone peer review.

The authors reproduce a prior 'machine bias' study and show that poor representation stems not only from insufficient between-group variation but also from variation assigned to the wrong groups, and they find that cultural fine-tuning improves alignment with the survey center without improving within-population differences. As LLMs are increasingly used to simulate human attitudes in social science research and synthetic survey data, this framework offers a more rigorous way to diagnose when model outputs misrepresent subgroups, which matters for AI fairness, alignment evaluation, and the validity of LLM-based simulations. It also provides reusable code, data, and trained models, potentially becoming a standard benchmark for population fidelity. The framework distinguishes three conditions for population representation and demonstrates that aggregate agreement metrics fail to capture the distinction between matching the survey center and reproducing within-population differences. The paper is an arXiv preprint (v1) and has not yet undergone peer review or generated community discussion.

A new arXiv paper (2609.36263) investigates how varying the amount of paired multimodal data at fixed total data budgets affects loss curves, finding that synergistic loss reduction is gated and requires a critical threshold of paired data before it occurs at all. The authors propose a new family of multimodal scaling laws that models total data-attributable loss as the sum of four power laws for redundancy, a unique channel per modality, and synergy, achieving 3.2% error on fit tests versus 10.4% for the best pairing extension of published laws. This work provides a more theoretically sound and empirically accurate framework for predicting multimodal model performance, which could guide data collection and pairing strategies in vision-language and other multimodal systems. It challenges the assumption in existing scaling laws that multimodality can be captured by a single empirical term, potentially affecting how practitioners allocate resources between paired and unpaired data. The study trains models in three different environments and sweeps data sizes and pairing budgets, showing that only paired data can reduce synergistic loss while unpaired data reduces redundant or unimodal information up to unimodal floors. The proposed law decomposes loss into four information channels and predicts multimodal loss more accurately than existing laws, though the abstract is truncated and no community discussion is available.

## [DecoyTrace Uses Chaotic-Map Decoys to Defend Serverless Federated Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.36330) ⭐️ 7.0/10

DecoyTrace introduces a proactive cyber deception defense for strictly serverless decentralized federated learning (DFL), deploying a mobile DecoyNode that generates decoy challenges via chaotic maps, distributes a dual clean/decoy model based on neighbor trust, and evaluates them with three-state semantic metrics. Evaluated across sixty configurations on the NEBULA platform (five datasets, three topologies, four attack/defense scenarios), it keeps F1-score within 0.03 of baseline on MNIST/FashionMNIST, matches or exceeds baseline on EMNIST and CIFAR-100, and stays 0.05–0.10 below baseline on CIFAR-10, while containment cuts CPU and network usage by up to two-thirds. Existing deception-based defenses were designed for centralized federated learning and fail to jointly handle local observation, poisoning propagation, source attribution, and containment in strictly serverless DFL, where removing the central server also removes the single observation point traditional defenses rely on. This work shows it is feasible to unify deception, identification, and containment in DFL, which matters for security and ML communities building peer-to-peer training systems resistant to backdoors and semantic poisoning. The defense relies on a mobile DecoyNode, chaotic-map-generated decoy challenges, a dual clean-versus-decoy model disseminated by neighbor trust, and three-state semantic metrics for confirmation, after which a distributed protocol isolates the source and performs model reset or recovery. The paper also identifies limitations: performance degrades on the visually complex CIFAR-10 convolutional scenario and in multi-attractor threat models.

## [Neighbor-Based Calibration Enables One-Round Membership Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.36331) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.36331) proposes calibrating membership inference signals by querying the target model on neighbors of the target point, eliminating the need to train reference models. The authors show that querying these neighbors against an early training checkpoint further sharpens the signal, and they validate the approach across three image classification datasets and three training setups. Reference-model-based calibration is the strongest known membership inference paradigm, but it scales poorly to modern large models whose training is too expensive to replicate. By removing the need for auxiliary models, this work makes strong privacy attacks feasible in realistic one-round settings, which matters for both privacy auditing and the security evaluation of large models. The core insight is that reference models only reveal how an example behaves under models not trained on it, and querying the target model on nearby samples yields the same information; the paper proposes two complementary ways to obtain such neighbors. The evaluation covers three image classification datasets and three training setups, achieving competitive attack performance at no additional training cost, though the approach is demonstrated only on image classification rather than large language models.

**Background**: Membership inference (MI) attacks determine whether a specific data record was part of a model's training set, typically by exploiting the fact that models tend to behave differently on data they were trained on. State-of-the-art attacks calibrate their signal per example using reference models — auxiliary models trained to exclude the target — which makes the membership signal much stronger. However, training such reference models is prohibitively expensive for modern large models, motivating the one-round setting where only a single trained model is available and per-example calibration is normally impossible.

## [Quantization Enables Private Dense Retrieval Against Malicious Servers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.36376) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.36376) introduces a two-round cryptographic protocol that provides both query privacy and retrieval integrity against a malicious server for dense retrieval in RAG systems. The protocol reduces private and verifiable retrieval to multiplication of a committed matrix by an encrypted vector, using low-bit quantization to make the computation practical. This work addresses a critical gap in privacy-preserving AI: existing dense retrieval systems trust the server to both keep queries confidential and return honest results, which is unsafe in privacy-sensitive domains like healthcare. By showing that private dense retrieval is practical for moderately sized corpora with minute-scale latency, it opens the door to deploying RAG systems where neither query nor retrieval integrity can be compromised. Evaluations across six embedding models, four language models, and corpora up to 2.68 million passages show that with a clipped quantizer, three-bit quantization largely preserves retrieval quality and downstream RAG accuracy, while a private query over a clinical reference-sized corpus requires one to three minutes of server time. The protocol relies on a committed matrix and encrypted vector multiplication, with the trade-off between cryptographic cost, retrieval quality, and RAG accuracy explicitly characterized.

The paper introduces CrystAF, an all-atom crystal flow-map generative model, and uses it together with the UMA interatomic potential to systematically compare three places where physics can be injected: during training, post-training, and inference. This work offers an actionable principle for physics-informed generative modeling: learn reusable physical alignment into the generator once, and reserve expensive inference-time physics for residual constraints. Because the same post-training strategy also improves the multi-step all-atom Clari-M and rigid-body MolCrystalFlow generators, the finding appears transferable across architectures and representations, which matters for ML researchers and computational chemists working on molecular crystal structure prediction. The comparison holds the generator and physical signal fixed, using the UMA interatomic potential as the physics source; post-training pays the physics cost once during training rather than repeatedly at deployment. The authors note that learning from relaxed targets provides little benefit, and that post-training and inference-time relaxation are complementary rather than competing, with inexpensive inference corrections still needed to remove clashes and restore stereochemistry the generator cannot represent.

## [Broader Positive-Pair Supervision Erases Change in Longitudinal Contrastive Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.36409) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.36409) shows that in person-level longitudinal contrastive learning, widening the span of positive-pair supervision systematically suppresses recoverable changing-state information, even when the amount of available history is held fixed. Using in-home sensing records spanning up to 2.7 years, the authors find that at the broadest supervision span less than 10% of the information recoverable from an untrained encoder remains, and they prospectively reproduce the effect in 199 GLOBEM participants. This identifies a previously underappreciated scaling problem in longitudinal self-supervised learning: more history does not automatically mean better representations, because broader invariance can erase the very change that makes longitudinal data valuable. It matters for representation learning, self-supervised learning, and especially longitudinal health sensing, where detecting behavioral or clinical change is often the core goal. The paper separates record span (how much history the learner sees) from supervision span (how far positive-pair supervision reaches across that history), showing the two are fundamentally different. It also finds that keeping positives local is not sufficient, since as records grow even distant states that are never paired become increasingly similar, and explicitly contrasting other observations from the same person reverses the loss without shortening the record.

## [RPD: Training-Free Reliable Parallel Decoding for Masked Diffusion Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.36452) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces Reliable Parallel Decoding (RPD), a training-free method that improves parallel token commitment in masked diffusion language models (MDLMs) by selecting candidates based on layerwise prediction stability and final confidence. Evaluated on LLaDA and Dream across mathematical reasoning and code generation benchmarks, RPD achieves the highest decoding throughput among compared methods while maintaining or improving accuracy. Parallel decoding is the key mechanism that gives diffusion language models their latency advantage over autoregressive models, but committing unreliable predictions together can degrade output quality. RPD addresses this reliability gap without additional training, making it directly applicable to existing MDLMs and potentially accelerating their adoption for code generation and reasoning tasks. The method's diagnostics show that confidence alone is insufficient for determining commitment order: confident predictions near the end of a sequence can be fixed before their supporting computations are established, and downstream predictions become less reliable as upstream uncertainty grows. RPD instead defers predictions with uncertain upstream context and commits the remaining candidates in parallel under a cumulative entropy budget over preceding masked positions, without relying on a fixed block schedule.

This allows them to predict multiple masked tokens in parallel within a single forward pass, offering sub-linear generation latency and bidirectional context. However, predictions made in the same forward pass are not necessarily mutually consistent, so deciding which tokens to commit together is a central challenge for decoding quality.

The paper proposes Chameleon, a channel-dependent state space model (SSM) that enables data-dependent, fine-grained interactions across variables while scaling linearly with the number of variables. The model leverages the missing measurement update in selective SSMs to model cross-variable interactions while preserving the SSM backbone for temporal modeling, and introduces a previously unexplored stochastic perturbation of reversible instance normalization to improve generalization. Researchers introduced STAIRCASE POLICY (S-WAM), a streaming inference and training framework that turns a flow-matching VLA into a JEPA-style World-Action Model and partitions a large action chunk into sub-chunks at staggered denoising stages. Near-term actions are executed as soon as they are available while later actions continue to be refined, and at each sub-chunk boundary the future latent is re-predicted from the latest observation to update all unexecuted actions. ## [Distributed Inference Alters Medical Model Reliability, Study Finds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.36525) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.36525) proposes a testing framework and a distributed-execution-sensitive benchmark that compares the same medical model checkpoint and input under a centralized HuggingFace reference versus matched distributed deployments. Across language, vision, and multimodal medical models, execution changes produced measurable output disagreements, with test success rates ranging from 0.21 to 0.43 for single-modality models and 0.32 to 0.98 for multimodal models. The work exposes an evaluation-deployment mismatch: medical AI models may pass offline centralized evaluation yet behave differently once deployed under tensor parallelism, mixed precision, kernel fusion, and multi-device communication. This matters for clinical safety and regulation, since reliability claims based on centralized benchmarks may not hold in real distributed serving environments. The benchmark evaluates the same checkpoint and input under a centralized HuggingFace reference and matched distributed deployments, extending medical-model evaluation from capability and security toward evaluation-deployment consistency. The reported success rates vary widely by modality, suggesting that multimodal medical models are especially sensitive to execution-stack changes.

## [PAIR uses counterfactual rollouts to fix context compression in long-horizon agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.36526) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.36526) introduces PAIR (Prompt Adaptation using Interventional Rollouts), a method that uses matched counterfactual continuations to identify individual context-compression events that degrade long-horizon agent execution and then revises the relevant sections of a fixed compression template. PAIR reportedly achieves the strongest cross-run reliability among compressed methods in every main benchmark-scope combination, consistently beating the competing prompt-adaptation baseline and bringing compressed execution close to the no-compression baseline without modifying the downstream agent. Context compression is essential for long-horizon LLM agents whose interaction histories grow without bound, but compression can silently degrade reliability rather than solvability, making failures hard to attribute. By isolating which individual compressions cause harm and adapting the compression prompt accordingly, PAIR offers a practical path to more reliable agent execution without retraining or modifying the underlying agent, which matters for researchers and practitioners building multi-step agent systems. The paper first shows that compression degrades reliability before solvability, and that severe degradation concentrates at isolated compression events rather than being spread evenly. PAIR diagnoses the effects of these harmful compressions and revises only the relevant sections of a fixed compression template, avoiding modification of the downstream agent; the method is evaluated across multiple benchmark-scope combinations for cross-run reliability.

**Background**: Long-horizon agents are LLM-based systems that execute many sequential steps, so their context windows fill with accumulated observations and interaction history; context compression summarizes or prunes this history to keep the agent within token limits. Existing prompt-adaptation approaches infer compression errors by comparing full-context and compressed trajectories, but such comparisons cannot isolate individual compressions and are confounded by agent stochasticity. ## [Interactive-Policy Distillation Bridges On-Policy and Off-Policy Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.36546) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper proposes Interactive-Policy Distillation (IPD), which uses a bidirectional propose-and-verify state machine to let student and teacher alternately act as proposer and verifier during student rollouts, generating mixed-source trajectories with source-split supervision. When distilling Qwen3-30B-A3B into Qwen3-1.7B-Base, IPD improves benchmark-averaged accuracy by +3.28 mean@8 and +3.28 best@8 over on-policy distillation (OPD), while using only about 1/4 of the training examples and steps. IPD addresses teacher unanchoring, a core failure mode of on-policy distillation where the student drifts into states the teacher would rarely visit, making its supervision unreliable. By unifying on-policy and off-policy distillation and improving data efficiency, the method could make distillation of large models into small models cheaper and more reliable for the LLM training ecosystem. The method applies different supervisions according to each token's source and includes a dedicated fused inference engine that co-hosts both models in one serving instance with separate KV caches, instantiating the state machine to distribute, collect, and process requests. The paper also studies loss variants and takeover/handback configurations, and shows robustness across different training data, though it remains an arXiv preprint without peer review or community validation yet.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Sep 30, 04:00

**Background**: Knowledge distillation trains a smaller student model to imitate a larger teacher model. On-policy distillation (OPD) has the student generate its own trajectories and queries the teacher for dense token-level feedback on those states, whereas off-policy distillation instead collects teacher-generated data and applies supervised fine-tuning to the student. OPD can suffer from teacher unanchoring, where the student's reasoning drifts far from the teacher's distribution, so the teacher is queried on states it would hardly visit and gives unreliable guidance.

The paper introduces a factorized scheduling principle (FSP) framework that decomposes a global scheduling rule into additive univariate and pairwise components with identifiability constraints, learning them via a policy-based objective combined with a temporal-difference signal defined on condition distributions. Experiments on synthetic and realistic scheduling tasks show strong performance, interpretability, and zero-shot generalization across different system scales. Scheduling is a core problem in reinforcement learning and operations research, and FSP offers a principled way to obtain policies that are both interpretable and transferable, potentially reducing the need for retraining when system scales change. This could benefit applications such as job scheduling, resource allocation, and network routing where transparency and generalization are critical. The framework maintains a simple priority-based structure during deployment, where states are represented as condition distributions and the scheduling principle is learned through a policy-based objective with a temporal-difference signal. Identifiability constraints are imposed on the additive components to ensure unique decomposition, and the method demonstrates zero-shot generalization across different system scales.

Training strong PRMs has been a major bottleneck in LLM post-training and test-time reasoning because step-level human annotation is hard to scale and Monte Carlo estimation is computationally expensive and can drift from the intrinsic correctness of steps. By inducing process supervision from outcome-only RL, TIPS offers a low-cost alternative that could make high-quality step-level verification far more accessible for reasoning-focused LLM alignment. TIPS uses group-relative advantage to optimize the entire generated response, so when checking intermediate steps helps determine the outcome, more accurate checks yield better outcome judgments and higher rewards, reinforcing step-level verification without explicit process supervision. The authors validate the method across math and agent benchmarks and four backbone families, and release code and data at https://github.com/RUCBM/TIPS.

The paper proposes a Normalize-Then-Precondition framework that hierarchically separates marginal scale from interaction geometry in matrix optimizers, yielding two new variants called NormPre-G and NormPre-L. NormPre-G uses global spectral preconditioning approximated by Newton-Schulz iterations, while NormPre-L uses localized spectral preconditioning approximated by randomized sketching, and both are shown to consistently outperform AdamW, Muon, and MANO across GPT-2 Small, LLaMA, and Qwen3 pretraining experiments under matched budgets. Matrix optimizers such as Muon are becoming a serious alternative to AdamW for large-scale LLM pretraining, so a principled framework that clarifies how to organize scale and geometry information could guide the design of the next generation of optimizers. If NormPre's gains hold at production scale, it could translate into faster convergence or lower compute cost for frontier model training. The authors establish O(T^{-1/2}) convergence guarantees for simplified versions of NormPre, and their spectral analysis characterizes a performance-efficiency trade-off between the global NormPre-G and the localized NormPre-L. Code is open-sourced at https://github.com/zx-gong/NormPre, though the convergence theory applies only to simplified variants rather than the full practical algorithms.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Sep 30, 04:00

**Background**: Muon is a matrix-aware optimizer that orthogonalizes the update for each weight matrix, typically via Newton-Schulz iterations, and has been scaled to production LLM pretraining by the Kimi/Moonshot AI team. Newton-Schulz iteration is a matrix-multiplication-only method for approximating the orthogonal factor of a matrix, which makes it efficient on GPUs. Spectral preconditioning refers to reshaping gradient updates according to their singular-value spectrum, and prior work has begun analyzing why this orthogonalization benefits Muon. NormPre builds on this line by revisiting Muon through its full-Gram representation and splitting the update into a marginally normalized part and a spectrally preconditioned interaction part.

## [Spotter: VLM Reflects on Failures to Guide Embodied Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.36808) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper proposes Spotter, a framework in which an embodied model executes continuously while a vision-language model (VLM) runs in parallel, monitors via a lightweight local screener, and intervenes only when an error is detected to reflect on and correct it. Tested with Qwen and GPT as the VLM, Spotter improves Cosmos Policy and π0.5 by 5.6 and 7.5 percentage points on RoboCasa, and raises π0.5 from 47.2% to 57.0% on RoboTwin 2.0 Hard and from 53% to 83% on a real robot. Current embodied models cannot self-repair failures because they are trained only on successful demonstrations, and prior VLM-led approaches place the VLM on the critical path, making execution slow. Spotter reverses these roles, enabling efficient error recovery that could make embodied AI systems more robust and practical for real-world robotics. Because the VLM steps in only when an error is confirmed, a successful episode with Qwen takes only 13 to 16 seconds longer than with the embodied model alone and about 70% less time than a VLM-led baseline using the same model. The framework is evaluated on RoboCasa, RoboTwin 2.0, and a real robot, with code available at https://github.com/zqc3117/Spotter.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Sep 30, 04:00

**Background**: Embodied models are AI systems that control robots by mapping sensory inputs to actions, often trained via imitation learning on successful demonstrations. Vision-language models (VLMs) are multimodal AI systems that jointly interpret images and text, extending large language models with visual understanding. Best-of-N selection is a test-time technique that samples multiple candidate outputs and picks the best one, but it relies on reliable verification. The paper argues that reflection—the kind of self-correction behind gains in language models—must come from a VLM because it can take in richer information such as episode history and text.

## [Gradient-Based Jailbreak Detectors Fail in Multi-Turn Dialogue](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.36849) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.36849) conducts a controlled evaluation of gradient-based jailbreak detectors, specifically GradSafe, in multi-turn dialogue settings, and proposes a Context Window Scanner extension that scores fixed-size windows of user turns and takes the maximum as the conversation-level score. The results show that against synthetic benign conversations the detector reaches an ROC-AUC of 0.98 on human-authored multi-turn jailbreaks, but on WildChat benign conversations the ROC-AUC drops to 0.76, and a threshold calibrated on synthetic data flags over 90% of benign conversations as unsafe. This work exposes a critical gap in AI safety tooling: detectors validated on single prompts or synthetic data may fail badly when deployed on real multi-turn assistants, where adversaries can spread unsafe intent across turns. It warns that reliable deployment of gradient-based detection requires calibration on realistic benign conversations, short-window scoring, length-aware thresholds, and evaluation across attack types and model architectures. Under realistic benign distributions, single-turn windows give the highest separability, while longer windows and accumulated context reduce performance; the detector is also sensitive to the attack-generation method and target model, with successful Crescendo attacks scoring comparable to or lower than benign conversations, and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct yielding near-random separability with a different optimal window size.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Sep 30, 04:00

**Background**: GradSafe is a jailbreak detection method that scores an input by the alignment between the gradient it induces in a safety-aligned language model and a fixed unsafe reference direction, avoiding the need for online moderation APIs or fine-tuned classifiers. Multi-turn jailbreak attacks such as Crescendo gradually steer a model across several dialogue turns, exploiting the fact that safety alignment is typically evaluated on single prompts. This paper asks whether gradient-based signals, which were designed for single prompts, still survive when unsafe intent is spread across a conversation.

The paper reports a trade-off: embedding perturbation primarily reduces flagged harmful content, whereas gradient attenuation primarily preserves explicit refusal behavior. ## [Dissipative Quantum Reservoir Computing Builds Digital Twin of High-Harmonic Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.36901) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2609.36901) introduces a dissipative quantum reservoir computing (DQRC) framework that builds a digital twin of driven many-body quantum systems, learning the input-output map directly from data while keeping a small open quantum reservoir fixed and training only a classical readout. The authors show that a minimal single-qubit reservoir reproduces the High-Harmonic Generation (HHG) response of a substantially larger Ising spin chain and matches or surpasses previously reported temporal convolutional and Kolmogorov-Arnold-network models on several metrics, with code released on GitHub. This work suggests that compact, physically realizable quantum reservoirs can serve as efficient digital twins for nonlinear, memory-dependent quantum dynamics, potentially reducing the cost of simulating strongly driven many-body systems. It bridges quantum machine learning and computational physics, offering a practical route to model attosecond-scale phenomena such as HHG without expensive full-scale simulation. The reservoir is a single fixed qubit open quantum system, and only a classical readout is trained, which simplifies implementation compared to training the full quantum dynamics. A single fixed reservoir also generalizes across a broad range of drives, indicating it learns a shared physical response structure rather than memorizing trajectories; the code is available at https://github.com/AI-and-Quantum-Computing/DQuRC.

CSF exploits contextual information asymmetry by varying the history while keeping the noisy target fixed, aligning a noise-mixed-history student's intermediate representations with a clean-history EMA teacher. Context-aligned AR DMD shares the causal mask and prefix across generator sampling, fake-score training, and real-score evaluation, performing clean-prefix few-step distillation and then adapting to generated histories without switching objectives or requiring separate consistency distillation.
