## [OPFL: Optimistic Verification of Federated Learning via Empirical Boundary](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37011) ⭐️ 7.0/10

OPFL introduces an optimistic verification framework for privacy-preserving federated learning that replays client training inside secure multi-party computation (MPC) and uses an offline-calibrated empirical boundary to distinguish benign numerical deviations from malicious manipulation. Experiments on LeNet, BERT, and Qwen show the boundary generalizes across datasets, input lengths, and GPUs, achieving 0% ASR against model poisoning and PGD-based attacks, and on a LeNet workload at p=0.01 it is about 98.6× faster than full MPC-based FL and 625.5× faster than a ZK-based approach. Federated learning lacks visibility into local training, making it hard to verify whether clients follow the prescribed procedure or submit poisoned updates, and OPFL addresses this without sacrificing data privacy. By making privacy-preserving verification practical through optimistic sampling and empirical boundaries, it could strengthen trust and security in real-world federated learning deployments across domains such as healthcare and finance. The core insight is that gradients computed under MPC and on local GPUs are not bitwise identical, but their absolute differences are stable and bounded, so OPFL calibrates an empirical boundary offline and audits only sampled training steps to cut MPC replay cost. The reported 0% ASR and speedups are demonstrated on LeNet, BERT, and Qwen workloads, though the abstract is truncated and full evaluation details, threat model assumptions, and boundary calibration overhead remain to be examined in the paper.

**Background**: Federated learning lets multiple clients collaboratively train a model without sharing raw private data, but because the server cannot see local training, malicious clients can submit manipulated updates in model poisoning attacks. Optimistic verification, inspired by systems that process data optimistically and only challenge invalid results within a window, reduces cost by auditing only a sample of steps rather than proving everything upfront.

## [LongSpark: Fixed-Cost Block-Diffusion Drafter for Speculative Decoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37029) ⭐️ 7.0/10

LongSpark introduces a block-diffusion drafter for speculative decoding whose decoding cost stays constant regardless of prefix length, by extracting fixed-size multiscale views from the target model's verification pass instead of maintaining a growing persistent state. The paper reports state-of-the-art end-to-end efficiency across multiple model scales, the lowest time-per-output-token on long-context tasks, and a reduction of the drafter's context state by several orders of magnitude. Existing state-of-the-art drafters become increasingly expensive as context grows, eroding the speedup that speculative decoding is meant to provide; LongSpark breaks this scaling by making the drafter's cost independent of prefix length. This could substantially improve latency and memory efficiency for long-context LLM serving, benefiting both inference providers and users running long-document or agentic workloads. The key insight is that a drafter only proposes candidates and the target model verifies and corrects every error before any token is committed, so the drafter need not scale with its prefix the way a standalone language model must. LongSpark achieves this via block diffusion with fixed-size multiscale views, though the abstract is truncated and full acceptance-length and quality trade-off numbers are not yet visible.

**Background**: Speculative decoding is an inference-time optimization for autoregressive LLMs in which a smaller draft model proposes several candidate tokens that a larger target model verifies in a single forward pass, preserving the target's output distribution while cutting latency roughly two to three times. Block diffusion drafting is a semi-autoregressive paradigm that splits sequences into blocks and applies parallel diffusion-based denoising, enabling parallel candidate generation. Autoregressive inference generates one token at a time, so drafters traditionally must maintain a state that grows with the prefix, which is exactly the cost LongSpark targets.

A new arXiv paper introduces SPEED-AE (SParse Equivalent Equation Discovery AutoEncoder), a framework that combines a pretrained Causal Representation Learning (CRL) method with a component-wise autoencoder to recover governing ODEs from high-dimensional unstructured observations such as images. The authors prove that for polynomial ODEs, this additional step restricts variable identifiability from polynomial to monomial diffeomorphisms, and experiments on Lotka-Volterra, Lorenz, and a two-pendulum system show improved disentanglement, closer-to-ground-truth ODE recovery, and state-of-the-art forecasting performance. The key insight is that variables learned by CRL methods are only identifiable up to component-wise diffeomorphisms, which generally do not yield the sparse equations that equation-discovery methods like SINDy require; SPEED-AE adds a component-wise autoencoder to learn transformations amenable to sparse discovery. With Qwen3.5-9B, VACE reaches 45.26% test accuracy on OfficeQA and a mean partial-credit score of 75.19% on AutomationBench, beating weight-only RL by 6.43 and 9.09 percentage points and ungated alternation by 4.59 and 6.95 points. The critic estimates the posterior probability of eventual success from later trajectory states and unfinished prefixes, providing dense per-prefix signals that require no completed rollouts, step-level annotations, or external reward labels.

## [CRJudgeBench Tests Whether AI Can Spot Plausible but Invalid Code Reviews](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37216) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduced CRJudgeBench, a benchmark of 1199 instances built from real pull requests and expert-verified perturbations, covering both trustworthy and plausible but untrustworthy code review comments. They also presented Sentinel, a repository-grounded agentic judge trained from Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct via iterative action-level learning, which achieves 76.60% accuracy on the 359-instance test set, beating GLM-5.3 by 6.13 points and its base model by 19.78 points. Existing code review benchmarks mainly evaluate review generation, issue discovery, or general comment quality, but not whether an agent can judge the technical trustworthiness of an individual comment. This work addresses that gap, which matters for AI-assisted software engineering because plausible but incorrect review comments can mislead developers and erode trust in automated review tools. The benchmark comprises 1199 labeled examples drawn from 124 pull requests across 9 repositories, and the dataset is available on Hugging Face. Sentinel actively gathers code evidence from the repository before making judgments, and the results show that even state-of-the-art general-purpose LLMs struggle to identify untrustworthy comments.

## [DatalogBench: New Benchmark Tests LLMs on Text-to-Datalog Synthesis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37233) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduced DatalogBench, a benchmark of 136 text-to-Datalog synthesis tasks curated from existing Datalog-based artifacts, evaluating six LLMs across four prompting configurations. Exact match peaks at 68.4%, with most failures under direct prompting occurring at compile time, typically because models invent auxiliary predicates they never declare or type consistently. This is the first systematic benchmark for text-to-Datalog synthesis, filling a gap in LLM evaluation for logical reasoning and program analysis tasks. The finding that failures cluster around compile-time errors and recursive reasoning gives developers actionable direction for improving LLM code generation and agent design. Synthesized programs are graded by execution on held-out inputs against an oracle validated by mutation analysis, and relation descriptions or an input-output example have only modest, model-dependent effects. Two coding agents reach up to 83.8% and eliminate nearly all compile-time failures, leaving mostly semantic errors concentrated in recursive tasks.

**Background**: Datalog is a declarative logic programming language, syntactically a subset of Prolog, that generally uses bottom-up evaluation and supports recursive queries; it underpins reasoning tasks such as program analysis and is used as a query language by databases like Datomic. Existing Datalog synthesizers require users to specify intent as input-output examples, whereas LLMs could allow synthesis directly from a natural-language question. Mutation analysis, used here to validate the grading oracle, works by deliberately introducing small changes to test whether a checker reliably detects faults.

## [V-JEPA Policy Builds World-Action Models on Frozen Predictive Visual Latents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37250) ⭐️ 7.0/10

V-JEPA Policy introduces a framework that builds a world-action model (WAM) on the latent space of a frozen V-JEPA 2.1 encoder, jointly learning an instruction-conditioned future-latent predictor and a flow-matching action expert from scratch in a single downstream stage. With 0.9B total parameters (0.6B trainable), it achieves competitive performance against representative WAM and vision-language-action baselines on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboCasa-GR1. This work suggests that a predictive visual latent space from large-scale self-supervised pretraining may be sufficient for effective world-action learning, without inheriting a full pretrained visual generative model. If validated, it could offer a lighter, more efficient path for robotics and embodied AI, and it identifies V-JEPA latents as more effective than discriminative, reconstructive, and video-understanding-oriented alternatives, especially under distribution shifts. The predictor's future-informed context key-value states condition action generation, and the framework is compared against other visual foundations under the same downstream framework and training budget. Pretraining the predictor on DROID video-instruction pairs without action labels and then adapting it into a WAM yields substantial gains in downstream control and out-of-distribution generalization; code is available at https://github.com/breez3young/VJEPA-Policy.

## [Loss-Guided Pretraining Data Selection for Time-Series Foundation Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37255) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.37255) introduces a static data-selection framework that scores each pretraining window with a reference forecaster and retains an intermediate interval within every source dataset. The method outperforms random selection across various TSFM architectures and even improves relative MASE and CRPS over full-data pretraining while using fewer candidate windows. This work addresses a key inefficiency in TSFM pretraining, where billions of observations are sampled without assessing their learning value. By showing that a small reference model can select data for larger targets, it could significantly reduce compute costs and improve model performance for time-series foundation models. The framework connects forecasting loss to optimization difficulty by proving that normalized squared loss controls the per-sample gradient norm under a local Jacobian condition, and it uses dataset-stratified selection to preserve sample diversity. Analyses reveal strong cross-scale and cross-architecture score correlations, suggesting a small reference model can often select data for larger targets if they share compatible difficulty orderings.

They also release UniAfford-Data, a dataset combining pixel-level 2D annotations, point-level 3D annotations, and language instructions under a shared object-affordance taxonomy. 2D and 3D affordance grounding have historically evolved as separate problems with different task definitions, supervision formats, datasets, and evaluation protocols, which limits transferable object-affordance semantics across visual and geometric spaces. Experiments show strong zero-shot generalization across 2D and 3D affordance benchmarks without target-specific fine-tuning, and ablations validate token routing, joint 2D-3D supervision, and decoder coupling.

## [Audit Finds Tool-Using Agent Benchmarks Fail to Verify Tool Contracts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37315) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.37315) audits tool-using agent benchmarks by treating each tool's advertised interface as an executable contract and checking the implementation against it. Across 34 mutating tools in four benchmarks, the authors confirmed seven tool defects and one evaluator property at pinned commits, and found that their checker missed most injected defects because no probe exercised the relevant clause. If benchmarks grade what a simulated tool call reports rather than what the tool actually did, then agent scores can be systematically wrong, and a defect beneath a score persists on every rerun. This undermines the reliability of leaderboards used to certify agents for settings where a wrong action carries real cost. The checker raised no false positives in 25 flags, flagged only 2 of 5 negative controls, and missed 29 of 33 scored defects even though a clause covered them. Its static half alone flags 14 of 17 confirmed sites, so the dynamic half mainly confirms and traces rather than discovers; for AgentDojo, at least 5 of 25 mutating tools diverge from their advertised surface, and on 1,120 paths isolating a tau2-bench telecom defect the evaluator rewards refueling a suspended line while failing the repaired tool.

## [Port-Hamiltonian Latent Deliberation Fixes Deliberation Drift Cliff](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37351) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2609.37351) identifies a 'Deliberation Drift Cliff' in continuous latent reasoning, where unconstrained recurrent models gain accuracy at short horizons (K ≤ 4) but collapse by 22%–62% at deeper steps (K ≥ 16). The authors propose Port-Hamiltonian Latent Deliberation (PH-LD) with a Direct-Gradient Pure-Tensor Helmholtz-Hodge Decomposition (DG-HHD), achieving 58.67% peak accuracy and retaining 35.27% at K=32 in a 15-arm Pareto benchmark. This work addresses a critical failure mode in test-time compute scaling for latent reasoning, a highly active area for improving AI reasoning without verbal chain-of-thought. If validated, PH-LD could enable more stable and efficient long-horizon latent deliberation, benefiting researchers building recurrent-depth or latent-space reasoning models. DG-HHD parameterizes the attracting flow as a tangent projection tensor network and orthogonally decouples non-zero circulation, achieving Hodge machine error of 1.65e-17 and contraction error of 5.55e-17 while eliminating runtime autograd dependencies for 1.84x vector field and 2.09x RK45 rollout speedups. Transferred to small language model multi-hop causal reasoning, it delivers monotonic compute scaling (49.33% to 51.56%) and suppresses out-of-distribution drift (cliff -0.66%), with all 30 Level 0 deterministic invariants certified.

**Background**: Test-time compute scaling lets a model spend more computation at inference to improve reasoning, and latent reasoning does this by iterating in a continuous hidden space rather than generating long chains of text. A new arXiv paper (2609.37371) introduces "adaptation compilation," a framework that reframes model adaptation as a joint prediction and decision problem. Instead of searching over candidate update programs for each new learning episode, a compiler learns from prior adaptations to predict a vector-valued counterfactual response surface over candidate programs and selects one before adaptation begins. This work suggests that adaptation search can be amortized across related learning problems, turning prior adaptation experience into a reusable basis for deciding how future learning should occur. If it holds up, it could make model adaptation more efficient and principled, benefiting practitioners who fine-tune large language models under different priorities such as acquisition, transfer, boundedness, and preservation. On Llama-3.1-8B, compiler-selected programs approach the performance of exhaustive search while outperforming global and objective-specific defaults; replication on Gemma-2-9B preserves program heterogeneity and selection headroom but shows that exploiting this headroom requires accounting for uncertainty when departing from strong defaults. ## [Do-JEPA Adds Causal Intervention Objective to Latent World Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37378) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Do-JEPA proposes a causal intervention objective for latent world models that, from a single saved simulator state, runs dynamics under an action a and a reference action a∅, then trains the model to predict the difference Δz = z^a − z^{a∅} between the two latent futures. The objective combines an effect loss, a support loss, a propagation loss, and invariance losses, and in a synthetic system with object-aligned variables it identifies the directly intervened object in 99.95% of test cases, versus a sparse action mask that sends the action to a nuisance slot in every case. Latent world models are typically trained only to predict what happens next, so their objective cannot separate what an action caused from what merely co-occurred with it. By intervening on what physically happens rather than on what the predictor can see, Do-JEPA improves causal understanding of action effects, which could benefit model-based reinforcement learning and robotics where agents must reason about the consequences of their actions. From pixels, the effect loss lowers latent effect error by 28.4% on an end-to-end LeWM model and physical effect error by 13.5% when trained and tested on natural action sequences, while on three independently generated CausalWorld benchmarks it lowers responsive effect error by about 20% under physics shifts and the latent context sensitivity of predicted effects by 66%. Trained from scratch it costs factual accuracy, but fine-tuning an existing model with it removes this cost.

**Background**: JEPA (Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture) is a self-supervised framework that learns by predicting abstract representations of inputs in a latent space instead of reconstructing raw pixels or tokens, aiming to capture what matters for understanding, planning, and reasoning. The authors derive a max-min formulation for learning this map and demonstrate it on image restoration, where one model handles multiple degradation types using a common set of clean target images. Standard optimal transport only handles a single source-to-target mapping, so multi-source settings are usually addressed by pooling sources, which aligns only at the aggregate level and can leave individual sources misaligned. This work offers a principled neural solution that could benefit image restoration, domain adaptation, and other tasks where one model must handle heterogeneous inputs without knowing their source at inference time. The method learns a shared transport map that minimizes average transport cost subject to aligning each source distribution with the prescribed target, formulated as a max-min optimization problem. The abstract is truncated and provides no quantitative results, and no community discussion is available to gauge impact.

## [LazySloth Speeds Up Long Video Comprehension with Bounded Lazy Tree Search](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37426) ⭐️ 7.0/10

LazySloth introduces a bounded LLM-based lazy tree search method that speeds up long video comprehension and retrieval by 2.9-8.3x compared to existing agentic methods through selective captioning of video portions deemed irrelevant by a VLM. It achieves similar or better accuracy across four benchmarks on Gemma 4 31B and Qwen3.6 27B, narrowing the gap to GPT-4o. It also shows open-source VLMs can approach closed-source performance when paired with smarter retrieval. Ablations show that replacing VLM scene understanding with CLIP-based retrieval costs 8.8-19.9% accuracy, while lazy tree construction matches eager construction at a fraction of the captioning cost. The approach is evaluated on two recent open-source base VLMs across four benchmarks, with the main limitation being dependence on the VLM's relevance judgments.

## [RBA Trains Readers to Abstain When Evidence Is Missing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37491) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper introduces Regime Boundary Alignment (RBA), a training method that teaches a single reader model to answer when retrieved context supports the gold answer and to abstain when that support is removed. Across three multi-hop QA datasets and three random seeds, RBA cut the unsupported-answer rate by more than 60 percentage points versus conflict-focused training while matching its supported accuracy, and on a held-out TriviaQA retrieval-miss slice it reduced unsupported answering from 100% to below 1%. This addresses a core failure mode of retrieval-augmented generation: models that keep answering even when the retrieved evidence is missing or insufficient, which is a major source of hallucination in production RAG systems. Because RBA requires no verifier, threshold, or regime label at inference time, it could be adopted as a drop-in fine-tuning recipe for building more trustworthy question-answering systems. RBA trains on matched variants of the same question and gold answer: the reader must produce the gold answer when the context supports it, including when conflicting evidence is also present, and abstain when the correct support is removed. Inference uses ordinary decoding with no extra components, and the method is evaluated on three multi-hop QA datasets plus a held-out TriviaQA retrieval-miss slice.

## [PriceCheck: Risk-Controlled Selective LLM Answering via Label-Free Checks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37493) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduced PriceCheck, a method that builds a compact family of decision rules from label-free checks (such as re-solving a problem) to decide when an LLM should abstain from answering. On mathematics tasks, the selected schedules served 76.1% of answers on average while keeping held-out selective risk below 1.5% across all 15 splits, outperforming reward models, a prompted judge, the generator's confidence, and a trained correctness classifier. This work shows that how verification checks are combined and stopped matters as much as how well a verifier ranks answers, offering a practical path to deploy LLMs with statistical guarantees on error rates among served answers. It is relevant to anyone building LLM systems that must decide when to answer automatically versus defer to human review. Each check carries a "price" — its agreement rates on correct and incorrect answers plus its cost per run — and prices fitted on a small, class-enriched labelled set compose into predictions of a schedule's coverage and cost. A calibration test then selects a schedule at a stated selective-risk target; across 118 diagnostic schedules, price-based coverage predictions achieved a rank correlation of 0.97 with observed coverage.

**Background**: Selective prediction is a paradigm in which a model may abstain from predicting when its estimated risk or uncertainty exceeds a threshold, trading coverage for lower error rates. ## [DScale Cuts Verification Padding in Block-Diffusion Speculative Decoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37532) ⭐️ 7.0/10

DScale introduces an adaptive verification method for block-diffusion speculative decoding that preserves the drafter's architecture, weights, and full draft length while adding a separate 112K-parameter predictor. On A100-40GB GPUs with Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-4B across four datasets and concurrency 8-32, it achieves geometric-mean throughput gains of 43.9% and 48.8% over DFlash, 22.2% and 37.7% over DSpark, and 24.4% and 32.0% over Domino, with lower request latency. This addresses real bottlenecks in high-concurrency LLM serving, where verification padding, rejected candidates, and incompatibility between variable prefixes and fixed-shape graphs waste compute. The lightweight predictor and graph-reuse mechanisms make it practical for production inference stacks, potentially improving throughput and latency for any deployment using block-diffusion drafters. The method uses path-aware tiles to reduce padding and dynamic verify-length (DVL) allocation to pack scored prefixes into half the native verification capacity, while fixed-address workspaces propagate changing boundaries through verification and acceptance without recapturing graphs. The 112K-parameter predictor requires neither confidence calibration nor hardware speed-curve preparation, and GPU profiling shows complete decode-step time on GSM8K drops by 30.8-52.5% versus DFlash.

**Background**: Speculative decoding accelerates LLM inference by having a small draft model propose multiple future tokens that a larger target model verifies in a single forward pass. Researchers propose MIRAGE, a topology-concealment framework that preserves the genuine communication topology of LLM-based multi-agent systems for task execution while shaping adversary-facing semantic evidence toward a carefully constructed phantom topology. MIRAGE constructs a phantom topology structurally distinct from the genuine one, materializes phantom edges as plausible semantic dependencies, and suppresses source-specific cues that could reveal genuine edges absent from the phantom topology. **Background**: Common-mode failure occurs when two or more nominally independent components fail from the same underlying cause, defeating redundancy-based safeguards. SPARQL is a query language for RDF graph data, and the case study examines a cross-catalogue integrity study of two open registers of Earth-orbiting objects.

## [AS²D decouples speculative drafting from target prefix for mobile audio understanding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37617) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (arXiv:2609.37617) proposes AS²D (Audio Speculative Speculative Decoding), a target-decoupled speculative decoding method in which an audio-conditioned drafter follows its own generation history while the target model independently verifies and corrects candidates. Implemented in MNN for Android and evaluated across four phones, seven datasets, and three tasks covering 12.2 hours of audio, AS²D improves pooled ASR throughput by 42–76% over target-only decoding, with only 5.7% of evaluation windows slower than target-only versus 58.1–63.0% for speculative baselines. Conventional speculative decoding serializes drafting and verification because the drafter must follow the target's evolving verified prefix, which limits parallelism. By showing that source-conditioned audio generation can relax this dependency, AS²D exposes substantial concurrency and could make on-demand audio understanding with large models practical on mobile devices, where latency and compute are tightly constrained. AS²D retains target-side verification and correction, so output quality is preserved while drafting and verification proceed concurrently; when no usable candidates exist, the target advances alone. Native on-demand execution with a 7B target achieves up to 78% higher throughput than target-only, and for ASR the method reaches 97.33–98.20% of a hindsight per-window oracle's pooled throughput across the evaluated drafter/budget catalog.

Deleting the same rows had little measurable effect, and the advantage grew when half the poison rows were corrected. The benefit held on a second base model and a second misaligned model organism, but the content of the replacement mattered: paraphrasing rows while keeping the bad advice showed no clear benefit, and instructing the rewriter to model a careful, harm-avoiding assistant added no measurable gain over plain corrections. A new arXiv paper (2609.37680) precisely characterizes the causal geometry of number comparison in Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, finding that the model largely relies on linear representations of numbers despite the presence of curved geometry in its representations. A new arXiv preprint (2609.37789) proves that common self-supervised learning methods can provably identify stochastic, prediction-relevant latent signals while discarding nuisance information. The authors trace this ability to two complementary principles: predictive mutual information maximization, which retains prediction-relevant information, and latent distribution matching, which constrains how that information is encoded, making the retained signal identifiable. Simulations with Gaussian predictors confirm the result, recovering the true signal up to an affine transformation even in dynamic, nuisance-laden environments. This addresses a fundamental conundrum in representation learning: since both stochastic variation in a prediction-relevant signal and true nuisance make observations partly unpredictable, it was unclear how SSL could distinguish them. The theoretical guarantee could strengthen confidence in SSL methods and guide the design of objectives that reliably separate signal from nuisance across domains such as vision, audio, and speech. The proof shows that SSL implicitly instantiates a latent-variable model with stochastic dynamics and observation-private nuisance, and that identifiability holds up to an affine transformation. The empirical confirmation is limited to simulations with Gaussian predictors, so it remains to be seen how tightly the theory transfers to deep networks and real-world data.

## [EOGP Compresses LLM Gradients for Scalable Influence Functions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37842) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces eigenbasis-corrected one-bit gradient projection (EOGP), a method that compresses stored training gradients to enable scalable influence function estimation in large language models. EOGP combines EK-FAC dimensionality reduction, PCA within the retained subspace, and one-bit quantization of the resulting coordinates, achieving competitive influence predictions with far less storage than baselines. Influence functions are a key tool for interpretability and training data attribution, but storing full gradients at LLM scale is prohibitively expensive. EOGP reduces per-example storage by up to 16x on GPT-2 and remains competitive with baselines using over 100x more storage on OLMo 2 models up to 32B parameters, making influence analysis more practical for large models. EOGP first uses EK-FAC to reduce gradient dimensionality, then applies PCA within the retained subspace to learn compression directions from training gradients, and finally applies one-bit quantization to the resulting coordinates so more coordinates fit within a fixed storage budget. The method is designed to preserve influence estimates for future queries unknown at storage time, and it is evaluated on GPT-2 and OLMo 2 SFT models from 1B to 32B parameters.

**Background**: Influence functions estimate how individual training examples affect a model's behavior by approximating the effect of removing or upweighting a training point, and they are widely used for interpretability and data attribution. Scaling them to LLMs is challenging because it requires repeated inverse-Hessian-vector products and access to training gradients, which are expensive to compute and store. EK-FAC is a second-order curvature approximation that makes inverse-Hessian-vector products tractable in large networks, while one-bit quantization is a known technique for aggressively reducing gradient storage or communication costs.

## [MIST Stress Test Shows Irrelevant Images Destabilise VLM Judges](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37863) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper introduces MIST (Misleading-Image Stress Test), a benchmark of 200 English sentences with figurative or literal readings, each paired with an aligned image, a misleading image, or no image, where guidelines require labels to be decided from text alone. Across thirteen VLM judges, an aligned image changed 20.5% of labels and a misleading one 19.4% — far above the 11.6% change caused by removing the ignore-the-image instruction — yet only 37% of differing labels moved toward the depicted sense, and human agreement stayed unchanged. The finding challenges the growing practice of substituting human annotators with VLM judges, suggesting that substitutability verdicts describe a specific evaluation configuration as much as the model itself. If merely the presence of an image — regardless of content — shifts labels, then multimodal evaluation pipelines and leaderboards may be measuring incidental conditions rather than genuine model capability. The effect was present in all thirteen judges but smaller in the seven that pass the alt-test than in the six that never do, indicating that alt-test performance correlates with but does not eliminate the instability. Notably, the aligned and misleading images produced nearly identical label-change rates for every judge, meaning the shift is driven by image presence rather than image semantics.

Researchers propose GRAFT (Gated Replacement of Answer-Failed groups with peer Trajectories), an off-policy-aware framework that replaces all-fail groups in RLVR with informative peer trajectories exchanged between heterogeneous models. Across three heterogeneous model pairs and five mathematical reasoning benchmarks, GRAFT improves both models over GRPO with the same per-model rollout budget, gaining 2.1 points on average and up to 4.5 points in model-level average performance. This addresses a core inefficiency in RLVR: when all rollouts in a group fail, GRPO receives no reward-based gradient signal, wasting compute. By exploiting the observation that heterogeneous models succeed on complementary prompts, GRAFT enables mutual learning without a designated stronger teacher, potentially improving sample efficiency for LLM reasoning training. GRAFT transfers both successful and unsuccessful peer responses with peer-computed advantages, controlling cross-model mismatch through sequence-level compatibility weighting and token-level importance ratio clipping. Stored peer trajectories preserve most of the gains, improving over GRPO by 1.8 points on average without simultaneous co-training.

An arXiv paper (2609.37916) introduces RLX, a single Rust codebase that unifies tensor compilation and distributed execution around one primitive-level, three-level intermediate representation (IR) with a transparent dispatch contract. The dispatch contract resolves each operator to native, common-IR, or rewritten lowering, and fails compilation when legalization is not possible; the system supports F16/BF16/F64/C64 and quantized INT4/INT8 flows with AMP/PTQ/QAT, and scales via tensor-/pipeline-parallel collectives over TCP and RDMA. It also extends beyond neural workloads to sparse and dense linear algebra (e.g., CSR LU/CG/matvec and LAPACK-backed factorizations) and 3D Gaussian splatting operators, and in the paper's benchmarks RLX-Metal is fastest on all-MiniLM-L6-v2 at every batch (16.6 ms at batch 32 vs. PyTorch-MPS 26.7 ms), with a top-throughput MNIST training entry of 946,487 img/s.

The paper introduces Rollout-Marginal Distillation (RMD), a two-stage method for long-horizon autoregressive (AR) video diffusion that first scores each generated chunk independently against a chunk teacher, then applies video-level Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD) to restore temporal coherence. Experiments show RMD maintains high visual quality far beyond its training horizon and outperforms video-level DMD baselines, with code and video results released at https://cjeen.github.io/RMD. Autoregressive video diffusion enables low-latency, streamable generation, but prediction errors accumulate over long rollouts, degrading visual quality. RMD addresses a specific flaw in existing video-level DMD — where joint scoring of a chunk with its imperfect past and future can favor matching artifacts over true visual quality — making it a valuable contribution for researchers working on long-form, real-time video generation. RMD retains the generated history for AR prediction but scores each chunk independently against a chunk teacher, so its quality correction is not compromised by imperfect temporal context; the subsequent video-level DMD stage compensates for the lack of temporal context in independent chunk scoring. The method is evaluated on long-horizon generation, showing quality retention well beyond the training horizon compared with video-level DMD baselines.

## [Dr. OPD Learns Token-Level Weights for On-Policy Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38025) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2609.38025) introduces Dr. OPD, a bilevel optimization framework that learns token-level weights for teacher supervision in on-policy distillation (OPD) instead of treating every teacher signal as equally important. The authors develop an efficient iterative solver that updates token weights in closed form and then takes one gradient step on the weighted OPD objective, and report that Dr. OPD improves average math performance by 9.7 points over vanilla OPD in strong-to-weak distillation, letting a smaller student surpass its larger teacher. On-policy distillation is a core technique for post-training large language models and for compressing frontier capabilities into smaller, deployable students, so improving how teacher supervision is weighted could directly benefit industrial model-compression pipelines. If the reported gains hold up, Dr. OPD suggests that not all teacher tokens deserve equal trust, which could reshape how distillation objectives are designed across math, code, and other reasoning domains. Dr. OPD is formulated as a bilevel problem where the student learns from weighted teacher supervision while the weights are chosen to maximize the student's expected reward, and under regularity conditions the authors prove the weighted update achieves higher expected reward than a vanilla OPD update. The method is evaluated on both strong-to-weak and same-size distillation for math and code, but it remains an arXiv preprint without peer review or community engagement signals, so its broader reproducibility and real-world impact are still uncertain.

Bilevel optimization is a hierarchical framework in which an outer objective is optimized subject to an inner optimization problem, and it has been applied to hyperparameter optimization, data cleaning, and meta-learning. Dr. OPD combines these two ideas by treating token weights as the outer-level variables and the student's weighted distillation update as the inner problem.

The paper provides a complete semantic and operational formalization of sequence variables as a computational domain for constraint programming, building on prior work that introduced the initial concept. It formally defines the sequence domain and its update operations, details the data structures needed to integrate sequence variables into trail-based CP solvers, and introduces consistency levels and specialized global constraints for routing problems. This work offers a more natural and elegant way to model vehicle routing problems with optional visits and insertion-based heuristics, which are awkward to express in classical successor-based CP models. The formalization includes the sequence domain definition, update operations, trail-based solver integration, consistency levels, and specialized global constraints. On held-out seeds, it improves mean capped final-round progress in Balatro from 16.83 to 20.00 and mean floor reached in Slay the Spire 2 from 18.17 to 28.83 compared with base harnesses. This work addresses a key bottleneck in long-horizon agent tasks, where each rollout is costly and feedback is delayed, making it hard for coding agents to diagnose failures. By showing that demonstrations can provide concrete guidance for diagnosis and modification, it offers a practical path to improve frozen LLM agents without retraining the underlying model. The coding agent examines human demonstrations alongside its own rollout history, extracts strategies and the conditions under which they apply, and turns them into reusable harness components. The comparison holds the evolution procedure and agent interaction budget constant, isolating the effect of demonstration guidance versus self-rollout evolution and retrieved textual knowledge augmentation.

## [KLineage Learns When to Apply GPU Kernel Optimizations by Deoptimizing Expert Code](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.28213) ⭐️ 7.0/10

KLineage introduces a method that learns the missing "when" knowledge for GPU kernel optimizations by walking expert implementations backward through validation-gated simplifications, reversing each accepted step into a reusable optimization skill. On five expert workloads across two NVIDIA architectures, these lineage-derived skills outperform recent memory-based LLM-kernel baselines in both final kernel quality and optimization efficiency under a fixed budget, and the framework also extends to Ascend NPUs. LLM-based agents increasingly generate GPU kernels but often fail to judge when an optimization is sound, because the required code state and dependencies are implicit in expert implementations. By explicitly capturing applicability conditions, KLineage could make LLM-driven kernel generation more reliable and efficient, benefiting performance engineering and AI systems work. Each learned skill records not only the optimization intent but also where it applies in code, what conditions made it valid, what effect it has, and what failures its assumptions avoid; a downstream LLM then materializes these skills on new code surfaces under the same compile/correctness/profile gate. The approach is validated on two NVIDIA architectures and shown to extend beyond NVIDIA GPUs to Ascend NPUs, with code publicly available at https://github.com/ict-agent/klineage.

**Background**: GPU kernels are the low-level programs that run on graphics processors, and optimizing them is critical for AI and scientific computing performance. KLineage addresses this by reversing expert optimizations into explicit, reusable skills that encode applicability conditions, rather than relying on forward trial-and-error rollouts.

## [REFT Diversifies RLVR Rollouts via First-Token Sampling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.28295) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2605.28295) introduces REFT (Rollout Exploration with First-Token Diversification), a lightweight modification to the RLVR pipeline that samples the first token of each response uniformly from the policy's top-N candidates and allocates rollouts evenly across those tokens. Evaluated on eight models ranging from 0.5B to 14B parameters across math reasoning and code-generation tasks under GRPO and DAPO, REFT consistently improves Pass@1, Pass@8, and Pass@64 while incurring the lowest rollout cost among competing diversification methods. Rollout diversity is a central bottleneck in RLVR training of reasoning models, and this work shows that a single, previously overlooked position—the first token—can broaden explored reasoning paths with minimal changes to the existing pipeline. Because REFT is a drop-in modification that improves accuracy at lower rollout cost, it could be widely adopted by teams training reasoning LLMs and may redirect future RLVR research toward token-level exploration strategies. The paper observes that the first-token distribution is sharply concentrated yet only weakly correlated with downstream correctness, meaning lower-probability first tokens can still yield equally accurate responses. REFT only changes the first-token sampling step, leaving the rest of the RLVR pipeline (including verifier scoring and policy updates) untouched, and it outperforms competing diversification methods at every evaluated budget.

## [Rater State Bias in RLHF Preference Data: An Audit Framework](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.16195) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2607.16195v3) identifies a structured confound in RLHF preference data called rater state shift, where annotators' preferences may drift under sustained stressful or distressing conditions, causing preference labels to encode rater state alongside judgments about response quality. The paper defines rater state shift, rater state confound, and correlated rater state bias, proposes survival level emotional authenticity as a candidate output signature, and presents five testable predictions with effect size thresholds plus an audit protocol and pilot study plan for publicly available instruction-tuned models. If rater state bias is real, it would not behave like ordinary disagreement or random label noise: it would be state-dependent, potentially shared across annotators under similar conditions, and might survive aggregation, reward modeling, and policy optimization, thereby contaminating the learned reward signal. This matters for AI alignment and for anyone building RLHF pipelines, because it suggests an under-explored source of bias that could systematically distort model behavior rather than merely adding noise. The paper argues that systematic rater state bias can survive aggregation and enter the learned reward signal, and it states five testable predictions with effect size thresholds for an initial audit, noting which predictions require proprietary data. The proposed survival level emotional authenticity signature is defined by lexical, pragmatic, discourse, and safety features whose reliability and validity remain to be demonstrated, and the authors explicitly do not infer the training history of any specific deployed model.

**Background**: RLHF (Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback) is a standard post-training pipeline in which humans compare pairs of model outputs, those pairwise preference labels are used to train a reward model, and the reward model then guides policy optimization. Preference data is therefore assumed to reflect the quality of the compared responses, and any systematic distortion in that data can propagate into the reward model and the final policy. ## [JUMP: Efficient Membership Inference on Fine-Tuned Diffusion Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.16207) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers propose JUMP (Joint Uncertainty Guided Mask Probing), an efficient membership inference attack for fine-tuned discrete diffusion language models (dLLMs) that jointly masks low-confidence positions and aggregates clipped target-reference reconstruction gaps. Across six MIMIR domains, JUMP raises mean ROC-AUC from 0.819 to 0.902 on LLaDA and from 0.851 to 0.942 on Dream, while requiring only three forward passes per example versus 32 for the prior multi-mask baseline. This work shows that fine-tuned diffusion language models leak membership information more readily than previously measured, and that a much cheaper attack can expose it, which matters for privacy auditing and safe deployment of dLLMs. It also extends the attack to a target-only setting, broadening the threat model beyond reference-based scenarios. JUMP uses the pre-fine-tuning checkpoint as a reference, selects low-confidence positions, masks them jointly, and scores all selected tokens with one query per model after mask selection. In the target-only variant, target-reference scoring is replaced by relative token preference, which compares the observed token with alternative predictions at the same masked position, achieving mean ROC-AUCs of 0.609 on LLaDA and 0.638 on Dream.

**Background**: Membership inference attacks (MIAs) determine whether a specific example was part of a model's training data, and are typically evaluated using ROC-AUC or true-positive rate at a fixed false-positive rate. Diffusion language models (dLLMs) generate text by iteratively denoising masked tokens in parallel, unlike autoregressive models that decode sequentially, which makes them attractive for efficient generation but also changes how privacy leakage can be probed. Prior MIAs on fine-tuned dLLMs aggregated reconstruction signals across many mask configurations, requiring repeated model evaluations and making attacks costly.

## [Decode-Branch Transformer Splits Prefill and Decode Computation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12385) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2608.12385v3) introduces the Decode-Branch Transformer, an architecture that keeps the primary path responsible for prompt prefill and KV cache writing while activating a separate decode branch only from the final prompt position onward. The two paths share attention, MLP, and output matrices but use separate token embeddings with lightweight coupling, and grouped decode reuses loaded weight tiles and the primary KV cache so added arithmetic does not proportionally raise memory traffic or decode latency. LLM serving cost is increasingly dominated by cumulative inference rather than one-time training, and prefill (compute-bound, parallel) and decode (memory-bound, sequential) have very different cost profiles. Decoupling them lets practitioners add learned computation to continuation prediction without inflating prefill cost or the weights read at each decode step, which could improve the efficiency-quality trade-off for large-scale serving. Across matched-token comparisons the method achieves lower validation loss across architectures and data settings, and in MoE models the primary and branch expert fan-outs become independent knobs for trading prompt cost, decode cost, and predictive quality. The paper studies two expert-allocation regimes—holding prefill or decode computation fixed—and exposes a prefill-decode-quality trade-off enabled by phase-specific expert allocation; however, it is an arXiv preprint with a truncated abstract and no community validation yet.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Sep 30, 04:00

**Background**: LLM inference has two phases: prefill, which processes the whole input prompt in parallel and is compute-bound, and decode, which generates output tokens one at a time and is memory-bound because each step must stream the model weights and the KV cache from memory. The KV cache stores key/value tensors from earlier tokens so they need not be recomputed, and conventional width or depth scaling increases both prefill and decode costs together because every added layer runs in both phases.

## [Robust POMDPs with Omega-Regular Objectives Reduced to Partially Observable Stochastic Games](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.24986) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper proves, for the first time, that reductions can be constructed in both directions between (s,a)-rectangular robust POMDPs with polytopic uncertainty sets and partially observable stochastic games (POSGs) under omega-regular objectives, establishing their semantic equivalence. This bidirectional reduction yields a range of new computational complexity results, including both upper and lower bounds, for solving RPOMDPs with different omega-regular objectives, with a corollary for RMDPs. This result connects two previously separate formal frameworks, allowing complexity and algorithmic insights from POSGs to be transferred directly to robust POMDPs, which are central to safe decision-making under model uncertainty. It is likely to influence future research in formal methods, AI planning, and verification communities working on robust decision-making under uncertainty. The equivalence holds specifically for (s,a)-rectangular RPOMDPs with polytopic uncertainty sets, a restricted but tractable uncertainty model; the reduction covers general omega-regular objectives that subsume reachability, safety, and LTL objectives. The derived complexity bounds are both upper and lower, and a corollary extends the results to robust MDPs (RMDPs).

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Sep 30, 04:00

**Background**: A POMDP is a sequential decision model where an agent cannot directly observe the true state but only receives noisy observations, and it is widely used in robotics and planning under uncertainty. Robust POMDPs (RPOMDPs) generalize this by assuming transition probabilities are not known exactly but lie within an uncertainty set, so policies must perform well against worst-case parameters. Omega-regular objectives are a broad class of temporal specifications, including reachability, safety, and linear temporal logic (LTL) formulas, commonly used in formal verification. Partially observable stochastic games (POSGs) extend POMDPs to settings with multiple interacting agents, and this paper shows that solving RPOMDPs is semantically equivalent to solving POSGs for such objectives.

## [BENEVDIAL Dataset Exposes Benevolent Bias Detection Gap in Human-Agent Dialogue](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29206) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2608.29206v2) operationalizes benevolent bias along two dimensions, tone and treatment, yielding three classes: neutral support, overt bias, and benevolent bias. The authors build BENEVDIAL, a class-balanced corpus of 362,880 multi-turn support dialogues spanning user and agent demographics, roles, and generators, and find that off-the-shelf safety detectors reliably flag overt bias but largely fail to identify benevolent bias, while prompted LLM judges improve sensitivity at the cost of misclassifying neutral support as benevolent bias. This work matters because it shows that fair monitoring of human-agent dialogue must look beyond surface cues such as hostile language to whether the agent's treatment is actually disparate, a gap that current safety tooling largely misses. As LLM-based agents increasingly mediate support conversations, undetected benevolent bias could quietly reproduce group-based inequalities while appearing warm and positive. The BENEVDIAL corpus is class-balanced and spans user and agent demographics, roles, and generators, enabling controlled evaluation across detector families. The paper reports a clear trade-off: explicit detection criteria raise LLM judges' sensitivity to benevolent bias but also increase false positives on neutral supportive statements, and this misclassification tendency is further exacerbated when demographic context is present.

**Background**: Bias in human-agent interaction is usually studied as hostile or overtly discriminatory language, but benevolent bias describes unequal treatment that hides behind a warm, positive tone, such as assuming what is best for someone and deciding on their behalf. Detecting it is hard because the surface text looks supportive rather than harmful, so standard safety classifiers trained on overt toxicity may not transfer. This paper addresses that gap by defining the phenomenon precisely, building a large controlled dataset, and benchmarking both off-the-shelf detectors and prompted LLM judges.

## [GLANCE: One-Pass Block Drafting Speeds Up VLM Speculative Decoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00355) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduced GLANCE, a one-pass block drafter for lossless speculative decoding in vision-language models, which drafts an entire block of tokens in a single forward pass over the target model's already fused vision-language states. In a production engine at a fixed round budget, GLANCE decodes up to 3.05x faster than autoregressive decoding and outperforms the production EAGLE3-VL head by about 11% on grounded tasks. Speculative decoding is a key latency-reduction technique for large models, but on VLMs the autoregressive drafter must stay small and cannot afford to attend to the image at every step, weakening drafts exactly where the image matters most. GLANCE breaks this self-reinforcing cycle without modifying the target VLM, potentially making multimodal inference substantially faster for researchers and practitioners deploying VLMs. GLANCE uses a block-diffusion head to draft a whole block in one forward pass, reading the multimodal context once regardless of draft depth, while the target verifies a wide candidate tree in one pass and commits exactly its greedy output, preserving losslessness. The authors also present an entropy law explaining when drafting pays off, predicting the longest accepted blocks on grounded tasks where the target's next-token entropy is lowest; code is available at https://github.com/js-lee-AI/GLANCE.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Sep 30, 04:00

**Background**: Speculative decoding accelerates autoregressive generation by having a smaller draft model propose multiple candidate tokens that a larger target model verifies in a single forward pass, preserving the target's output distribution while cutting latency. Vision-language models jointly process images and text, extending text-only LLMs to multimodal tasks such as visual question answering and image captioning. Block diffusion generates text by denoising whole blocks of tokens in parallel rather than one token at a time, which GLANCE adapts into a drafting head for VLM decoding.

## [SRPO: Setwise Relative Policy Optimization for Multi-Agent Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.08452) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.08452v2) proposes Setwise Relative Policy Optimization (SRPO), a policy optimization framework for multi-agent LLM systems that updates policies at the level of a team decision rather than per individual response or per whole trajectory. SRPO defines an "active set" — the minimal set of newly sampled outputs consumed by one state transition — and combines member log-ratios into a single cardinality-normalized set ratio, assigns one shared relative advantage, and clips the set once. Existing multi-agent RL methods either treat each agent response as an independent update or treat an entire trajectory as one training example, which can assign the same final outcome to outputs that played different roles in different team decisions and thus produce misleading policy updates. By tying each update to the decision that produced the next state, SRPO could improve credit assignment and training stability for multi-agent LLM systems used in mathematical reasoning and multi-turn search. A singleton active set corresponds to division of labor, while a larger set corresponds to joint co-evolution, and the set composition can change across decisions; SRPO normalizes the combined policy change by set size and clips it once. Experiments on mathematical reasoning and multi-turn search show effectiveness, and ablation studies analyze the normalization choice and training behavior under changing active-set sizes.

**Background**: Multi-agent systems coordinate multiple LLM agents that divide roles and refine candidate solutions, enabling complex reasoning and tool use. Reinforcement learning for such systems typically relies on policy optimization methods like PPO, which compute advantages and clip policy ratios to stabilize updates. SRPO extends this idea by defining the unit of update as the set of outputs jointly consumed by a single state transition, rather than an individual response or a full trajectory.

## [AgentGrad: Intervention-Guided Prompt Optimization for Multi-Agent LLM Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.08572) ⭐️ 7.0/10

AgentGrad is a new prompt optimization framework for LLM-based multi-agent systems that replaces existing textual gradient methods with sequential intervention and semantic textual gradient abstraction. It identifies the specific agent responsible for each failure by modifying one agent's behavior at a time, then uses that agent's modified output as agent-level supervision to extract fine-grained gradients. Experiments show state-of-the-art results on five MAS benchmarks while cutting wall-clock optimization time by 2.5x and cost by 21.8% on average versus the next-best baselines. Prompt design is the primary lever for improving multi-agent systems when workflow topology is fixed by expert design, safety, or compliance constraints, so better optimization methods directly translate into more capable and cheaper agentic AI deployments. By fixing the gradient extraction and aggregation stages, AgentGrad offers a more generalizable and efficient way to tune each agent's prompt, which should interest researchers and practitioners building LLM agent pipelines. The method's two core innovations are sequential intervention, which verifies that modifying a chosen agent actually resolves the failure before extracting a gradient, and semantic textual gradient abstraction, which clusters semantically similar gradients so unrelated failure modes are not mixed together. The reported gains are measured across five MAS benchmarks, though the paper is an arXiv preprint and the abstract does not detail benchmark composition or model choices.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Sep 30, 04:00

**Background**: Textual gradient methods are a leading paradigm for automatic prompt optimization: instead of numeric gradients, an LLM produces natural-language feedback that describes how a prompt should change, analogous to gradient descent in text space. In multi-agent systems, several specialized LLM agents each carry their own system prompt and collaborate through a fixed workflow, so deciding which agent's prompt to edit and how to combine feedback from many failures is a central challenge. Prior work selected target prompts without verifying that the edit would fix the failure and randomly grouped gradients, which often mixed unrelated failure modes and hurt generalization.

A new arXiv paper (2609.13463v2) proposes Continual Search, an iterative framework that repeatedly nudges an LLM judge across successive turns to keep hunting for unresolved diagnostic evidence instead of settling on a one-shot diagnosis. The authors also introduce MegaRCA-Mix, a benchmark of 50 human-annotated failure trials for long-horizon, execution-heavy tasks, and report that Continual Search raises Opus-4.8's F1 on it by 29%, from 0.471 to 0.608. As AI agents take on longer tasks and generate massive execution logs, reliable automated root-cause attribution becomes a bottleneck for deployment, since outcome-level failure signals alone give little guidance on where to intervene. The finding that effective search can let lower-tier models surpass higher-tier ones within the same family suggests diagnostic strategy may matter more than raw model scale for agent reliability. The core problem is that relevant evidence in long traces is sparse, distributed across distant actions, and disconnected from the visible failure, so one-shot LLM judges tend to lock onto a plausible diagnosis early and leave critical evidence unexamined. Evaluation spans four existing RCA benchmarks plus the new MegaRCA-Mix, and improvements are reported consistently across multiple benchmark suites and model families.

A new arXiv paper (2609.13747v2) shows that in continuous latent reasoning, keeping cumulative latent states with equal weights, rather than only frontier-step states, allows a Transformer to guide attention correctly at a smaller hidden width and preserve more intermediate reasoning steps. Experiments with two-layer and GPT-2 Transformers reproduce this predicted width advantage and show unequal weights fail first on the least-weighted states. ## [TranSGrid Benchmark Exposes Gaps in Systematic Generalization Tests](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19212) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper introduces TranSGrid, a reasoning-centered testbed that unifies deductive, inductive, and abductive reasoning within a single task to probe what existing systematic generalization benchmarks overlook. Testing seven Transformer models on 4,800 TranSGrid instances, the largest model solved 79.6% of a held-out test set but only 55.3% of TranSGrid and 15.8% of the hardest subset. The findings suggest that widely used systematic generalization benchmarks may overstate model capabilities because they simplify away inductive and abductive reasoning demands. This could push the AI/ML community toward more comprehensive benchmark design and a more realistic assessment of Transformer reasoning limits. The performance gap persists even within the training length range, showing that productivity alone is insufficient to evaluate systematic generalization. When the authors reintroduced either simplification—limiting interactions among action effects (reducing inductive demand) or making goals action-explicit (reducing abductive demand)—solve rates returned to roughly the held-out test set level, indicating that either simplification alone collapses TranSGrid into an ordinary test set.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Sep 30, 04:00

**Background**: Systematic generalization is the ability to solve novel problems by recombining known atomic elements, and it is considered central to human intelligence but hard to study rigorously. Existing studies often rely on simplifications such as elemental composition, productivity-based tests, and action-explicit goals, which make the capability easier to measure but may omit essential aspects. Deductive reasoning derives certain conclusions from premises, inductive reasoning generalizes rules from examples, and abductive reasoning infers plausible explanations for observations—three complementary forms of reasoning that TranSGrid combines.

Open-weight models are LLMs whose parameters are publicly released, allowing anyone to run them locally, while open-source agentic frameworks such as LangGraph, CrewAI, and SmolAgents let developers build autonomous multi-step agents on top of them. The authors derive a minimum-overlap formula showing ρ ≥ 0.25 suffices for non-borderline judges, and propose a zero-cost stratified allocation scheme that halves false-rejection rates relative to random sampling. As LLM-as-a-judge becomes the default way to scale evaluation of generative AI systems, this work shows that annotation budget allocation—not just judge quality—can silently invalidate deployment decisions, affecting anyone who uses human agreement to certify a judge before shipping it. The actionable thresholds and allocation scheme offer immediate practical guidance for evaluation teams operating under tight annotation budgets. The minimum-overlap formula indicates ρ ≥ 0.25 is sufficient for non-borderline judges, but borderline cases remain fundamentally hard to validate regardless of overlap. The stratified allocation scheme is zero-cost and only halves false-rejection rates when the strata are informative; validation covered 10 LLM judges across four evaluation matrices spanning visual assessment, causal reasoning, and summarization.

Existing memory benchmarks focus on retention and retrieval, while multi-agent benchmarks emphasize coordination and end-to-end completion, leaving topology-conditioned memory boundaries largely unmeasured. The paper introduces Decision-Sufficient State Representations (DSSR), a framework that decomposes the reader's loss in LLM agent state representations into budget loss and write-time regret, and trains the writer to minimize the latter. In TextWorld cooking games, a 128-token state holding the necessary facts wins nearly every game, while prompted language-model writers win at most 17%, with almost all loss attributed to write-time regret that grows with the delay before a fact is needed. This work provides a principled way to measure and reduce information loss in LLM agent memory management, which is critical for long-horizon tasks where agents must retain relevant facts over many steps. The finding that training the writer from the reader's own loss yields significant gains (+7.0 points) suggests a practical path to improving agent performance without increasing context length. The forward-rolled score used by DSSR predicts game outcomes with a correlation of ρ = 0.48, whereas scoring a candidate as a fixed context (as hindsight methods do) yields ρ ≤ 0.07. Training adds +7.0 [+1.9, +12.2] points of success when facts are needed soon, but the gain shrinks as delay grows and is significant only at the shortest delay, a limit traced to credit assignment across later rewrites.

The method randomly drops a portion of the student's reasoning trajectory during training while the teacher still observes the full trajectory, and it consistently improves average performance across teacher-student model pairs of different scales and six mathematical reasoning benchmarks, plus two out-of-domain benchmarks. PISA arises in two common cases: high student confidence can weaken corrective gradients even when the teacher disagrees, and tokens that depend on earlier reasoning can receive learning signals as weak as those for simple local continuations. Trajectory Dropout strengthens corrections for overconfident predictions and adds supervision at prefix-sensitive positions, but the paper's evaluation is limited to mathematical reasoning and two out-of-domain benchmarks rather than a broad task suite.

A new arXiv preprint (2504.14015v2) introduces "causal pieces," a concept inspired by "linear pieces" in artificial neural networks, to analyse feedforward spiking neural networks (SNNs) with single-spike coding. The authors prove that within each causal piece, output spike times of current-based leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) neurons with large membrane time constants are locally Lipschitz continuous with respect to inputs and parameters, and they derive a lower bound on approximation error that depends on the number of causal pieces. The theoretical results apply to feedforward SNNs with single-spike coding and current-based LIF neurons with large membrane time constants, and hold for networks with both excitatory and inhibitory synapses. Empirically, the authors find that parameter initialisations yielding more causal pieces on the training set strongly correlate with training success on benchmarks including Yin-Yang, Fashion-MNIST, and EuroSAT, and simulations with standard single-spike LIF neurons suggest the findings extend beyond the theoretically analysed regime.

In a controlled grid of three schema generators crossed with six query models, the schema source accounts for 79.5% of exact match (EM) variance versus only 1.6% for the query model, and the best configuration (Gemini 2.5 Flash schemas + Gemini-2.0-Flash queries) reaches 80.39 EM, 11.5 points above the strongest reported baseline of 68.89 EM. The finding that schema design dominates query model choice by a wide margin suggests that research and engineering effort in LLM-based QA over structured data should prioritize knowledge representation and schema construction rather than solely scaling or swapping query models. This has implications for text-to-SQL systems, LLM-based data integration pipelines, and any application that reasons over evolving semi-structured tables such as Wikipedia infoboxes. Replacing the schema and its derived prompt scaffolding shifts EM by 14.7 to 20.0 points, whereas replacing the query model under a fixed schema shifts it by only 4.4 to 12.1 points; the authors distill three candidate schema-design principles—balanced normalization, semantic naming, and consistent temporal anchoring—explicitly framed as correlational hypotheses rather than proven causal rules. An open-weights configuration also reaches 79.52 EM, close to the best proprietary setup.

A new arXiv paper (2601.22736v3) introduces an uncertainty-aware causal decision-making framework that decomposes causal effect bounds into two parts: the range of values that could be eliminated by collecting more samples, and the range that, with high probability, cannot be eliminated by more observational data. The authors show this partitioning can be obtained by solving max-min and min-max optimization problems, and they use neural causal models to approximately recover the decomposition in practice. By separating these sources, the framework can help practitioners decide when to resort to non-observational studies or measure unmeasured confounders, which is relevant to AI/ML and statistics communities working on reliable decision making from observational data. The framework distinguishes the range of causal effect values that might be eliminated by more samples from those that, with high probability, cannot be eliminated, using max-min and min-max optimization and neural causal models for approximation. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets show the algorithm can determine when collecting more samples will not help identify the best action.

The framework constructs a fixed-length latent message through several iterations of sequential visual observation, where each step processes a localized crop and refines the existing token sequence. The encoder and decoder share a single transformer and are trained end-to-end using flow-matching reconstruction plus semantic representation-alignment objectives, with experiments indicating that semantic alignment helps ground representations while sequential tokenization drives object-centric structure.

## [PAC-CF: Calibrating Irreversible Pruning in LLM-Guided Search](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.14345) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces PAC-CF (Probably Approximately Correct Conformal Filtering), a method that calibrates pruning thresholds in LLM-guided search using conformal prediction to provide finite-sample guarantees for retaining useful branches under evaluator bias. PAC-CF formulates elimination as an (ε,δ)-PAC problem under bounded evaluator bias and calibrates a score-gap threshold on held-out tasks using post-search verifier labels. Conditional on exchangeable native-controller tasks with nonempty protected exposure, conformal calibration gives finite-sample coverage for retaining at least one verifier-defined valid continuation at every protected frontier; at deployment, only candidates whose gap exceeds the frozen threshold are removed.

## [SymDrift: One-Shot Generative Modeling under Symmetries](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.06140) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduce SymDrift, a framework that makes the drifting field itself symmetry-aware for one-shot generative modeling of physical systems. It proposes two complementary strategies: a symmetrized drift in coordinate space based on optimal alignment, and a G-invariant embedding that removes symmetry ambiguity by construction. SymDrift enables one-shot inference that reduces computational overhead by up to 40x compared to existing baselines, making it promising for high-throughput applications such as virtual drug screening and large-scale reaction network exploration. It addresses a fundamental symmetry-specific limitation of drifting models, which previously could not match the drifting field obtained from symmetrized target distributions without expensive symmetrization. The paper shows that an equivariant generator does not generally produce the same drifting field as the one obtained from the symmetrized target distribution, and that addressing this would require expensive symmetrization of the empirical distribution. Empirically, SymDrift outperforms existing one-shot methods on standard benchmarks for conformer and transition state generation, while remaining competitive with significantly more expensive multi-step approaches.

A new arXiv preprint (2605.08144v2) introduces NoiseRater, a network trained via bilevel optimization that scores individual Gaussian noise instances conditioned on the data sample and timestep, then uses those scores to reweight the diffusion loss. Experiments show that top-scored noise improves performance over i.i.d. sampling while bottom-scored noise degrades it, and that this instance-level selection is complementary to existing timestep scheduling and weighting schemes. Diffusion training has long treated the timestep as the main axis of design, but this work shows that which specific noise realization is drawn at a given timestep also matters, opening a new lever for improving training efficiency. If validated, instance-level noise valuation could reduce compute needed to reach a given quality and influence how future diffusion training pipelines sample noise. The rater is learned through bilevel optimization: its scores reweight the diffusion loss in the inner loop, and the rater itself is updated in the outer loop to reduce validation loss after inner-loop updates. The paper reports that noise utility is contextual—depending jointly on the image, class, and timestep—and that gains largely persist when combined with existing scheduling and weighting methods; code is released at github.com/JoeZhao527/Noise-Rater.

## [PRISM: A Geometric Risk Bound for Decomposing LLM Drift](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.11608) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2605.11608v2) introduces PRISM, a closed-form upper bound on the cross-entropy risk gap between a target LLM and its proxy variant, derived from the fact that the prediction head is linear and by comparing feature sets through an orthogonal map. The bound provably splits into three measurable axes—scale, shape, and head—each naming a distinct failure mode and intervention point, and it ranks quantized and fine-tuned variants from a single forward pass with mean Spearman above 0.8 across two model families and five benchmarks. Model releases increasingly ship dozens of post-training variants (quantized, LoRA-adapted, distilled), yet existing checks either report benchmark degradation or feature similarity without linking the two. PRISM bridges that gap with a single diagnostic that tells practitioners which axis is failing and where to intervene, and its differentiable shape term doubles as a regularizer that curbs catastrophic forgetting better than experience replay. The analysis shows low-bit quantization distorts the shape term and, at the lowest bit-widths, inflates activation scale, while quantizing the output embedding inflates the head term that dominates the bound at high bit-widths. Notably, only eight reference sequences are enough to recover the variant ranking that the raw risk gap itself needs over a hundred sequences to achieve.

Existing evaluation tools fall into two camps—benchmark and likelihood screens that detect degradation, and representation similarity metrics such as CKA and SVCCA that describe how internal features shifted—but nothing formally connects feature movement to loss change.
