## [Missing Old Logits Break Off-Policy Correction in Asynchronous Agentic RL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.12070) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2605.12070v3) identifies the 'missing-old-logit' problem in asynchronous reinforcement learning for LLM agents, where delayed updates and partial rollouts lose the historical training-side logits needed for PPO-style off-policy correction. The authors propose three exact old-logit acquisition strategies—snapshot-based version tracking, a dedicated old-logit model, and synchronization via partial rollout interruption—and adopt a revised PPO-EWMA method that yields significant gains in training speed and optimization performance. Asynchronous RL is becoming the dominant paradigm for training LLM agents because it decouples sample generation from policy optimization and improves rollout throughput, but the missing-old-logit problem silently breaks the intended semantics of decoupled off-policy correction. This work gives practitioners a concrete diagnosis and repair toolkit, which matters for anyone building distributed RLHF or agentic RL systems where clipping and masking thresholds interact undesirably. The paper shows that the total importance ratio should ideally decompose into a training–inference discrepancy term (aligning inference-side and training-side distributions at the same behavior-policy version) and a policy-staleness term (constraining the update from the historical policy to the current policy). When old logits are lost, these two factors become entangled, and the authors compare the system trade-offs of exact acquisition strategies versus approximate correction that avoids extra system overhead.

**Background**: PPO (Proximal Policy Optimization) is a widely used reinforcement learning algorithm that stabilizes updates by clipping the importance sampling ratio between the behavior policy and the target policy. In RLHF and agentic RL for LLMs, generating rollouts dominates cost, so systems often run asynchronously—generating samples with an older policy version while training on a newer one—which introduces data staleness and requires off-policy correction. Old logits are the historical training-side log-probabilities needed to compute that correction correctly; when asynchronous pipelines with delayed updates and partial rollouts discard them, the correction becomes semantically wrong.

## [Scalable Heterogeneous Graph Foundation Models for Power Flow](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.23194) ⭐️ 7.0/10

This paper introduces a large-scale heterogeneous graph-learning workflow built on HydraGNN for data-driven optimal power flow (OPF) surrogate modeling and graph foundation-model (GFM) development. Using roughly three million heterogeneous graphs from ten PGLib-OPF cases spanning 14 to 13,659 buses, the authors compared six heterogeneous GNN families under a common hyperparameter optimization campaign on the Frontier supercomputer, yielding two compact HeteroSAGE and HeteroHEAT models (~1.6-1.7 million parameters) with the lowest observed validation MSE. Fast and reliable OPF approximation is critical for power system operation, but heterogeneous OPF graph models have typically been evaluated with architecture-specific implementations or limited training corpora. This work provides a common, scalable implementation for distributed preprocessing, multi-GPU training, HPO, and downstream adaptation, which could accelerate the adoption of graph foundation models in smart grid applications. Strong and weak scaling tests using up to 1,024 Frontier nodes showed that 256 nodes (1,024 AMD MI250X GPUs) provides the best time-to-solution balance for the measured workload. Two downstream tasks on the IEEE 118-bus case—classification of nominal versus extreme-overload conditions and N-1 single-component-outage regression for bus voltage magnitude and phase angle—showed that partial fine-tuning offers the strongest balance between predictive performance and computational cost.

**Background**: Optimal power flow (OPF) is a fundamental optimization problem in power system operation that determines the best operating point while satisfying physical and security constraints; the AC version is nonlinear and non-convex, making fast approximation valuable. PGLib-OPF is an open-access benchmark library of AC OPF test cases maintained by an IEEE PES task force, widely used to compare OPF algorithms. HydraGNN is a distributed PyTorch framework for multi-headed graph convolutional neural networks that supports heterogeneous power-grid graphs, and graph foundation models aim to pretrain on large graph corpora and adapt to downstream tasks, analogous to foundation models in NLP and vision.

## [AMS KV Compression Prevents Region Wipe-out in Long-Context LLM Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.23200) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces Adaptive Mass-Segmented (AMS) KV Compression, a region-aware quota allocation framework that partitions the KV cache based on the spatial distribution of attention mass, ensuring structurally vital reasoning segments receive guaranteed memory quotas. It incorporates an EMA-based smoothing mechanism to stabilize segment boundaries during iterative decoding and is designed as a plug-and-play layer compatible with existing scorers like TOVA, Expected Attention, KeyDiff, R-KV, and TriAttention, as well as paged-KV serving frameworks such as vLLM. This work addresses a specific failure mode called Region Wipe-out, where global Top-k eviction severely removes contiguous reasoning blocks and derails logical coherence in long-context tasks. By shifting from token-level competition to region-aware quota allocation, AMS could improve the reliability and performance of long-context LLM inference across mathematical reasoning, code completion, open-domain QA, and sparse retrieval, benefiting researchers and engineers deploying efficient long-context models. AMS adaptively partitions the KV cache and uses an EMA-based smoothing mechanism to prevent jitter in segment boundaries during iterative decoding. It is orthogonal to existing scorers and system-compatible with modern paged-KV serving frameworks like vLLM, supporting efficient gather-and-compact KV execution without introducing additional steady-state attention overhead.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Sep 30, 04:00

**Background**: The Key-Value (KV) cache stores key and value states of previously generated tokens to avoid recomputation during autoregressive generation, but its size grows linearly with sequence length, creating a memory bottleneck for long-context LLM inference. Existing KV compression methods typically evict tokens based on importance scores using global Top-k selection, which can inadvertently remove contiguous reasoning blocks. AMS addresses this by allocating memory quotas based on attention mass distribution across regions, ensuring that structurally important segments are preserved.

## [AdvantageFlow: Regularized Advantage-Weighted RL for Flow Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.26013) ⭐️ 7.0/10

AdvantageFlow introduces a forward-process reinforcement learning algorithm for rectified flow models that minimizes an advantage-weighted prediction loss regularized by the rollout policy, convexifying the objective and stabilizing optimization. The authors validate it on text-to-image generation with Stable Diffusion 3.5 Medium and FLUX.1, comparing against both forward- and reverse-process RL algorithms. Reinforcement learning fine-tuning has become a key way to align generative models with human preferences, but applying it to rectified flow models has been challenging due to unstable optimization. A stable, principled RL objective for flow models could make preference-based fine-tuning more accessible for state-of-the-art text-to-image systems. The method frames its objective as fitting a local reward-improving target distribution, with rollout regularization arising as a variance reduction step. Evaluation is limited to text-to-image generation on two models, so generalization to other domains or flow architectures remains to be shown.

**Background**: Rectified flow models are neural ODE-based generative models that learn transport mappings by aligning data along nearly straight paths between distributions, offering an alternative to diffusion models. Advantage-weighted regression is an off-policy RL technique that weights data by advantage values during policy optimization. AdvantageFlow combines these ideas to bring stable RL fine-tuning to rectified flow models such as Stable Diffusion 3.5 Medium and FLUX.1.

A new arXiv paper (2605.30152v2) introduces a temporal-graph-learning (TGL) controller that jointly decides when a proactive assistant should intervene and which context to use, replacing repeated LLM inference. TGL runs at 11.13 ms per event on a GPU server, achieving the highest AUC among nine trigger architectures and roughly 4–7× trigger-stage speedups over two single-forward LLM triggers, while improving downstream F1 by a mean of 16.7 points across 14 backbones. Proactive assistants currently pay LLM inference costs even when they stay silent, which is wasteful and blocks on-device deployment. Showing that a small graph model can handle both triggering and context selection could make always-on proactive agents far cheaper and practical to run locally, reshaping how agent architectures are designed. The key insight is that user activity has a native graph structure: events involve persistent entities whose recurrence connects interactions over time, so triggering and context selection map directly to predictions on event and entity nodes. TGL also runs at 13.99 ms on a consumer laptop with an approximately 220 MiB BF16 resident footprint, enabling on-device deployment.

## [Entropy-Cut Metropolis-Hastings Improves Sampling-Based Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.30327) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces Entropy-Cut Metropolis-Hastings, a new sampler that identifies key decision points in a reasoning trace using the base model's next-token entropy and resamples from those positions instead of uniformly random cuts. It consistently outperforms baselines and RL-trained models on MATH500, HumanEval, GPQA Diamond, and AIME26, including best-of-N at the same token budget. This work makes training-free reasoning via power distribution sampling more practical by focusing computational effort on consequential decisions, potentially reducing the need for expensive RL post-training. It could significantly impact how reasoning models are deployed, especially in resource-constrained settings. The method uses entropy jumps as a proxy for decision points and provably scales mixing time with the number of decisions rather than the number of tokens, which can be much larger. Empirical results show consistent improvements across multiple benchmarks without additional training or verifiers.

## [RobotValues Benchmark Tests Household Robots in Value-Conflict Scenarios](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.03312) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduced RobotValues, a benchmark of 8K value-conflict scenarios where household robots must choose among actions prioritizing different human values such as autonomy, efficiency, privacy, and social appropriateness. Evaluating 10 vision-language models (VLMs) used in robotics, they found models exhibit default value preferences—favoring safety and accommodation while underselecting privacy-prioritizing actions—and fail to override these defaults 80% of the time on average when prompted to prioritize conflicting values. This work highlights a critical gap in robot evaluation: current benchmarks focus on task completion or safety, but real domestic environments require robots to navigate conflicting human values. The findings suggest that deploying household robots without value-alignment evaluation could lead to decisions that systematically neglect certain values like privacy, affecting users and shaping the broader field of human-robot interaction and AI value alignment. The benchmark was constructed through LLM-assisted scenario generation, stakeholder-grounded value extraction, image generation, and automatic quality control, with each instance containing a realistic synthetic household image and multiple plausible robot actions. The abstract notes the benchmark contains 8K scenarios, though search results mention a 10K version, and the evaluation focused on 10 VLMs used in robotics.

The paper introduces CHERRL, a Controllable Hacking Environment for Rubric-based RL that injects known biases into an LLM-as-a-Judge to reliably reproduce reward hacking, observe reward divergence, and pinpoint hacking onset. It also presents an agentic detection system (RHDA) that automatically identifies hacking onset from training logs, with code and environment released at github.com/THUAIS-Lab/CHERRL. Reward hacking in rubric-based RL is subtle and entangled with multiple judge biases, making it hard to analyze or mitigate in real training runs; a controllable testbed gives alignment and RL researchers a clean way to study mechanisms and defenses. This matters as LLM-as-a-Judge scoring becomes a standard reward source for open-ended tasks, where undetected hacking can produce unsafe or ineffective policies. CHERRL works by injecting known biases into the judge so that hacking can be reproduced stably, and the authors analyze different judge biases along two axes: discoverability and exploitability. The RHDA detection agent is evaluated against ground-truth hacking onsets derived from training logs, and the environment is publicly released for reuse.

## [ActiveSAM Accelerates Open-Vocabulary Segmentation with Frozen SAM 3](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.16996) ⭐️ 7.0/10

ActiveSAM is a training-free inference framework that turns the frozen SAM 3 backbone into an active-vocabulary segmenter by first estimating an image-conditioned active set of class prompts from a low-resolution presence preview, then running full-resolution mask prediction only on retained prompts. Across eight OVSS benchmarks it outperforms the state-of-the-art SegEarth-OV3 by +2.1 mIoU on average while achieving 7.3-12.2x speedups on large-vocabulary datasets. Open-vocabulary semantic segmentation with SAM 3 is bottlenecked by running full-resolution decoding over the entire dataset vocabulary, even though each image contains only a few active classes. ActiveSAM removes this inefficiency without any weight updates, oracle labels, or per-dataset tuning, making it practical for noisy-input domains such as autonomous driving and embodied AI. The framework canonicalizes and expands class prompts, uses evidence-proportional grounding to select the active set, applies bucketed prompt multiplexing with the frozen SAM 3 decoder, and resolves overlapping concept responses via exclusive concept decoding that compares each pixel's joint score vector against class signatures estimated once per vocabulary from unlabeled images. It also achieves the highest accuracy under image corruptions simulating real-world distribution shift.

**Background**: SAM 3 (Segment Anything Model 3) is Meta's unified foundation model for promptable concept segmentation, which detects, segments, and tracks objects using text or visual prompts such as noun phrases or image exemplars. Open-vocabulary semantic segmentation (OVSS) aims to segment an image into semantic regions according to text descriptions, including classes not seen during training. Training-free inference frameworks reuse frozen pretrained models without updating weights, offering a practical path to reducing inference cost.

## [Skill-MAS Evolves Meta-Skill to Bridge Inference and Training Multi-Agent Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18837) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Skill-MAS proposes a novel third path for automatic multi-agent system (MAS) generation that decouples experience retention from parametric updates by treating high-level orchestration capability as an evolvable Meta-Skill. It refines this Meta-Skill through a closed optimization loop combining Multi-Trajectory Rollout and Selective Reflection, and experiments across four complex benchmarks and four distinct LLMs show performance gains with a favorable cost-performance trade-off. This addresses a key dilemma in LLM-based MAS generation: inference-time systems repeat identical searches without learning, while training-time systems are limited by smaller models and hard to scale to frontier LLMs. By enabling experience retention without gradient updates, Skill-MAS could make automatic MAS generation more practical and scalable for complex tasks. The closed optimization loop consists of Multi-Trajectory Rollout, which samples a behavioral distribution for each task under the current Meta-Skill, and Selective Reflection, which adaptively selects priority tasks and applies hierarchical contrastive analysis to distill systemic experience into generalizable, strategy-level principles. The evolved Meta-Skills are reported to be highly robust and transferable across unseen tasks and different LLMs.

Researchers introduced Temporal Self-Imitation Learning (TSIL), a reinforcement learning framework that mines temporally efficient successful trajectories generated during training and converts them into reusable supervision. Across 30 long-horizon tasks spanning robot manipulation and interactive navigation, TSIL consistently improved task success rates, learning efficiency, behavioral efficiency, and robustness to unstable training conditions. This is relevant to AI/ML researchers working on robotics and long-horizon decision-making, where sample efficiency remains a major bottleneck. TSIL progressively refines learning using configuration-conditioned adaptive temporal targets derived from fast successful trajectories, while preserving and replaying efficient behaviors through efficiency-weighted self-imitation learning. ## [Distilled RL Merges Teacher Supervision into LLM Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.17247) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper proposes Distilled Reinforcement Learning (Distilled RL), a post-training method that integrates teacher supervision directly into the RL objective to provide fine-grained guidance instead of relying on coarse outcome rewards. It introduces three components — reverse importance sampling with clipping, negative sample reset, and sequence-level geometric normalization — and reports substantial gains over standard RL and on-policy distillation (OPD) in both within-family and cross-family distillation settings, with code released on GitHub. LLM post-training currently splits between RL, which struggles with credit assignment and acquiring new knowledge, and OPD, which is largely confined to within-family distillation. By selectively transferring teacher knowledge rather than unconditionally imitating logits, Distilled RL could broaden cross-family distillation and improve how reasoning and alignment capabilities are transferred to smaller or differently-sourced models. The method's three components — reverse importance sampling with clipping, negative sample reset, and sequence-level geometric normalization — are designed to avoid unconditional imitation of teacher logits while still extracting useful guidance. A concise case study shows the student acquiring knowledge previously unavailable to it, and experiments measure improvements on both pass@1 and pass@k.

**Background**: Post-training adapts a pretrained LLM to improve reasoning, adaptation, and alignment. Reinforcement learning typically uses only a final outcome reward, making it hard to know which intermediate tokens deserve credit, while on-policy distillation trains the student on its own generated sequences using token-level log-probabilities from a teacher, usually via KL divergence. KL-divergence-based imitation tends to work well only when teacher and student are similar, which is why OPD is often limited to within-family distillation.

## [LOCKS: Page-Local Low-Rank Key Summaries for Efficient Long-Context Decoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24555) ⭐️ 7.0/10

LOCKS introduces a method that stores a rank-r spectral summary per page of attention keys, reconstructs within-page logits, and selects pages by log-sum-exp mass without reading candidate keys or values. It stays within about one point of FullKV on LongBench-v1, matches FullKV aggregate quality beyond 100K context at a 2048-token budget while attending about 2% of tokens, and reduces complete decode-step time by 1.8x at 512K context on GH200. Long-context LLM serving is bottlenecked by the KV cache, which is read at every decode step, so reducing these reads without sacrificing quality directly improves throughput and latency. LOCKS could influence future KV cache compression research and enable larger batches or longer contexts on existing hardware. Across ranks 2-8, the summaries use only 4-10% of full-KV bytes, and with full KV offloaded to Grace memory, LOCKS reaches 3.82-4.22x the faster dense backend's aggregate throughput at 64K-256K by serving larger batches. The method tracks the read-every-key exact-LSE oracle on RULER down to the smallest budgets and retains quality furthest under tight budgets on AIME26 and MATH-500.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Sep 30, 04:00

**Background**: The KV cache stores key and value tensors for all previous tokens so the model can attend to them during generation, but its size grows with context length and it must be read at every decode step, making it a major bottleneck for long-context serving. Low-rank approximation of attention keys has been explored in prior work such as Linformer and Loki, while log-sum-exp is a smooth approximation of the maximum often used for attention selection. LOCKS combines these ideas by fitting a low-rank basis per page rather than sharing one projection across all pages.

## [LAIP unlocks spatial grounding in audio-visual retrieval models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24786) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces LAIP (Localization via Audio-Informed Pooling), a framework that replaces the standard global pooling module in large audio-visual retrieval models with a lightweight Audio-informed Spatial Pooling (AiSP) that queries intermediate visual tokens using frame-aligned audio. This recovers fine-grained spatial information otherwise discarded by the retrieval pipeline, achieving state-of-the-art results on AVSBench and AVATAR, nearly doubling AVATAR performance with average CIoU improving from 13.21 to 26.22. This work shows that large-scale audio-visual retrieval models, trained only for global alignment, already encode latent spatial structure that can be exploited for sound source localization without dense pixel-level annotations. It offers a cheap, plug-in way to add spatial grounding to existing retrieval backbones, which could benefit weakly supervised audio-visual localization research and applications. The key insight is that spatial detail is progressively lost in the upper layers of retrieval backbones due to global pooling, while intermediate visual tokens retain highly structured spatial information; the largest gains are observed for PE-AV, a stack with underlying temporal aggregation. The method operates under weak supervision, avoiding costly dense spatial annotations, and is evaluated on the AVSBench and AVATAR benchmarks.

## [Domain Adaptation Can Undermine Trustworthiness of Small Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00042) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2608.00042v2) presents the first systematic cross-domain, cross-architecture empirical study of how domain adaptation affects the trustworthiness of small language models, testing three architectures (TinyLlama 1B, Gemma-2 2B, Llama 3.2 1B), three domains (healthcare, legal, finance), two training-data conditions, and four fine-tuning strategies across 216 configurations with three random seeds. It finds that baseline QLoRA adaptation barely changes TruthfulQA MC2 (mean |ΔTQA| < 0.02), adversarially perturbed data improves domain adaptation quality (Δloss ≈ -0.040) without hurting trustworthiness, but Dark Experience Replay and Task Arithmetic LoRA increase mean HarmBench ASR by +0.171 and +0.155 respectively in safety-aligned models. The results challenge the common assumption that replay-based and arithmetic-merge strategies automatically transfer safety alignment to domain-adapted small models, which matters for anyone deploying SLMs in high-stakes settings like healthcare, legal services, and finance where factual calibration and adversarial robustness are critical. It also suggests that practitioners cannot rely on safety-preserving fine-tuning methods as a guarantee of trustworthiness. The study evaluates trustworthiness via TruthfulQA MC2 for factual calibration and HarmBench ASR for adversarial robustness, and reports that Safety-DPO was effectively neutral (mean ΔASR < 0.001) while Dark ER and TA-LoRA raised HarmBench ASR by +0.171 and +0.155 on average in safety-aligned models, with individual configurations exceeding +0.45. These findings indicate that some popular parameter-efficient fine-tuning strategies can substantially increase adversarial harm susceptibility even when domain performance improves.

## [Functional Compatibility Determines Whether Neural Learning Persists](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.22462) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2608.22462v3) identifies functional compatibility—the extent to which incoming learning can coexist with behavior that must be preserved—as an experimentally manipulable causal determinant of persistent neural learning. Starting from identical neural states, the authors varied compatibility while matching unrestricted learning opportunity and imposing a common retention requirement, finding that persistence increases with compatibility across independent directions, convolutional and transformer architectures, vision and text, and a ten-seed replication. This work reframes the long-standing stability-plasticity dilemma from a problem of preventing forgetting to a question of determining which new learning can coexist with existing function and persist, potentially giving continual-learning researchers a new causal lever to design algorithms around. Because the effect holds across architectures and modalities, it suggests compatibility is a general principle rather than an artifact of a specific setup. The authors matched unrestricted learning opportunity and imposed a common retention requirement to isolate compatibility as the causal variable, but note that learning rules and retention constraints determine how much compatible opportunity is retained, while nonlinear geometry limits the matched intervention at larger update norms. The study includes a ten-seed replication to support robustness of the finding.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Sep 30, 04:00

**Background**: Artificial neural networks suffer from catastrophic forgetting, the tendency to abruptly lose previously learned information when trained on new data, which is the core obstacle in continual learning. The stability-plasticity dilemma describes the tension between retaining old knowledge (stability) and acquiring new knowledge (plasticity), and prior work has largely focused on preventing forgetting rather than on what makes new learning persist.

## [OPDVR Unifies On-Policy Distillation and Verifiable Rewards Without Extra Hyperparameters](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.24696) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers propose On-policy Distillation with Verifiable Reward (OPDVR), which reformulates the implicit reward of sampled-token on-policy distillation (OPD) based on trajectory correctness and applies a ReLU gating mechanism so correct trajectories get non-negative rewards and incorrect ones get non-positive rewards. Experiments on six reasoning benchmarks show OPDVR consistently outperforms standard OPD, and the code is released at https://github.com/LeapLabTHU/OPDVR. This work addresses a known limitation of both paradigms: RLVR provides only sparse task-level feedback, while OPD gives dense token-level guidance but ignores trajectory correctness and is capped by teacher performance. By turning sampled-token OPD into a proper RLVR method that works with any policy gradient algorithm such as GRPO, OPDVR offers a hyperparameter-free recipe for LLM post-training that could simplify industrial distillation and reasoning-training pipelines. The key trick is a ReLU gate applied to the reformulated implicit reward, which aligns the distillation signal with task success while preserving the teacher's distributional guidance, and it requires no weighted combination or heuristic switching. The paper reports gains on six reasoning benchmarks, though the abstract does not specify model sizes, teacher models, or the magnitude of improvements.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Sep 30, 04:00

**Background**: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student model on trajectories sampled from its own evolving policy while a teacher provides dense token-level log-probability supervision, which avoids the distribution mismatch of static imitation of teacher-generated text. Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) instead uses automatic rule-based checkers, such as unit tests or math answer matching, to give binary task-level rewards, as popularized by DeepSeek-R1's use of GRPO. Each approach has a complementary weakness: OPD lacks task-level correctness signals and cannot exceed the teacher, while RLVR's sparse rewards provide little guidance on individual tokens.

The framework uses hybrid dense and lexical retrieval to gather evidence, and its ECS combines semantic relevance, entity matching, orthology information, source reliability, and literature association signals; notably, 80% of retrieved documents are query-exclusive, suggesting evidence quality complements rather than replaces retrieval relevance. ## [TraceML Dataset Diagnoses Why Auto-Research Agents Lag Behind Humans](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26086) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers released TraceML, a version-level schema and dataset pairing 4,465 human Kaggle trajectories across 134 competitions with 430 paired human and 207 agent trajectories from two agent scaffolds (Codex and MLEvolve). Each code version is labeled with its score, timestamp, action type, intent, edit size, and score effect, revealing that agents collapse into narrow loops while human experts alternate between data work, validation, model changes, and ensembling. Outcome-based benchmarks only grade final submissions and discard the development process, so they cannot explain why auto-research agents underperform humans on long-horizon ML tasks. TraceML shifts evaluation from final scores to process-level diagnosis, which could reshape how agent scaffolds are designed and evaluated for autonomous ML development. Codex spends its steps re-weighting ensembles and tuning submissions, while MLEvolve mutates its model in place; neither pivots at the human rate nor reopens abandoned work. A short planning prompt distilled from human practice moves the named behaviors toward the human profile and lifts scores, but the effort profile stays agent-shaped, showing instructions only close the part of the gap reducible to instructions.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Sep 30, 04:00

**Background**: Auto-research agents can now run machine-learning development unattended for hours, revising data pipelines, models, and validation from their own feedback, yet they still finish below strong human competitors on most competitions. Kaggle is a platform hosting data science competitions where participants iteratively build and submit models, making it a natural testbed for comparing human and agent development processes. TraceML introduces a version-level schema that records every code version with its score, timestamp, action labels, intent, edit size, and score effect, and releases an open-source toolkit that converts any command-line agent run into a TraceML trajectory.

## [Performative Privacy: When Differential Privacy Maximizes Utility](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28198) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2608.28198v3) introduces 'performative privacy,' a framework combining performative learning with differential privacy, where data leakage reduces future participation. Through theoretical analysis and numerical experiments on a repeated mean-estimation model, the authors show that a finite privacy budget can outperform non-private estimation in the long term when the leakage-participation feedback loop is strong enough. This provides the first formalization of the long-assumed claim that protecting user data preserves trust and participation, potentially improving long-term utility. It suggests differential privacy can be optimal not only as a protection mechanism but also from a pure utility standpoint, which could influence how privacy-preserving machine learning systems are designed and justified. The model considers agents who repeatedly contribute data for mean estimation but may leave the system when their data is leaked, with privacy implemented via differentially private mechanisms that create a trade-off between estimation noise and future participation. The result is a theoretical and numerical finding, and as a preprint it has not yet undergone peer review or community discussion.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Sep 30, 04:00

**Background**: Differential privacy is a mathematically rigorous framework for releasing statistical information about datasets while protecting individual privacy, typically governed by a privacy budget that quantifies how much information can be learned. Performative learning studies systems whose deployed predictions affect the data they later observe, creating a feedback loop between model and data. Mean estimation is a basic statistical task where a sample is used to estimate the mean of an unknown distribution. This paper connects these concepts by treating privacy as a mechanism that shapes future data collection.

## [Flow-JEPA Uses Flow Matching for Robust Latent World Model Dynamics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29029) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Flow-JEPA (F-JEPA) is a new flow-based latent dynamics model that generates sequences of future latent states conditioned on the current observation and actions, replacing pointwise transition regression with stochastic trajectory-level prediction. It raises mean success from 86% to 92% under clean observations and from 67% to 86% under localized out-of-distribution visual noise. The work addresses a known but unresolved weakness of JEPA world models — severe performance degradation under out-of-distribution noise — which matters for deploying latent planning systems in robotics and other real-world settings where sensor corruption is common. It also suggests conditional flow matching as a viable alternative to deterministic autoregressive prediction for dynamics modeling in JEPA architectures. A Gaussian distribution serves as the flow source, exposing the vector field to perturbed latent trajectories so it learns to transport them toward clean future representations, while the reconstruction-free JEPA framework is retained. The performance advantage reportedly persists across varying perturbation severity and inference settings, though the abstract does not quantify computational overhead or scaling limits.

The paper proposes online surrogate repair (OSR), a closed-loop algorithm that uses sparse high-fidelity evaluations to update a surrogate model throughout a longer, cheaper agent search. ## [Kalman Delta Networks add uncertainty tracking to linear attention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.07816) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduce Kalman Delta Networks (KDNs), a family of linear-attention models that formulate associative memory as a linear-Gaussian state-space model and use the Kalman gain to balance new observations against stored memory reliability. Two hardware-efficient variants, Diagonal KDN and Isotropic KDN, retain one uncertainty value per key channel and per head respectively, and at 750M and 1.3B parameter pretraining scales both consistently improve perplexity and mean downstream accuracy over state-of-the-art linear-attention baselines. Linear attention compresses token history into a fixed-size recurrent memory, making each update a trade-off between writing new information and preserving useful associations, and existing models like DeltaNet, Gated DeltaNet, and KDA predict write strength without explicitly tracking memory uncertainty. By making updates uncertainty-aware, KDNs could improve long-context inference quality for efficient attention architectures that are increasingly used as alternatives to softmax attention. The formulation recovers standard delta-rule updates by replacing the tracked covariance with a token-predicted isotropic surrogate, and the Diagonal and Isotropic variants admit associative scans with logarithmic parallel depth, requiring only O(d_k) and O(1) auxiliary state per head. The work is a preprint without community discussion yet, so results have not been independently verified.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Sep 30, 04:00

**Background**: Linear attention reduces the quadratic cost of standard softmax attention by summarizing past tokens into a fixed-size recurrent state, which enables efficient long-context inference but forces the model to decide how strongly each new token should overwrite existing memory. The Kalman filter is a classic recursive algorithm from control theory that estimates a system's hidden state from noisy measurements while explicitly tracking the uncertainty of that estimate, weighting new evidence more when existing beliefs are uncertain. DeltaNet-style models apply a delta rule to update this memory, but they predict write strength directly from the current token rather than reasoning about how reliable the stored memory already is.

## [Workspace Tokens: Lightweight Robotic Memory via VLM Saliency Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20820) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.20820v2) introduces 'workspace tokens,' a lightweight latent memory for robotic policies trained by using a vision-language model (VLM) to identify task-salient current and historical information, then distilling it into a compact token via a set-reconstruction decoder loss. At deployment, the workspace token serves as a drop-in replacement for observations, letting reactive policies solve memory-intensive long-horizon manipulation tasks without any in-the-loop VLM queries. Long-horizon manipulation has been a persistent bottleneck for robotic policies, and existing memory approaches either condition on full histories (causing spurious correlations) or rely on expensive in-the-loop VLM queries that are impractical on real hardware. By moving VLM reasoning to train time and distilling it into a lightweight latent, this work offers a practical path to deploy memory-augmented policies efficiently, and it generalizes the idea of a 'latent harness' for transferring strong reasoning models into reactive robot controllers. The workspace token is trained with a two-stage procedure: a VLM first labels which current and historical information is necessary for the task, and a set-reconstruction decoder loss then distills that supervision into the token. Experiments in both simulation and on hardware show the token is not only more lightweight than conditioning on curated past image frames, but also yields better policy performance, motivating latent history curation over explicit modality conditioning.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Sep 30, 04:00

**Background**: Vision-language models (VLMs) are large multimodal models that can reason about images and text, but querying them at every control step is computationally prohibitive for real robots. Knowledge distillation is a technique that transfers knowledge from a large, expensive model into a smaller, efficient one. Memory-augmented policies aim to give robots a sense of task history so they can handle long-horizon tasks where the current observation alone is insufficient, and this paper combines these ideas by distilling VLM saliency into a compact latent memory.

## [Coreset Selection Loses to Random Sampling Under Fair Wall-Clock Budgets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22894) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.22894v2) introduces an end-to-end benchmark that charges both subset selection time and downstream training time to the same auditable wall-clock budget, spanning 4 datasets (CIFAR-10 to ImageNet-1K), 11 selectors, 5 fractions, and 3 seeds with over 1,500 released runs. Across eight wall-clock budget anchors on CIFAR-10 and Tiny ImageNet, no sophisticated selector wins any anchor — every winner is class-balanced random sampling, repeated random sampling, or full-data training. This finding challenges the practical value of a large body of coreset selection research, suggesting that many reported gains disappear once selection overhead is honestly accounted for. It has direct implications for data-efficient ML practitioners, benchmark designers, and anyone choosing between smarter subset selection and simply training on more data for fewer epochs. In fixed-budget duels on ImageNet-1K, training on all data for fewer epochs beats every selection strategy probed while also costing the least, and a per-dataset cost audit shows selection cost is dominated at every scale by a fixed full-dataset scan that cannot be amortized by choosing a smaller fraction. The paper also documents 9 correctness fixes to a widely used codebase, one of which shifts a standard Herding baseline by nearly 6 accuracy points, and quantifies when selection does pay back through subset reuse.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Sep 30, 04:00

**Background**: Coreset selection aims to pick a small, representative subset of a labeled training set so that model training becomes cheaper, and it is traditionally evaluated by downstream accuracy at a fixed subset size. That protocol ignores the time spent selecting the subset and the training recipe behind each reported number, which can hide substantial overhead. Class-balanced random sampling, by contrast, simply draws equal samples from each class at random to mitigate majority-class bias, and it requires almost no computation. Wall-clock budget refers to real elapsed training time rather than step or token counts, making it a stricter and more deployment-relevant measure of efficiency.

## [SE-LLM-OCP: LLM-Guided Optimal Control for Narrow-Space Parking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24631) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduced SE-LLM-OCP, a unified framework in which a large language model proposes sparse high-level maneuver decisions while an optimal-control module enforces vehicle dynamics and collision constraints, decomposing narrow-space parking into a sequence of short-horizon trajectory-optimization problems. When the low-level solver fails, the LLM aggregates failure evidence from the solver and validation stages to guide online replanning, and offline the system automatically evolves a structured decision-making knowledge base from accumulated failures. Narrow-space autonomous parking is a known hard, nonconvex problem where pure optimal-control solvers often fail and pure LLM trajectory generation cannot guarantee physical feasibility, so this hybrid approach could make parking both safer and more robust. The demonstrated transfer of the same maneuver representation to a different kinematic platform (a differential-drive robot) suggests the framework may generalize across vehicle types rather than being tied to one model. The LLM only outputs sparse discrete maneuver plans rather than dense trajectories, leaving feasibility enforcement to the optimal-control solver, and solver failures are treated as useful feedback signals rather than dead ends. Validation was performed in simulation on a car-like vehicle model and a differential-drive robot, so real-world deployment and hardware validation remain untested.

SE-LLM-OCP combines the two by letting the LLM handle discrete maneuver decisions while a classical solver handles low-level trajectory optimization, with failure evidence feeding back into both online replanning and offline knowledge-base evolution.

## [XPhysICS: Cross-Physical-Domain Threat Grounding for ICS Security](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30805) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers present XPhysICS, a methodology that abstracts documented cyber-physical threats from one industrial control system into provenance-linked descriptions of manipulated roles, expected physical consequences, and required observations, then applies deterministic grounding checks against a target system contract. The study evaluates 83 threat abstractions across continuous-process and manufacturing sources, testing 78 abstractions against target contracts spanning water treatment, water distribution, hydropower, and chemical processes, with selected cases exercised through controlled simulator-role perturbations. ICS attacks are typically documented in plant-specific terms, making it hard to know whether a threat observed in one facility remains meaningful in another; XPhysICS addresses this gap by separating explicit target checks and traceable evidence from mere semantic similarity. This could help security analysts transfer threat intelligence across critical infrastructure sectors such as water, energy, and chemicals, where physical processes differ but underlying attack patterns may recur. XPhysICS relies on an analyst-guided abstraction step whose vocabulary and schema version, together with a target contract, must be fixed before deterministic grounding checks can run; accepted results are represented as validation slices recording mapped roles, signals, dependencies, and context. The paper also tests compatibility with several analysis styles, including the released upstream GeCo implementation, and conducts a three-objective, one-target realizability study using a paper-derived search reproduction.

## [Temporal-Attention Heads Specialize Sparsely During Video Diffusion Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31654) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A checkpoint-resolved census of every temporal-attention head across nine Open-Sora STDiT training runs (306M to 1.03B parameters) found that only about 4-13% of heads in full-grid runs develop pronounced cross-frame attention concentration (CFAC), while aggregate CFAC stays flat or declines. The reproducible signal is positional but block-level: selected heads repeatedly arise in the first temporal block, though individual head coordinates do not reproduce across seeds. This work shows that population averages can mask sparse, structured temporal organization inside video diffusion transformers, which matters for interpretability and for anyone trying to monitor or steer training dynamics. It also offers a transferable methodology—checkpoint-resolved, per-head analysis under fixed selection rules—that could be applied to other factorized video diffusion transformers and, with adapted routing metrics, to joint spatio-temporal architectures. Each head was scored with an entropy-normalized measure of cross-frame attention concentration under a preregistered change-point and effect-size selection rule, and among the analyzed 760M selected heads, attention maps converged to a small repertoire of local frame-routing motifs (self-frame diagonals and adjacent-frame bands) even when the responsible coordinates differed across runs. Correlation and ablation analyses did not establish a causal link to generated video quality, and the authors explicitly bound their claims accordingly.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Sep 30, 04:00

**Background**: Video diffusion transformers generate video by denoising latent frames, and temporal attention is the mechanism that lets information flow across frames so motion and consistency are preserved. Open-Sora is an open-source project that builds such models using the STDiT (Spatial-Temporal Diffusion Transformer) architecture, which factorizes spatial and temporal attention. Prior understanding of temporal attention came almost entirely from analyzing fully trained models, leaving open when and where this structure emerges during training; this study addresses that gap by tracking checkpoints throughout training.

The paper introduces a new dataset of 217.6 hours of Super Nintendo (SNES) gameplay video paired with 485 hours of clean soundtracks, matched via audio fingerprinting, and trains an encoder-decoder transformer that feeds video features directly into a MusicGen decoder. It compares three video encoding strategies—textual descriptions (T5), independent frames (ViT), and spatiotemporal patches (ViViT)—finding that frozen encoders match or outperform fine-tuned ones, with frozen ViViT achieving the best overall results. The model outperforms all baselines on objective metrics despite having up to 18% fewer parameters, surpasses GVMGen in a listening study (N=96), and performs comparably to OSSL, suggesting practical value for game audio generation and multimodal music research. The dataset uses audio fingerprinting to align clean soundtracks with gameplay audio, and the decoder is always fine-tuned while encoders are tested both frozen and fine-tuned. Frozen encoders match or outperform fine-tuned counterparts on every metric, and the frozen ViViT achieves the best overall results, though the application remains niche and the evaluation is limited to SNES-era gameplay.

Researchers introduced EyeVQA, a unified visual question answering benchmark built from 21 ophthalmic datasets containing 20,000 question-answer pairs across six disease groups and seven question types, including point location and bounding box tasks. Benchmarking fourteen general-purpose, scientific, and medically specialized VLMs under a zero-shot protocol, the best model scored only 62.8 overall, with large gaps in spatial grounding and cross-task generalization. Researchers introduce DRAM (Delta-rule Recurrent Associative Memory), a plug-and-play memory module that attaches to a wide range of pretrained robotic manipulation policies and gives them long-horizon memory without architectural modification or backbone retraining. It maintains a fixed-size associative memory via gated delta-rule linear attention with a modified update that processes all tokens within each frame in parallel, and only the memory module and action expert require task-specific post-training. Most pretrained robotic policies condition only on the current observation or a short temporal window, which limits them on history-dependent, long-horizon manipulation tasks. DRAM offers a low-cost, architecture-agnostic way to retrofit existing policies with memory, potentially making deployed robot systems more capable without expensive full-model retraining. DRAM keeps memory at a fixed size using gated delta-rule linear attention, and its architecture-agnostic readout injects historical context into action prediction across different policy architectures. Experiments show it consistently improves frozen pretrained policies over short-context baselines and alternative compact memory designs, though the abstract is truncated and no community discussion is available to validate the full results.

## [REUSE Framework Controls Adaptive Overfitting in Self-Improving Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.33180) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper introduces REUSE (Risk-controlled Evaluation Under Sequential Evolution), a certified evaluation and promotion framework that lets a fixed benchmark support repeated adaptive decisions while providing statistical guarantees. For a user-specified error level α, REUSE guarantees that with probability at least 1−α every promoted modification is a genuine population improvement, and in live self-improvement experiments it reduced false promotions from up to 20.7% to 0%. As recursive self-improvement (RSI) systems increasingly rely on finite benchmarks to decide which modifications to keep, adaptive overfitting can make apparent progress illusory, so REUSE offers a principled way to distinguish genuine improvement from benchmark gaming. This matters for AI safety and evaluation researchers who need trustworthy signals to guide self-improving agents. REUSE works by strictly limiting the evaluation feedback returned to the search process and accounting for possible promotion histories within the error budget, and the paper develops statistical theory including simultaneous error control, valid lower bounds on cumulative improvement, and a characterization of the fundamental limits of adaptive evaluation reuse. The abstract is dense and lacks empirical results beyond the live experiments, so broader validation remains to be seen.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Sep 30, 04:00

**Background**: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) is a hypothesized process in which an AI system improves its own ability to improve itself, potentially compounding into an intelligence explosion, though no such explosion has been observed so far. In practice, RSI systems often use a fixed benchmark to score candidate modifications, but repeatedly reusing the same finite evaluation set creates a multiple-comparisons problem: candidates are proposed based on feedback from the same data, so the search can adaptively overfit and look better than it truly is. Existing corrections for multiple comparisons usually assume candidates are chosen independently of the evaluation set, which does not hold in this adaptive setting.

## [DRM: Diffusion Reward Model Captures Multimodal Human Preferences](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.33803) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduce DRM (Diffusion Reward Model), which recasts reward modeling as conditional density estimation over p(r|x,y) using a lightweight Diffusion Transformer conditioned on a frozen LLM encoder. Across five benchmarks, DRM matches or surpasses point-estimate, distributional, and generative reward model baselines, and downstream RLHF experiments show improved policy performance when DRM is used as the training-time reward. Reward models are central to aligning LLMs with human preferences, but dominant designs collapse each prompt-response pair into a single point estimate or a fixed parametric family, which cannot represent the inherent multimodality of human judgment. DRM's distributional approach could influence future reward model design and enable uncertainty-aware decision-making in RLHF pipelines. DRM places no parametric assumption on the output distribution, and at inference N samples form an empirical reward distribution that can be aggregated into a scalar, a variance, or quantiles. The same architecture handles both multi-attribute regression and pairwise preference data, and uncertainty-aware rejection plus lower-confidence-bound (LCB) aggregation demonstrate benefits beyond a scalar reward.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Sep 30, 04:00

**Background**: Reward models are trained to score LLM outputs according to human preferences and are used to guide alignment techniques such as RLHF. Most existing reward models output a single scalar or assume a fixed distribution (e.g., Gaussian), which cannot capture cases where the same response is reasonably judged in multiple ways. Diffusion models are generative models that learn to denoise Gaussian noise into data samples, and Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) replace the traditional U-Net backbone with a Transformer to better capture global structure. Conditional density estimation models the full conditional distribution p(y|x) rather than a single point estimate, which is the statistical framing DRM adopts for rewards.

## [Counterfactual Rollout Replay Gives SWE Agents Free Process Rewards](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.33875) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.33875v2) introduces Counterfactual Rollout Replay (CRR), a training-time procedure that uses forkable executable environments to obtain step-level return contrasts for software engineering agents. With a 14B policy, CRR improves pass@1 on SWE-bench Verified, SWE-bench Live, and SWE-rebench, achieving 41.7% versus 36.7% for extended outcome-only GRPO on SWE-bench Verified in an equal-wall-clock comparison. This offers a way to get dense, step-level training signal for SWE agents without human process labels or a learned process reward model, addressing a key bottleneck in outcome-only reinforcement learning. It could make RL training for coding agents more sample-efficient and easier to scale, and it composes with existing process-reward and trajectory-search methods. CRR selects a small set of decision points, restores each state, samples an alternative action, and rolls the branch forward under the policy, replacing the advantage at selected steps with the difference between the realised terminal return and the sampled counterfactual return. The 'free' in the name refers to supervision costs, not replay compute, and the method requires affordable, reliable state restoration; stochastic continuations and expensive or imperfect replay remain limitations.

## [Random Probe Estimates Quantization Error Without Calibration Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.33923) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.33923v2) shows that a single random Gaussian probe gives an unbiased estimate of a layer's squared Frobenius quantization error, because round-to-nearest error is spectrally flat. The authors apply this to RAM, a budget-targeted mixed-precision quantization method that uses no calibration data, scoring every tensor at six bit-widths and allocating bits via a knapsack solver under an exact byte budget. This enables mixed-precision quantization without any calibration data, which is a major practical bottleneck for deploying large models. Across seven architectures from 8B to 122B parameters, RAM achieves 3.5–13.6% lower median WikiText-2 perplexity than size-comparable uniform 4-bit builds on tested MoE models, and a single probe pass can serve any byte budget. Across 1,683 tensors from a 35B MoE and a 9B dense model, effective dimensionality is 0.93–0.96 times the i.i.d. noise value of the same shape, and on the MoE the median is unchanged from 2-bit to 8-bit. One probe measures per-tensor sensitivity to within 4–7%, twenty probes reach 1.3–1.4%, and the propagated probe rank-correlates 0.81–0.83 with the GPTQ layer objective from real activations, while the isolated estimator is uncorrelated with it.

**Background**: Quantization reduces the memory and compute cost of large language models by storing weights and activations at lower bit-widths, but different tensors tolerate different levels of precision. This paper shows that quantization error is spectrally flat, meaning a random Gaussian probe can estimate sensitivity without any calibration data, and a knapsack solver then allocates bits under a byte budget.

## [GradLev Parallelizes Test-Time Training via Costate Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.34174) ⭐️ 7.0/10

GradLev proposes a token-parallel test-time training (TTT) method that uses a causal auxiliary network to predict costates (activation gradients) across all tokens in parallel, then applies associative scans to compute adapted weights and forward activations while propagating gradients backward. The approach provides exact consistency guarantees, meaning it exactly recovers the sequential online gradient descent learner, and the auxiliary predictor is discarded at deployment so the model updates natively token-by-token. Test-time training allows models to adapt their weights at inference time for better predictions, but its inherently sequential gradient writes make it hard to parallelize on modern hardware. GradLev's exact parallelization could make TTT far more practical for long-context and online-learning settings, potentially influencing how future sequence models are trained and deployed. The method relies on the observation that, given layer inputs and activation gradients (costates), online gradient descent admits exact parallel scans for both forward evaluation and reverse backpropagation. A consistency loss supervises the costate predictor against the gradient targets produced by the scans, and the auxiliary network is only used during training, not at inference.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Sep 30, 04:00

**Background**: Test-time training (TTT) is a technique where a model updates part of its weights, often called fast weights, after observing each token during inference, effectively storing temporary memory of the sequence. Because these updates are sequential, they are inefficient on GPUs, which favor parallel operations. Associative scans are parallel prefix algorithms that can compute recurrences in parallel when the underlying operation is associative, and costates refer to activation gradients in the backward pass of neural network training.

## [GenNVS: Geometry-Enhanced Novel View Synthesis via Disentangled 3D Prior](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.34579) ⭐️ 7.0/10

GenNVS is a new framework that improves single-image novel view synthesis by modeling foreground objects and background separately with 3D Gaussian Splatting, then aligning them through a coarse-to-fine geometric optimization to form a unified 3D scene. This scene conditions a video diffusion model via a Dual-Stream Masking mechanism that jointly exploits rendered validity masks and geometry-aware warping, yielding better visual quality and geometric accuracy than recent methods. Single-image novel view synthesis is a core problem in computer vision and graphics, and GenNVS directly tackles the geometric ambiguity that causes diffusion-based methods to lose spatial coherence of foreground objects. If it generalizes, the approach could improve applications such as 3D content creation, scene editing, and AR/VR, where plausible geometry from a single photo is highly valuable. The method uses a disentangled 3D prior to align foreground and background 3D Gaussian Splatting representations, and the Dual-Stream Masking conditions the video diffusion model on both rendered validity masks and geometry-aware warping. The paper reports favorable results in visual quality and geometric accuracy while naturally supporting flexible scene editing, though it remains a specialized arXiv preprint without community discussion.

**Background**: Novel view synthesis is the task of generating images of a scene from viewpoints not present in the input images, and it is central to computer vision and graphics. 3D Gaussian Splatting is a volume rendering technique that represents a scene as many 3D Gaussians and enables real-time radiance field rendering, while video diffusion models generate video by iteratively denoising latent representations. GenNVS combines these ideas, using 3D Gaussian Splatting to build a geometric prior that guides a video diffusion model for single-image view synthesis.

## [Action Upcycling Reuses Discarded Action Chunks to Speed Up Robot Policies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.34911) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.34911v2) introduces Action Upcycling, a training-free algorithm that reuses the tail actions a chunked robot policy would normally discard, extending the execution horizon until action velocity begins to fluctuate. Experiments on simulated and real-world manipulation tasks show it reduces policy calls by 1.2–1.7x with no loss in success rate across multiple Vision-Language-Action Models (VLAs) and even a World Action Model (WAM). Action chunking is now standard in modern robot policies, but the reactivity-versus-efficiency trade-off forces frequent, expensive policy calls. Because Action Upcycling requires no model internals, no extra sampling, and no training, it applies to any chunked policy at negligible cost and is orthogonal to other acceleration methods like few-step sampling and streaming action decoding, opening a new axis for policy acceleration. The key insight is that discarded actions remain close to their replanned versions as long as action velocity stays smooth, so the horizon can be extended until velocity fluctuates. The method is training-free and architecture-agnostic, requiring no access to model internals or additional samples, and it was validated on both simulated and real-world manipulation tasks.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Sep 30, 04:00

**Background**: Action chunking is a technique where a robot policy predicts a sequence of future actions (a chunk) from a single observation, executes only a prefix of that chunk, and discards the rest before replanning. The length of the executed prefix, called the execution horizon, controls a trade-off: a short horizon keeps the robot reactive but requires frequent policy calls, while a long horizon is more efficient but less responsive. Recent test-time methods adaptively select the horizon per chunk, but they either read model internals (requiring architecture-specific signals) or draw extra samples, which adds computational cost.

A new arXiv paper (2609.34965v2) proposes two inductive biases for diffusion-based restoration of physiological signals: a shift-covariant wavelet representation and dense per-sample phase conditioning inferred from the corrupted input. The phase conditioning is dense and per-sample, derived from the corrupted observation rather than a clean reference, and the cyclostationarity index is training-free, meaning it can be computed on existing data to decide whether the added conditioning is worthwhile. The antithetic coupling reduces sampling variance and cuts network evaluations by roughly 5x while maintaining comparable performance.

**Background**: Cyclostationarity means a signal's statistical properties repeat periodically with an underlying cycle phase, as in heartbeats or brain rhythms. Wavelets are brief, wave-like oscillations used to represent signals at multiple scales, and shift covariance means a time shift in the input produces a corresponding, predictable shift in the representation.

## [Elastic Forcing Removes Score Models from Autoregressive Video Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.35491) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper proposes Elastic Forcing, a post-training method that learns the rollout distribution directly from reference videos by minimizing maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) in frozen self-supervised video representation spaces, eliminating both the bidirectional diffusion teacher and the online fake-score model used in Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD). Using the same architecture and initialization as Self-Forcing, the 1.3B model improves the VBench Total score from 83.80 to 84.64 while retaining 17 FPS, and removing auxiliary score models enables 14B model post-training on eight H200 GPUs. This work shows that few-step autoregressive video generation can be trained without any score models, which significantly reduces memory and compute overhead and makes large-scale (14B) post-training feasible on modest hardware. It also opens the door to learning new visual styles, semantic concepts, and spatial priors directly from reference videos rather than relying on a target-specific diffusion teacher. The framework uses a hybrid Nyström–Monte Carlo estimator to balance approximation bias and sampling variance, and relies on memory-efficient replay and gradient subsampling to make the objective practical. The reported gains are on a 1.3B model with 17 FPS retained, and the abstract does not provide detailed comparisons against other distillation baselines.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Sep 30, 04:00

**Background**: Few-step autoregressive video generation typically uses Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD), which requires a bidirectional diffusion teacher and an online fake-score model to align the student's output distribution with the teacher's. Maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) is a kernel-based statistical distance that measures how different two probability distributions are, and it can be estimated from samples without training a separate classifier or score network. The Nyström method approximates large kernel matrices with a subset of samples, while Monte Carlo estimation uses random sampling to approximate expectations, and combining them helps control both bias and variance in the MMD estimate.

Researchers propose F4R (Failure for Rising), a failure-driven real-to-sim-to-real closed-loop framework that automatically diagnoses real-world robot failures, reconstructs them as interactive object-centric table-top simulation environments, and refines vision-language-action policies via failure-conditioned sim-real co-training plus targeted reinforcement learning. F4R relies on an agent to identify and diagnose failures from rollouts, then reconstructs each failure as an object-centric table-top environment that preserves task-relevant spatial and physical conditions, after which the improved policy is redeployed and new failures feed back into the next cycle. The method works by composing per-segment cost representations so that the cumulative estimate captures the extra input cost incurred when context from earlier segments is re-read by every later call, and newly observed evidence refreshes the forecast as execution unfolds. ## [Jev Fails at Training-Free Human Activity Recognition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.36154) ⭐️ 6.0/10

A new arXiv study evaluates Jev, a fixed general-purpose probabilistic decision model, on 1,800 class-balanced accelerometer windows from the WISDM, UCI341, and PAMAP2 datasets, with no labeled examples, retrieval context, or HAR-specific parameter updates. Jev's strongest sensor representation reaches macro-F1 scores of only 0.038, 0.118, and 0.089, far below the 0.686–0.907 achieved by supervised HAR models. The negative result challenges the assumption that general-purpose decision models can replace or complement trained HAR classifiers without task-specific training, and it suggests that the sensor-to-model interface should be evaluated as part of the model rather than treated as neutral preprocessing. This has implications for wearable sensing, mobile health, and any application hoping to reduce dependence on labeled sensor data. Adding more numerical features did not improve Jev and actually reduced recognition on all three datasets, while augmenting the same numerical evidence with a deterministic semantic rendering only partially recovered performance, though the experiment does not isolate semantics from accompanying serialization and redundancy changes. Jev is fast and inexpensive to query, but its probabilities are not reliably calibrated for recognition, and a post-hoc fusion analysis showed a small improvement on WISDM that did not replicate on UCI341 or PAMAP2.

**Background**: Generative recommendation represents items as semantic IDs (SIDs) — discrete code sequences produced by vector quantization of continuous embeddings. Vector quantization maps continuous vectors to a finite codebook of prototype vectors, and the common Top-1 hard assignment updates only the nearest codeword per item, which concentrates gradients on frequently selected codewords and leaves most of the codebook under-trained. This under-training causes SID collisions, where different items map to the same identifier, degrading recommendation quality.

## [Distinguish or Homogenize: Last-Chance Policy Identification Under Resource Depletion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.36741) ⭐️ 6.0/10

The paper introduces Last-Chance Policy Identification (LCPI), a formal framework in which an agent under irreversible resource depletion can either spend resources to distinguish among latent fault models or change the system state so that remaining models share a common acceptable continuation. It defines the Last Identifiable Margin (LIM) as the feasibility boundary between these two options, provides an Exact-LIM recursion for deterministic diagnostic graphs, and proposes Risk-Budgeted Compatibility Planning (RBCP) for noisy finite-horizon recovery. This reframes fault diagnosis and planning by making the mapping from fault models to acceptable policies a function of the agent's own actions, rather than a fixed given. It could affect how autonomous systems, microservice incident recovery, and safety-critical planners decide when diagnosis is worth its cost and when state change can make it unnecessary. For deterministic diagnostic graphs the paper derives an Exact-LIM recursion, while for noisy finite-horizon recovery RBCP searches a compatibility-aware frontier under a hard worst-case failure constraint. Experiments on abstract microservice topologies and MiniGrid latent-damage navigation show RBCP improves risk-feasible recovery within the failure budget, and a cost-matched sham control that preserves model incompatibility eliminates the gain entirely.

The design turns boundary variation into feature modulation: geometry can change the embedding through a controlled pathway, but it cannot change the number, order, or support of local tokens. It uses a history-only predictor to estimate the future connectivity graph and a graph Gaussian source whose Laplacian-based covariance encodes dependencies derived from past connectivity, with a conditional velocity field transporting source samples to future graph residuals while explicitly distinguishing transport time from physical EEG time. This work addresses a key open question in distributional forecasting: whether graph-informed source distributions offer practical advantages over isotropic noise and strong deterministic predictors. If validated, it could improve how neuroscientists model time-varying brain connectivity and inform the design of flow-based generative models for structured time-series data. The framework combines conditional flow matching with graph Gaussian sources, where the source covariance is built from a Laplacian derived from past connectivity. The study explicitly identifies the conditions and controls needed to distinguish useful residual transport from gains attributable to deterministic prediction, learned representations, and sampling effects.

Conditional flow matching is a generative modeling technique that learns a velocity field transporting samples from a simple noise distribution to a target data distribution, and it has become popular for fast, simulation-free training of continuous normalizing flows. PrimeSeeker introduces latent anchor reasoning, a primitive that decomposes deep search into anchor resolution (recovering an unnamed retrieval anchor from descriptive specifications) and relation transfer (carrying that anchor into a subsequent information demand). Using this formulation, the authors built 9,221 expert trajectories and trained a 30B search agent that achieves strong results across five deep-search benchmarks. Existing synthetic question generation scales difficulty through global proxies such as larger evidence graphs, more hops, and longer trajectories, which only indirectly reflect the local retrieval skills an agent actually needs. The framework constructs web-grounded anchor structures and jointly derives a question plus a reference evidence skeleton; extractive highlights of tool observations guide expert generation but are removed before supervised fine-tuning, while the skeleton is reused to audit reference-step coverage for reinforcement-learning rewards. The resulting trajectories show low retrieval redundancy, and fixed-budget evaluation achieves strong solution coverage with substantially fewer tool calls than long-horizon systems.

Against a cross-entropy-only control with the same optimiser and schedule, PACT is significantly more accurate at two of three seeds, halves the seed-to-seed spread, and lowers NLL by 26%; no single term raises raw accuracy on its own.

## [Name-Only Directory Routing Beats FTS5 for One-Shot Code Search](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.35918) ⭐️ 6.0/10

A new arXiv paper evaluates name-only directory routing, where a language model follows directory and file names to locate annotated code files. Across 82 audited issues from 11 repositories at pinned pre-fix commits, routing recovered 0.465 of gold files within eight candidates, compared with 0.352 for FTS5 and 0.245 for a fixed full-issue rg query, a paired gain of 0.113 over FTS5. Finding the right files is an early bottleneck for coding agents, and this result suggests that cheap, name-based hierarchical navigation can surface relevant candidates that lexical search misses. If it generalizes, it could inform how agentic coding tools combine structural signals with full-text search during issue resolution. Under a shared 16K-token context budget, routing delivered 0.443 of annotated lines versus 0.246 for FTS5 on 55 fully aligned cases, and combining routing with FTS5 reached 0.491 file recall at the eight-file limit, though the gain over routing alone was uncertain. Routing averaged 8.9 seconds per issue versus 7 milliseconds per FTS5 query after a 0.9-second build, and the study cannot attribute the gain to hierarchy or show that it improves issue resolution.

## [TMLN Frames Continual Learning as Optimal Control on a Riemannian Manifold](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.35926) ⭐️ 6.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2609.35926) introduces TMLN (Trajectory-Modulatory Landscape Navigation), a normative navigation policy that formalizes continual learning as an optimal control problem over a curved loss landscape. TMLN uses a memory-efficient diagonal empirical Fisher Information Matrix to define a localized Riemannian manifold and dynamically modulates a preconditioner using the normalized historical trajectory of parameter values, avoiding additive penalties. Catastrophic forgetting remains a central obstacle to deploying neural networks in non-stationary, sequential settings, and TMLN offers a theoretically grounded alternative to rigid Euclidean weight regularization. If the reported reduction in the loss barrier between consecutive tasks holds up, it could influence how preconditioning and geometry-aware methods are designed for continual learning. The method relies on a diagonal approximation of the empirical Fisher Information Matrix, which is memory-efficient but spatially limited, so TMLN compensates by modulating the preconditioner with the normalized historical trajectory of parameter values. Empirical evaluations are reported on class- and domain-incremental benchmarks, showing a significant reduction in the loss barrier between consecutive tasks.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Sep 30, 04:00

**Background**: Continual learning studies how neural networks can learn a sequence of tasks without forgetting earlier ones; when they do forget, the failure is called catastrophic forgetting. Classical remedies add weight-regularization penalties that keep important parameters close to their old values, but these penalties are scalar and Euclidean, ignoring the curvature of the parameter space. The Fisher Information Matrix measures how much information the data carries about each parameter and is often used to define a Riemannian metric, while Riemannian optimization exploits that metric to take more stable, geometry-aware gradient steps.
